0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a young pastor, and it is as practical and urgent as anything Paul ever wrote. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to deal with a crisis: false teachers were infecting the church with “different doctrine”, with myths and endless genealogies, with a distorted use of the law, and with a harsh self-denial, passed off as spiritual, that forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul’s letter is his pastoral briefing for a young man who has been given a very hard assignment in a very important city.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, a great centre of trade and religion, home to the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It was a city Paul knew intimately: he had spent nearly three years there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19–20), and the church he planted was one of the most strategic in the Roman East. Now, years later, that church was in danger. The false teachers were not outsiders; they had come from within, perhaps former elders or teachers who had “made shipwreck of their faith” (1:19–20). Timothy’s task was to confront them, silence them, and restore the church to sound doctrine and ordered life.

The letter’s great themes belong together. Sound doctrine comes first: “the gospel of the glory of the blessed God” (1:11) is the measure of every teaching. There is the ordering of the church: prayer, worship, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the honour due to elders. There is the call to godliness, a word that appears more often in 1 Timothy than in any other New Testament letter: the practical Christlikeness that is the goal of all true teaching. And there are the “trustworthy sayings”, five across these letters (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Tit 3:8): short summaries of the faith that sound like early confessions, already familiar in the church before Paul wrote them down.

Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters? Many scholars think a later follower wrote them in his name, arguing that their vocabulary and style differ from Paul’s other letters, that their church order with elders and deacons looks later, and that their travels cannot be fitted into Acts. But each letter names Paul as author, they were received as his by the early church, and the church order they describe is simple: plural elders and deacons, which Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23; Phil 1:1). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to trusted co-workers on new subjects. And the travels fit if Paul was released from the imprisonment with which Acts ends, as the early church believed, and then travelled again, to Macedonia (1:3), Crete (Titus 1:5) and elsewhere, before a final arrest. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote them, in the mid-60s.

And what was Timothy’s role? Not a bishop of Ephesus in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate, sent with apostolic authority for a time, Until I come (4:13), to correct false teaching and see that qualified elders led the church (3:1–7; 5:17–22).

Above all, this is a letter about the church as “the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth” (3:15). The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is the family of the living God, called to hold up the truth in a world drowning in falsehood. That is what gives urgency to every instruction about doctrine and order and godliness: what is at stake is not an organisation but God’s truth in his world. The household of God must be governed well, because the God who lives in it is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (6:15).

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to stop men whose myths, genealogies and confident talk about the law produced speculation instead of love. The law is good when used for its purpose: to convict sinners, measured by the gospel of God’s glory.

Then Paul turns to himself as the proof of that gospel: if Christ’s patience reached a persecutor, it can reach anyone. The chapter ends with a charge to Timothy to fight the good fight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An official greeting to a son in the faith: Paul writes under orders, giving mercy before instructions.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

These letters call the Father ‘Saviour’ (he planned salvation, and the Son carried it out), and only the letters to Timothy add ‘mercy’ to grace and peace: compassion for a struggling minister.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was young and no fighter by nature (4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7). He needed an apostle’s authority visibly behind him.

Now: ‘Christ Jesus our hope’ tells anyone in a hard post where to look when the situation offers nothing to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to silence men whose myths, genealogies and misuse of the law bred arguments instead of love (vv. 3–7). The law is good when used lawfully, and its list of sins tracks the Ten Commandments (vv. 8–11). Then Paul offers his own story as the proof of the gospel he guards (vv. 12–17), and charges Timothy to fight the good fight, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander (vv. 18–20). A chapter about false teachers turns out to be a chapter about mercy, because the only safe guardian of the gospel is a man who knows he needed it more than anyone.

The setting. 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters, because they are written to Paul’s co-workers about leading churches. After his first Roman imprisonment (Acts 28), Paul seems to have been released and to have travelled again, around AD 62–64, leaving Timothy in Ephesus and Titus in Crete. Timothy was still relatively young (4:12), perhaps timid (2 Timothy 1:7), and often unwell (5:23). Ephesus was now troubled by exactly the false teachers Paul had warned its elders about at Miletus (Acts 20:29–30). The wolves Paul foretold had come, and some of them were elders of the church.

An apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent with authority, carrying the word of the one who sent him. The letter is personal, a father writing to a son, but it is also official, and the men Timothy had to correct needed to know that these instructions carried Christ’s authority and not merely an old friend’s opinion.

By command of God. The word is epitagē, used of royal orders. Paul did not volunteer and was not elected; he was commanded. That matters to a young man, probably not a fighter by temperament, left with a job he did not choose. Neither of them is in charge of this church. They are both under orders.

God our Saviour. Here Saviour is said of the Father, a title characteristic of these letters (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3): the Father is Saviour in that salvation was his design before the world began; the Son in that he accomplished it. It echoes the Old Testament, where the LORD is the Saviour of Israel and there is no other (Isaiah 43:3, 11). And it had an edge in Ephesus, where emperors and Artemis herself were hailed as saviours. Paul gives the title to the living God alone, in a letter that would be read aloud a short walk from her altar.

Christ Jesus our hope. Not our example or our teacher, though he is both: our hope (Colossians 1:27). What we wait for is not first a place or a feeling but him: to see him and to be with him for ever (1 John 3:2). Before he names a single problem, Paul names the direction to look, for anyone left in a hard post they would leave tomorrow if they could. The one who commands is the same one who is coming back.

My true child in the faith. The word is gnēsios: genuine, legitimately born, the real thing as against a counterfeit. Timothy was Paul’s spiritual son, probably converted on Paul’s first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–20), and genuinely like his father in faith and service (Philippians 2:20–22). Ephesus was full of men who wanted to be teachers (v. 7); Timothy is the genuine article, and Paul says so publicly, a father’s hand on a nervous son’s shoulder in front of the whole room.

Grace, mercy, and peace. Paul’s letters to churches say grace and peace; mercy (eleos) is added only in the letters to Timothy (some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add it at Titus 1:4 as well). Grace is God’s favour to the undeserving; mercy is his pity on the miserable; peace is the wholeness that follows. Mercy is the right word for a tired minister, whose standing with God is not measured by how well he is coping. God gives it to people who are not coping, and he gives it first, before the instructions.

From God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. One preposition, “from”, governs both the Father and Christ. They are the single source of grace, mercy and peace, and only God gives these. So without stopping to argue it, Paul places Christ on the side of God and not of creatures. The man who will call himself the foremost of sinners later in this chapter prays to a Saviour who is himself God.

Did Paul really write this letter? Many modern critical scholars doubt that Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters, pointing to differences of vocabulary, church organisation and theology from his earlier letters. But the letters claim Paul as author repeatedly and personally (1:12–16; 2 Timothy 4:9–21); the early church received them as Paul’s (Marcion, who cut much else from his Bible, left them out, but they are echoed by Polycarp and named as Paul’s by Irenaeus); differences of vocabulary are well explained by different subject matter, a different stage of life, and possibly a different secretary (perhaps Luke, who alone was with him, 2 Timothy 4:11); and a letter written under a false name, with forged personal details, such as the request for a cloak and some parchments, would have been regarded as a deception and rejected. Scholars still debate the question, and the arguments deserve a fair hearing; but the case against Paul is not compelling. We receive them as Paul’s, and as Scripture.

Is this letter for me if I am not a pastor? Yes. It is addressed to Timothy, but it was read to the whole congregation, and most of it concerns them: how they pray (chapter 2), whom they choose as elders and deacons (chapter 3), how they treat widows, older men and younger women (chapter 5), what they do with money (chapter 6). A church member needs to know what sound teaching sounds like, so that he can recognise it and test what he hears; what a faithful elder looks like, so that he can choose one and honour him; and how God wants his household run, because he lives in it. Reading a letter to a minister is also the best way to learn how to pray for one.

How do I find, or become, a spiritual father or mother? Timothy had a mother and grandmother who taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and then Paul. You do not need an apostle. Look in your own church for an older believer whose life you respect, and ask for an hour: to read the Bible together, to talk about how they have walked with Christ, to pray. Most will be surprised and glad. And if you are older, do not wait to be asked. Pick one younger believer, of the same sex where the friendship will be close, and simply begin: invite them to a meal, ask how their soul is, open the Scriptures. Paul did not run a programme. He took a young man with him.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and joined Paul on his second journey. The letter seems to come from after the events of Acts, probably after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early to mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With no thanksgiving, Paul goes straight to the problem: teaching that breeds speculation instead of love, and a misuse of the good law, measured against the gospel entrusted to him (vv. 3–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

The goal (telos) of the whole charge is love (v. 5). Doctrine exists to produce love; and the law, good when used lawfully (v. 8), convicts sinners and drives them to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul judged the Ephesian teaching by what it produced: endless speculation rather than God's household well run (v. 4).

Now: The list of sins in vv. 9–10 must be read where Paul put it: five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner alive.

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No thanksgiving. In most of his letters Paul begins by giving thanks for his readers; here he goes straight to the problem. Of his other letters, only Galatians and Titus so clearly lack one, and in Galatians the gospel itself was being abandoned. Paul loves this church (Acts 20:36–38), but a father who sees a fire in the house does not begin with pleasantries.

Remain at Ephesus. Urged (parakaleō) means pleaded; remain (prosmeinai) means stay on. Paul had asked him face to face, and now he puts the charge in writing, where Timothy can reread it on hard days. This journey to Macedonia is not recorded in Acts, which supports the view that Paul was released after his first imprisonment.

Charge certain persons. The word for charge (parangellō) means to give an order with authority, a key word in this letter (1:5, 18; 4:11; 6:13). Timothy is not asked to start a discussion with these men. He is to tell them to stop. Paul knows who the “certain persons” are and does not name them yet, perhaps hoping they will repent first; he will name two at the end of the chapter. Some were probably elders of the church itself (Acts 20:30).

Any different doctrine. One compound verb, heterodidaskaleō, found in the New Testament only in this letter: to teach other-ly, to teach a different thing. It does not necessarily mean teaching outright falsehood. It means teaching something of a different kind from what was handed down (6:3). There is a fixed body of truth, “the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3), and a teacher’s job is to deliver it, not to improve it.

Myths and endless genealogies. Myths (mythoi) are invented stories; genealogies are lists of ancestry. The precise content is debated. The false teaching seems to have had a Jewish flavour (v. 7; Titus 1:14): elaborate speculations built on the Old Testament family trees and legends, and possibly early speculation about chains of spiritual beings between God and the world. Paul does not bother to describe it: he judges the teaching by what it produces, not by its details.

Endless. That word (aperantos) is the giveaway: never reaching a conclusion. Such subjects make the pursuer feel sophisticated and never require him to do anything. A man can spend twenty years on the names in a genealogy and never once be told to forgive his brother.

Speculations rather than the stewardship. Two words set against each other. Speculations (ekzētēseis) are controversial questions, enquiry that never lands; their fruit was argument and division (6:4–5). Stewardship (oikonomia) is the management of a household, and more widely God’s own plan for running his household and saving his people, received by faith. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV (“godly edifying”), read oikodomē, edification, but the better reading is stewardship.

A plan with a Head. Paul used the same word, oikonomia, when he wrote to this church of “a plan for the fullness of time”, to unite all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10). God’s plan for his household has a centre, and the centre is Christ. That is why the genealogies were never meant to be endless: in Scripture they run somewhere, and Matthew’s list stops at Jesus, who is called Christ (Matthew 1:16). The false teachers kept the family trees and lost sight of the Son they were written to reach.

What are the myths and genealogies today? Anything that turns the Bible into raw material for a system it does not teach, and keeps people busy without making them holy. Date-setting for the Lord’s return and charts that decode current events. Hidden numerical codes in the text. Conspiracy theories baptised with proof-texts. Endless online controversies whose main fruit is a following. Elaborate claims about angels and demons, or about the hidden meaning of names, that Scripture never makes. The test is Paul’s: where does it lead? If it leaves you more anxious, more superior and more argumentative, and no more prayerful, loving or obedient, it is speculation, however clever it sounds.

How do I tell healthy study from speculation? Healthy study stays with what Scripture actually says, reads each passage in its setting, and is content to stop where the Bible stops (Deuteronomy 29:29). It aims at the questions the text is answering, not the ones it leaves aside. It makes you know Christ better and love people more. It can be deep and demanding: Paul’s own letters are not light reading. But it lands. You close the book with something to believe, to repent of or to do. Speculation never lands, and its favourite questions are the ones God chose not to answer.

Should I stay in a hard church? Paul asked Timothy to stay in a difficult place, and that is a word to those of us who leave too quickly. A church with problems is not a reason to go; a church with problems may be exactly where God wants a faithful member. But this is not a rule that you must stay anywhere at any cost. Timothy stayed in order to correct error, and he had an apostle’s authority behind him. If the gospel itself has been abandoned and the leaders will not hear correction, or if you or your children are being harmed and the church will not act, leaving is not unfaithfulness. Take counsel from mature believers before you decide, and leave, if you must, without bitterness.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, where Paul had spent about three years.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aim of our charge. This is the key sentence of the paragraph. The word for aim is telos: the goal, the point of the whole exercise. The point of sound doctrine is not winning arguments but producing a certain kind of person.

Is love. Not correct opinions, not a settled congregation, not the defeat of the opposition. Love (agapē), in sharp contrast with the speculations of verse 4, which produced quarrels. That is a startling thing to write at the head of a letter about to spend six chapters on doctrine and church order. Paul is telling us what doctrine is for.

Love with a face. Paul does not leave the word undefined. Ten verses later he names the love this charge exists to reproduce: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1:15). “By this we know love,” John writes, “that he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16). A man whose doctrine of the cross is accurate but who is cold toward people has learned what happened at the cross without learning to love as Christ loved there.

A pure heart. Love flows from three springs, and each guards against a particular false kind of love. Pure (katharos) means clean, unmixed. The heart in Scripture is the centre of the person: thought, desire and will together. A pure heart is one cleansed by God (Psalm 51:10) and wholly given to him, wanting one thing. Without it you get love as a performance, done for an audience or for what it returns.

A good conscience. Conscience (syneidēsis) is the faculty that sits in judgment on our own actions. A good conscience is one that does not accuse us, because we have been cleansed by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 9:14) and are walking in obedience. At verse 19 a wrecked conscience is what sinks a man; the false teachers had consciences seared as with a hot iron (4:2). Without a good conscience you get love as compensation: the busy kindness of someone trying to make up for a guilt he will not face.

A sincere faith. Sincere (anypokritos) means without a mask; the hypokritēs was the actor on the Greek stage. Paul uses the same phrase of the faith that lived first in Timothy’s grandmother and mother (2 Timothy 1:5). Without it you get love as religion: the correct behaviour of a person who does not actually trust God. Yet all three springs are his gift. God does not only command love; he is love, and he has shown it. The pure heart he asks for, he creates; the good conscience he requires, he cleanses with his Son’s blood; the sincere faith he looks for, he gives.

What does teaching grow? So Paul’s test for teaching is not merely whether it is true, though it must be, but what it grows: speculation and controversy, or people who love. Hold any teaching you are drawn to, and any you are inclined to fight about, against that measure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean doctrine is unimportant so long as people love. Love here is the fruit of sound teaching, not a replacement for it: the same chapter will hand two men over to Satan for false teaching.

Does love mean I should never confront false teaching? No. This verse comes in the middle of a command to stop false teachers, and it explains why the command was given. Error harms people, and love will not stand by and watch sheep being harmed. The father who lets his child drink poison because correcting him feels unkind does not love him. What love changes is the manner: gently, patiently, without quarrelling, correcting opponents in the hope that God may grant them repentance (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Love also changes the aim. You are not trying to win; you are trying to heal.

How can I have a good conscience when mine keeps accusing me? A good conscience is not one that has never been guilty. It is one that has been cleansed. Bring the specific thing to God, confess it plainly, and believe what he says: the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Where you have wronged someone, put it right as far as you can. Then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for. If the accusation returns after you have confessed, it is no longer your conscience doing its proper work; it is the accuser, and you answer him with the cross. And keep your conscience tender by obeying it quickly the next time it speaks.

In everyday life. Recall the last theological conversation you had that grew heated, and test it by Paul’s three springs. Did I want God’s glory and the other person’s good, or did I want to win? Was I arguing loudly about one thing to avoid facing another? Was I performing? Then, as one whose conscience Christ’s blood has cleansed, do one thing that verse 5 would recognise: write to that person, or pray for them, or ask their forgiveness for the tone if not the content.

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By swerving from these. The verb is astocheō: to miss the mark. The image is an archer, and the target was named in verse 5. These men did not attack the target from outside. They aimed at it and missed, which is a more uncomfortable diagnosis than malice, because it can happen to anyone who stops checking where he is pointing.

Vain discussion. Wandered away (ektrepō) is used of turning off a road, and in medical writers of a limb wrenched out of joint. Vain discussion (mataiologia) is empty talk: not false necessarily, but empty. Like a dislocated limb, their teaching still moved, but it could no longer bear weight.

Desiring to be teachers of the law. Teachers of the law (nomodidaskaloi) is the word used of the Jewish teachers of the law (Luke 5:17; Acts 5:34). And the order of the sentence is the whole diagnosis. First comes the desire to be a teacher; a subject was needed, and the law provided one. These men wanted the standing that comes with teaching and then went looking for something to teach, which is not confined to the first century. There is one Teacher who never spoke a word he did not understand, and who never sought the standing that his teaching earned. The crowds marvelled that he taught as one who had authority, and he used that authority to wash feet and to die for the men who had been listening.

Confident assertions. They do not understand their own words, nor the matters they pronounce on; yet the verb (diabebaioomai) means to insist strongly. Being certain without understanding is the reliable mark of this kind of teacher. Confidence in the truth is not the fault; Paul himself can say, “I know whom I have believed” (2 Timothy 1:12). But genuine understanding usually makes a person more careful, not less. The more a man truly knows of God, the more often he says, “I do not know.”

Paul had been this man. Before Damascus, Saul of Tarsus was as confident in the law as any man of his generation (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5–6), and he understood neither what he was saying nor the things he asserted, because the law he taught was pointing to the Christ he was hunting. What cured him was not a better argument but a meeting: the risen Jesus spoke his name. It is still the only cure for certainty without understanding, and it lets Paul write of these men with severity but without contempt.

Is it wrong to want to teach? No. Paul will say in 3:1 that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task. The difference is in what is wanted. One man wants the work: to feed people, to make Christ known, to see a church grow in love. Another wants the platform: to be listened to, quoted, deferred to. You can usually tell which you are by what happens when someone else is asked instead of you, and by whether you are willing to learn before you teach (James 3:1). A good teacher is first a good listener to Scripture and to wiser people.

How do I know if I am confident without understanding? Three signs. You find it easier to explain why others are wrong than to explain the passage in front of you. You have never seriously read the best case for the view you oppose. And you are rarely heard to say, “I am not sure,” or, “I was wrong about that.” The remedy is not timidity. It is to sit longer with the text before you speak, to check your reading against the faithful teachers of the church, and to hold firmly what Scripture says plainly and lightly what it does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is good. Paul now guards against a misunderstanding: that the problem is the law itself, and the sooner the church is clear of the Old Testament the better. A teacher named Marcion drew that conclusion in the second century; Paul heads it off at once. The law, here especially its moral commands, is good (kalos): excellent, beautiful, holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12), because it reflects the character of the God who gave it.

If one uses it lawfully. There is a deliberate play in the Greek: nomos used nomimōs. The law must be used as the law itself intends. The false teachers were using it as a source of speculation, or perhaps as a ladder for earning God’s favour; its proper use is to expose and restrain the sin of the lawless.

Where the lawful use leads. A law used lawfully does not leave a man admiring his own record; it sends him to a Saviour. The commandment that promised life proved to be death to Paul (Romans 7:10), and it drove him to Christ, who is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4): the goal the law was leading to. The false teachers made it a puzzle and so never arrived there.

Where Christians differ: what is the place of the law for Christians? Some say the Old Testament law has no role for Christians at all; others make it a way of earning favour with God. Faithful Christians weigh this differently, and some who love the gospel are wary of any talk of law for believers because they fear it breeds legalism. This commentary’s view: The Reformed tradition, following Scripture, speaks of three uses of the moral law. First, it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). Second, it restrains evil in society (the use in view here, vv. 9–10). Third, it guides believers in grateful obedience (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2). The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1–14); the civil laws of Israel expired with Israel’s state, though their principles of justice remain instructive. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains God’s will, but it is never the way of justification.

The remedy for bad use is good use. The instinct when something good is being handled badly is to withdraw it, as some churches have done with election, with the law, with the Holy Spirit. Paul does not respond to the abuse of the law by abandoning it; he explains what it is for. Good use always costs more effort than avoidance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are saved by keeping the law. No one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16). Justification is acquittal in God’s court: the sinner is not made sinless overnight but pardoned and accepted, because Christ’s obedience and death are counted as ours (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Every commandment was kept, perfectly and gladly, by the Son. Nor does it mean the law is bad because it cannot save. The fault lies in us, not in the law: our sinful nature left the law too weak to save us, and what it could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

If I am not under the law, why should I read it? Because you are not under it as a covenant of works, a way of earning life, but you are still under God, and the law tells you what he loves. A believer reads the commandments the way a child reads a letter from his father: not to find out how to be adopted, but to learn how to please the one who already adopted him. Christ did not abolish the law but fulfilled it (Matthew 5:17), and the Spirit writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). The same commandments that once condemned you now describe the family likeness the Spirit is forming in you.

Do I need to keep the food laws, festivals and sacrifices? No. Those belonged to the ceremonial law, which was a shadow of the things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The sacrifices pointed to his one sacrifice and ended when it was offered (Hebrews 10:1–14). The food laws marked Israel off from the nations, and Christ has made the two one (Mark 7:19; Ephesians 2:14–15). You read those chapters to see Christ in them, not to obey them as rules. The moral law is different, because it is grounded in God’s own character and in creation, and it is repeated throughout the New Testament. The Sabbath commandment needs a word of its own. This commentary holds that its rest is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), so that Christians gladly set the Lord’s Day apart for worship and rest as a gift, not under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience on it (Romans 14:5); many godly brothers in the Westminster and 1689 tradition hold it as a continuing Sabbath, and they are to be honoured.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not laid down for the just. Laid down (keitai) is a legal term: enacted, on the statute book. Paul does not mean a righteous person may ignore God’s commands. He means the law as accuser is not aimed at people already doing what it requires. Those justified in Christ do not live under its condemnation (Romans 8:1), though they delight in its moral content (Romans 7:22).

The lawless and disobedient. The list falls into two halves that track the two tables of the Ten Commandments, duties toward God and duties toward neighbour. The first six words come in three pairs describing sin against God: those who reject authority, those without reverence for God, and those who treat sacred things as common.

Who strike their fathers. Now the second table, in the order of the commandments. The words (patrolōais kai mētrolōais) mean father-killers and mother-killers, or those who beat their parents: the fifth commandment at its most violent extreme (Exodus 21:15). Murderers follow: the sixth.

Men who practice homosexuality. The seventh commandment, broadened to all sexual sin. The sexually immoral (pornoi) are those who engage in any sexual relations outside marriage. Men who practise homosexuality translates arsenokoitai, a compound of male and bed, which Paul may have coined from the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13: arsenos koitēn, a male bed. It refers to same-sex sexual acts, not only to exploitative forms, and the historic Christian reading should be stated plainly rather than hidden or softened.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative or abusive practices, such as pederasty, and not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Many who argue this are moved by love for gay friends and family, and the question deserves care. This commentary’s view: The word arsenokoitai comes from the Levitical prohibition, which concerns the act itself, regardless of the relationship. Romans 1:26–27 describes mutual desire, not only exploitation. Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union belongs to the marriage of one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6): Jesus roots marriage in creation itself, God making them male and female, not in the customs of a culture. This is held with compassion: same-sex attraction is a real struggle for many, it is not itself the same as acting on it, and all of us stand in this list as sinners. The hope is the same for all: “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Where Paul put it. But the verse must also be read where Paul put it, alongside liars and men who hit their parents, five verses before he calls himself the foremost of sinners. This is a passage about whom the law puts on trial, and the answer includes the writer. Any use of verse 10 that leaves the user feeling comfortable has misread the paragraph it sits in.

A list of people Christ came for. Six verses on, the same pen writes that “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1:15), using the very word that stands in this list (v. 9). Every kind of person named here is the kind of person the Son of God came for. The law charges the lawless so that the gospel can declare them not guilty, and it can do so only because Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Every one of these commandments was kept by Christ: he honoured his mother from the cross, he gave life and did not take it, he was pure, he stole nothing and gave everything, he never once lied. And the man who was all that the law requires was numbered with the lawless, so that the lawless who trust him could be numbered with the just.

Enslavers. The eighth commandment in its most extreme form. Enslavers (andrapodistai) are kidnappers, slave-traders, men who steal human beings to sell them, a crime the law punished with death (Exodus 21:16). The worst theft is to steal not a purse but a person. Writing inside an empire built on slavery, Paul puts slave-trading in a list of things contrary to sound doctrine. That condemns the Atlantic slave trade too, which men professing Christ carried on for three centuries against the plain words of this verse.

Liars, perjurers. The ninth commandment, false witness. Perjurers (epiorkoi) are those who swear falsely, the lie told under oath where justice depends on the truth.

Sound doctrine. The list gives examples and is not complete: “whatever else”. Then comes a phrase these letters keep repeating: sound (hygiainousa, related to our word hygiene) is a medical word, healthy, wholesome (6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; Titus 1:9). Paul’s standard for teaching is not merely accuracy but health; false doctrine spreads like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17). And these sins are contrary not to good manners but to sound doctrine: what a church believes and how its people live cannot be separated.

What if I am a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction? It means you are not in this list for your temptations; you are in Christ, and the list is about practice. Being tempted is not sin: our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Your calling is the one every Christian has, to say no to sexual sin and yes to Christ, whether in faithful celibacy or, for some, in marriage to someone of the opposite sex. That is costly, and the church must not pretend otherwise. It must be a family to you: homes open to you, friendships deep enough to carry the weight, no jokes or contempt tolerated. Many faithful believers walk this road, and Christ is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.

Did the Bible approve of slavery? Not of the slavery most people picture. The trade that seized Africans and shipped them across the Atlantic was man-stealing, and this verse and Exodus 21:16 condemn it outright. Old Testament servitude among Israelites was mostly a form of working off debt, limited in time and protected by law (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; 23:15–16). The law also allowed foreigners to be held permanently (Leviticus 25:44–46), a hard text Christians should not hide: like divorce, it was an institution the law regulated and restrained because of hardness of heart rather than one it created (Matthew 19:8). In the New Testament Paul did not lead a revolt against Roman slavery, which would have been swiftly crushed, but he planted the gospel that dissolved it: masters and slaves equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28), a runaway sent back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), slaves told, on the most likely reading, to gain their freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21). The Christians who fought to end the trade were reading these verses rightly.
verseByVerse.note: The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the first table (God) to the second (neighbour).

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In accordance with the gospel. This is the standard against which the whole chapter has been measuring. What is sound doctrine (v. 10)? Whatever agrees with the gospel. The law exposes sin; the gospel announces the remedy.

The gospel of the glory. The KJV renders it the glorious gospel, but literally it is the gospel of the glory: the gospel whose content is God’s glory. And the glory is seen in a face: “the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4). At the cross you see God’s holiness, which would not overlook sin, and his love, in which he paid for it himself, both at full strength at once (Romans 3:25–26).

The blessed God. A phrase Paul uses only in this letter (here and 6:15). The word is makarios, the word that opens the Beatitudes: happy, supremely fortunate. Applied to God it means he is perfectly and self-sufficiently happy, the Father delighting in the Son and the Son in the Father in the fellowship of the Spirit from all eternity. His joy was full before the first morning of creation, and out of that fullness he sent his Son, not to fill an emptiness in himself but to bring us into the fellowship he had always enjoyed.

Entrusted. The verb is the language of a deposit placed in someone’s keeping, the idea he will press on Timothy: “guard the deposit” (6:20). Paul did not devise this message and does not own it (Galatians 1:11–12), and only someone who knows that can safely correct anybody else’s doctrine. And that word is the turning point of the paragraph. Paul has been describing men who wanted to be teachers. Now he remembers that he was made one.

Is it irreverent to call God happy? No; it is Paul’s own word, and it guards us against two errors. One pictures God as stern and joyless, tolerating us with a frown, so that the Christian life becomes a matter of keeping a grim master satisfied. The other pictures him as needy, as if he made us because he was lonely and saves us because he could not bear to be without us. Neither is the God of the Bible. He is holy and he is happy, and these are not in tension: his joy is joy in what is good. That is why his commands are not burdensome, why his presence is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11), and why the servant who is faithful is told to enter into the joy of his master (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s own conversion is the gospel told as a life: mercy to a persecutor, a trustworthy saying, and a doxology (vv. 12–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

‘Of whom I am the foremost’, not was. The nearer a man comes to the light, the more dust he sees on himself, and only a man who sees himself so can correct others without contempt.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The persecutor became the pattern (v. 16): Christ's patience with him is the outer limit that no later case exceeds.

Now: The doxology of verse 17 comes from a man remembering his own conversion and unable to finish the sentence without worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has given me strength. The first thing Paul thanks Christ for is strength. The verb (endynamoō) means put power into. Paul’s ministry was not his own achievement but Christ’s power in him (Philippians 4:13).

In the flow. Verses 12–17 are not a detour from the false teachers but the heart of Paul’s answer to them: the men of verse 7 wanted to be teachers of the law, and here is the most zealous teacher of the law in his generation telling what actually happened to him.

He judged me faithful. Not because Paul had earned it; he was a persecutor. The Lord does not find faithful men; by grace he makes them, and then he entrusts them with his work.

Appointing me to his service. Service (diakonia) is ministry, the word from which deacon comes. A gracious appointment, given on the Damascus road: “he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name” (Acts 9:15; 26:16).

Formerly a blasphemer. Three words, and they escalate. Blasphemer: he had spoken against the name of Christ, and had tried to force others to do it (Acts 26:11). Persecutor: he had gone house to house dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:3). Insolent opponent is hybristēs, related to our word hubris: the violent man who takes pleasure in humiliating people. It is the ugliest of the three, and Paul chose it about himself.

I received mercy. The verb (eleeō) is passive: he was shown pity. He did not find mercy, earn it or ask for it. He was not seeking Christ; he was seeking Christians. Christ did not wait for Saul to soften; he met him at full speed on the road to Damascus, with letters of arrest in his bag.

Ignorantly in unbelief. This is not an excuse; he has just used three brutal words about himself. He thought he was serving God (Acts 26:9; Romans 10:2). The Old Testament made provision for sins committed unwittingly, and none for sins committed “with a high hand”, in open defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). Paul was on the first side of that line: catastrophically wrong, and sincerely so. Not innocent. Reachable. Jesus prayed for his crucifiers in the same terms: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

Grace overflowed. The verb is enormous: hyperpleonazō, super-abounded. Where his sin had been extreme, grace was more extreme: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Faith and love. Faith and love were not what Paul contributed in response; they arrived in the flood. Faith in place of his unbelief; love in place of his violence. Both are found in Christ Jesus: joined to him by faith, as a branch draws its life from the vine, we receive what is his (John 15:4–5). Here is the answer to verse 5, where love from sincere faith was named as the goal. Such love is not produced by teaching alone. It is poured in by grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s ignorance earned God’s mercy. Ignorance is not innocence; Paul still calls himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). His ignorance means only that his sin was not the deliberate, knowing rejection of the Spirit that Jesus calls unforgivable (Mark 3:28–29). The mercy itself was God’s free choice. His call did not merely invite Saul; it brought him. God spoke, and the dead heart answered (Galatians 1:15–16).

Could I have committed the unforgivable sin? If you are worried that you have, you have not. The sin Jesus warned of (Mark 3:28–30) was committed by men who watched the Spirit’s work in Christ and deliberately called it the devil’s, and who were so hardened that they had no desire to repent. It is a settled, knowing hostility to Christ, not a single dreadful thought, a terrible season of backsliding, or a past as violent as Paul’s. The very fear that you have gone too far is evidence that the Spirit is still at work in you. Paul blasphemed, persecuted and enjoyed hurting people, and he was received. Come to Christ now, and you will find that he does not cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Can God really use someone with my past? Yes: God did not merely forgive Paul but put him in the front line, among the very people he had hunted, though some offences have lasting consequences and roles such as eldership require a good reputation over time (3:2, 7). (See Hebrews 11:29–31 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. Name the most hostile person you know toward Christ, and pray for more than their restraint: pray that Christ would do to them what he did to Saul. Then thank him, specifically, for what you were when he found you.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy. Trustworthy (pistos) is the same word as “faithful” in verse 12. This is the first of five such sayings in the Pastoral Letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and the phrase appears to mark a line already well known in the churches, which Paul now endorses with his apostolic authority.

Full acceptance. The phrase means wholehearted reception: not only agreed with but embraced, the way a starving man does not merely agree that bread is nourishing.

Came into the world. He was somewhere else first. In passing, Paul says that Christ existed before he was born (John 1:9), and that he became man: the eternal Son did not stop being God, but took a real human body and soul, so that one person is truly God and truly man (John 1:14; Philippians 2:6–7). He walked into a world of sinners, not to inspect them but to save them.

To save sinners. Not merely to teach or to set an example, but to rescue from sin and its penalty (Matthew 1:21; Luke 19:10). And sinners: not the promising, not the religious, not the nearly good (Mark 2:17). This is the gospel in a sentence, and the only qualification for it is the one thing everyone has.

The foremost. Then Paul adds words of his own. Foremost (prōtos) is first, chief, worst. And the tense is the thing: not “I was”, but “I am”. Decades into his apostleship, this is still Paul’s settled estimate of himself. Mature believers see their sin more clearly, not less. Over the years Paul called himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:9), then “the very least of all the saints” (Ephesians 3:8), and now the foremost of sinners.

Nearness to light. This is not humility put on for show, nor a measured claim to be the worst man who ever lived. The nearer a man comes to the light, the more dust he sees on himself. John Bunyan took the title of his own spiritual autobiography from this verse: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. And John Newton, the slave-ship captain who became a minister of the gospel, is remembered as saying near the end of his life that his memory was nearly gone, but he remembered two things: that he was a great sinner, and that Christ was a great Saviour.

How Paul uses it. Paul is about to discipline two men (v. 20), and he does it from this position. A man who genuinely considers himself the foremost sinner in the room can correct other people without contempt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ came to save every person, so that all will be saved in the end; he came to save sinners, and those he came to save he actually saves (Matthew 1:21; John 10:11, 27–29).

Isn’t it unhealthy to call myself the worst of sinners? Not when it is said the way Paul says it, in the same breath as “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”. Self-hatred looks at sin and stops there; it ends in despair or in self-punishment. Paul looks at his sin in order to look at his Saviour, and it ends in a doxology two verses later. Nor is it a false humility that refuses to see God’s work in you: Paul also says he worked harder than all the apostles, though it was not he but the grace of God (1 Corinthians 15:10). The healthy Christian holds both: I am a great sinner, and I am greatly loved. Each truth keeps the other from going wrong.

What if I do not feel that bad? The question is not how you compare with Paul, but how you stand before God. A respectable sinner is still a sinner, and the danger of feeling “not that bad” is that you never come to Christ as one who needs saving. Paul’s first opinion of himself was that he was blameless (Philippians 3:6); that was his worst condition, not his best. The door of this verse is marked “Sinners”, and the only people who cannot go through it are those who think the sign does not apply to them.

In everyday life. When you next find yourself despising someone, the political opponent, the neighbour, the church member who has failed publicly, say this verse under your breath with your own name in it. It changes the tone of what you say next. And if you are carrying a sin you think is too heavy for this verse, read it again: it does not say that Christ came to save sinners, except the worst. The man who called himself the worst wrote it.
verseByVerse.note: The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His perfect patience. God had a reason for choosing such an enemy, and the reason was you. Perfect patience (tēn hapasan makrothymian) is the whole extent of his long-suffering, the slowness to boil that endures provocation. Christ was patient with Saul for the whole time Saul was doing his worst, and that patience gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4).

An example. The word (hypotypōsis) is a pattern, an outline drawn so that others can see the shape of a thing. If Christ’s patience stretched to a man who hunted his people and tried to make them curse his name, nobody who comes after can reasonably say their case is too hard. Whatever sin anyone brings, Christ has already been patient with worse.

To the King of the ages. Then the sentence breaks into a doxology, a burst of praise. It springs not from thinking about God in the abstract but from Paul’s memory of his own conversion. That is a fair test of whether we have understood the gospel or merely learned it. King of the ages: he reigned before the first age began and will reign when the last has ended, and he rules every age between, including this troublesome one in Ephesus, and including yours.

Immortal, invisible, the only God. Immortal (aphthartos) is incorruptible, unlike everything else Timothy is dealing with, his own frail body included. Invisible: no one has ever seen God in his essence (John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16). That is the difficulty of pastoral work: the one you serve cannot be seen, while the opposition is entirely visible. The only God (Deuteronomy 6:4): in a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis, that is not a philosophical statement but a stand. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “wise”, probably borrowed from Romans 16:27; the earlier reading is “the only God”.

Forever and ever. Literally “to the ages of the ages”, one of the strongest phrases Greek has for endlessness. And “Amen” means “so be it”. Paul expects the congregation to say it back.

Is it fair that a man like Saul should be forgiven? No, and that is the point: mercy is never fair, or it would not be mercy. But it is not unjust either. God did not pretend Saul’s violence had not happened. Every blow he struck at Christ’s people was a blow at Christ himself (Acts 9:4), and Christ bore the punishment for it on the cross, so that God is just when he forgives (Romans 3:26). The objection usually hides something in us: the elder brother’s complaint that the prodigal gets a feast he did not earn (Luke 15:28–30). Nobody at that feast earned it. The only people who stay outside are the ones who insist on being paid what they deserve.

What if I was converted quietly as a child? Is my story worth anything? Yes. Paul’s story is the outer limit, set there so that the worst may hope. But a child brought up in the faith and kept from great sins has received just as much mercy; it was simply given earlier, before the damage could be done. Being kept is as much grace as being rescued. Your story displays Christ’s patience in a different way: patience with all the small, stubborn sins of a long ordinary life, and faithfulness through every year of it.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? Because the invisible God has made himself known. John says that the only Son, himself God and at the Father’s side, is the one who has made the unseen Father known (John 1:18). Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). You meet him in the Scriptures, which testify to Christ, and you know him by faith, through the Spirit, who opens the eyes of your heart. The invisibility of God is not his absence. It is his greatness: he is not one more object in the world, and he cannot be captured in an image, but he has come close in his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge handed on to Timothy, and a warning from two men whose faith was wrecked (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First: Conduct or Doctrine

In verse 19 conscience is thrown away first, and faith is wrecked as a result; and even the severest discipline, handing over to Satan, is meant to restore: ‘that they may learn’ (v. 20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was to fight by the prophecies once made over him (compare 4:14).

Now: Shipwreck is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience tells him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This charge I entrust. Paul returns to where the chapter began. Entrust (paratithēmi) is to deposit with someone for safekeeping. As the gospel was entrusted to Paul (v. 11), he entrusts the charge to Timothy, who must entrust it to faithful men who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). That is how it has always travelled, one faithful person to another, until it reached you.

The prophecies. We are not told what was said when Timothy was set apart (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6), but he is to fight by it, to use it as ammunition on hard days. When a man wonders whether he should be doing this at all, one answer is to remember what was said when he began.

The good warfare. Wage warfare (strateuomai) is to serve as a soldier, a note that will return (6:12; 2 Timothy 2:3–4). Ministry here is not administration; it is a campaign against an enemy, fought in the strength Christ gives (v. 12). He is the captain of the good warfare, who fought the battle that mattered on the cross and won it.

Holding faith and a good conscience. These are the two things named in verse 5, and here they are two weapons.

Shipwreck. Rejecting (apōtheomai) is deliberately pushing aside, and “this” is the good conscience. Paul, who had been shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:25), uses a vivid image: they threw their conscience overboard, and their faith broke up on the rocks.

The conscience goes first. The order is one of the most practical things in the chapter. Paul does not describe men who reasoned their way out of Christianity and then began living badly. He describes men who kept doing what they knew to be wrong, and whose doctrine followed their conduct onto the rocks. Sooner or later, a man who lives wrongly changes his beliefs to excuse his life. Not everyone who leaves the faith takes this road, and honest doubts deserve honest answers; but some who say they lost their faith for intellectual reasons lost their conscience first.

Hymenaeus and Alexander. Two names, after a whole chapter of “certain persons”. Hymenaeus later taught, with Philetus, that the resurrection had already happened, and upset the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17–18). Alexander may be the coppersmith who did Paul great harm (2 Timothy 4:14), though the name was common.

Handed over to Satan. The phrase is used elsewhere of putting someone outside the church’s fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:5): out of the sphere where God’s people gather under Christ’s protection, and back into the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). This is excommunication, the most serious act of church discipline. It is not a sentence to hell.

A defeated enemy on a short chain. Handing a man over to Satan could only do him good if Satan is not free, and he is not. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). The devil still prowls, but inside the limits his conqueror sets (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and even the enemy’s ground can become a school in which Christ teaches a blasphemer to stop.

Learn not to blaspheme. The stated purpose changes how the whole sentence reads. Learn (paideuō) is to be trained, as a child is trained: the aim is to correct, not merely to punish. Life outside the church might bring them to repentance. And blasphemer is what Paul called himself in verse 13, before he received mercy. Their false teaching was blasphemy because it treated the name of the holy God as a common thing, inside his own house. Paul hands them over hoping that what happened to him will happen to them.

Where Christians differ: do prophecies like these continue today? Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians see the prophecies over Timothy as a model for prophetic words in churches today. This commentary’s view: The New Testament prophets belonged to the foundation-laying era of the church, alongside the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), when Scripture was still being given. With the completion of the canon, God guides his church through the sufficient written Word, not through new revelations (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). This is held charitably: brothers who differ often love Christ deeply, and God still guides through his Word, wise counsel, providence, and the inward witness of the Spirit to Scripture. But no word claiming to be prophecy may add to or stand alongside Scripture.

What were these prophecies? Spirit-given words, in the apostolic age, that marked Timothy out for his ministry, probably spoken when the elders laid hands on him (4:14). They belonged to that founding time. Today the church recognises a man’s call to ministry by his gifts, character and fruit, tested by Scripture, not by new prophecies.

Were Hymenaeus and Alexander true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read “made shipwreck of their faith” that way. The more likely reading is that they held the faith outwardly but never truly trusted Christ; as John says of such people, “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). Paul’s discipline was meant to bring them to repentance, that they might learn not to blaspheme. The warning is for every believer to hold faith and a good conscience.

What if I am afraid my own faith could be shipwrecked? The fear itself is a good sign; the men in this verse were not afraid, they were careless. Christ keeps his sheep, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he keeps them by means, one of which is this warning. So do what verse 19 says. Keep your conscience clean: when it accuses you, do not argue with it or bury it; take the thing to the cross, confess it and turn from it. Keep near the means of grace, the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. And tell a trusted believer when you are drifting. Ships rarely sink in one wave; they take on water slowly, and someone who loves you can see the list before you can.

What does church discipline look like today? It begins quietly, as Jesus taught: a private word, then one or two others, and only then the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Most discipline ends at the first step, with repentance and restoration. Excommunication is the last step, for serious, unrepented sin or for persistent false teaching, and it is carried out by the church under its elders, not by individuals. It means the person is no longer received as a member or at the Lord’s Table. It does not mean hatred or shunning in every form: you may still greet them, and you should pray for them and call them back, warning them as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15). And it must never be used to silence the victims of abuse or to protect leaders; that is a perversion of it.

In everyday life. Is there one thing you have been doing that you know is wrong and have stopped thinking about? That is where shipwrecks start. Name it to God today, at the cross, and if it involves another person, put it right this week. A sin you hate and keep fighting is a different thing: the fight itself is the Spirit’s work, and the conscience that grieves over it is still afloat.

For worship. The gospel has come down to us through a long chain of trembling hands, Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, and on through every century, and not one link was strong in itself. Christ kept it. Even his discipline is mercy, a hand reaching after the wanderer, and the blasphemer who wrote these lines is the proof that it can bring him home.
verseByVerse.note: To hand someone “over to Satan” means putting him out of the church, in the hope that he will be brought to repentance.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,<sup>2</sup>To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.<sup>3</sup>As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine,<sup>4</sup>nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.<sup>5</sup>The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.<sup>6</sup>Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion,<sup>7</sup>desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.<sup>8</sup>Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,<sup>9</sup>understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers,<sup>10</sup>the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,<sup>11</sup>in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.<sup>12</sup>I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service,<sup>13</sup>though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief,<sup>14</sup>and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>15</sup>The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.<sup>16</sup>But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life.<sup>17</sup>To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>18</sup>This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare,<sup>19</sup>holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith,<sup>20</sup>among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.

2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Paul turns to the church’s gathered life. First, prayer for everyone, including rulers such as Nero, because God our Saviour desires all people to be saved, and there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Then conduct in worship: men pray without anger; women are adorned with good works rather than wealth.

Finally the most debated verses: women are to learn, but not to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, on grounds from creation, not Ephesian culture. This commentary holds the complementarian reading and insists that a restriction on a role is never a verdict on a person’s worth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prayer comes first: every kind of prayer, for every kind of person, rulers included. Paul grounds it in the heart of the gospel: one God, one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom, and Paul sent as his herald to the nations.
verseByVerse.theology:
‘Desires All People to Be Saved’

Verse 4 has been read as all kinds of people, or, often in the Reformed tradition, as God’s revealed will (what pleases him and what he commands) set beside his decreed will (what he has purposed to happen). Either way there is one mediator, and his ransom is a substitute’s (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Nero, the church was told to pray, and give thanks, for kings (v. 2; compare Jeremiah 29:7).

Now: The aim is modest: a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Paul thought that enough to pray for.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 2 sets the church’s public worship in order. First, prayer for all kinds of people, rulers included, grounded in one God and one mediator who gave himself as a ransom for all (vv. 1–7). Second, men and women in worship (vv. 8–15): men are to pray without anger; women are to adorn themselves with good works, and to learn quietly; and Paul does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, grounding this in creation and the fall (vv. 11–14). He closes with a hard sentence about childbearing (v. 15). At the centre stands the one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself.

The setting. The false teachers in Ephesus seem to have been exclusive in outlook, contentious in spirit, and particularly influential among some women (5:13–15; 2 Timothy 3:6–7), and may have forbidden marriage (4:3). Paul’s instructions answer each: pray for everyone; stop quarrelling; women are to learn, but not to take over the teaching office; and marriage and motherhood are good. The emperor was Nero (AD 54–68), who would soon begin persecuting Christians.

First of all. Having dealt with the false teachers, Paul turns to the church’s conduct, and the first item is not strategy against the opposition but prayer for outsiders. “First of all” means first in importance: in the light of the battle for the truth, the church must pray. A church that fights error but does not pray for the world has already lost what the narrow-minded false teachers wanted it to lose: its care for outsiders.

Four kinds of prayer. The four words overlap. Supplications (deēseis) are requests arising from need. Prayers is the general word. Intercessions (enteuxeis) is a word used of bringing a petition before a king on someone’s behalf. And thanksgivings, the surprising one, since those to be given thanks for include Nero. Together they describe not a brief mention of the government before the real business, but the church on its knees, bringing the world before the throne.

For all people. No one is excluded from the church’s prayers. The context, which immediately names kings, shows that Paul means all kinds and classes of people, not least those we might be tempted to leave out.

For kings. Kings includes the emperor; high positions are governors, magistrates, officials. A church in Ephesus is to pray, and give thanks, for the emperor who would shortly use Christians as living torches in his gardens, and under whom, as the early church remembered, Paul himself would be executed. It matches Romans 13:1 and Jeremiah’s word to the exiles: “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). God’s people have usually lived under governments they did not choose, and this is the standing instruction. On leadership and submission in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

A peaceful and quiet life. Peaceful is free from outward disturbance; quiet is settled within. The purpose is modest: not influence for the church, but room to worship and to let the gospel spread. That is a smaller ambition than a modern church often has for its nation, and Paul thought it enough to pray for.

Godly and dignified. Godliness (eusebeia), reverent devotion to God shown in life, is a key word of these letters. The purpose of peace is not comfort but godliness: Paul asks for quiet so that Christians can be holy in public, and their neighbours can see what a life given to God looks like.

Praying for the power that judged him. The church’s Lord stood before a Roman governor (6:13), was condemned by Roman authority and nailed up by Roman soldiers, and he prayed for the men who did it (Luke 23:34). A church that prays for Nero is doing what its Master did. And it prays through him: its intercessions reach God only because there is one mediator (v. 5), who lives for ever to intercede for his people. Our prayers for rulers are heard because he prays for us.

What do I actually pray for a ruler I think is wicked? Pray what Paul prays. For their salvation first: Nero was beyond the church’s reach, but not beyond God’s, and the prayer that a persecutor might be converted was answered spectacularly in Paul himself. For wisdom and justice in their decisions. For restraint on their evil, and for protection of the weak who suffer under it. For peace, so that the church can worship and the gospel can run. And give thanks for whatever good they do, and for the order that even a bad government preserves, because the alternative is chaos. You can pray all this without pretending to admire them.

Does praying for rulers mean I must never oppose them? No. Praying for a ruler is not the same as agreeing with him. Christians may vote, campaign, protest lawfully and speak out against injustice, as the prophets confronted kings and Paul appealed to Caesar for his rights (Acts 25:11). Where a ruler commands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). But prayer changes the spirit in which we do all this. It is very hard to hate a man you have prayed for by name every week, and very hard to put your hope in politics once you have spent time before the King of the ages.

In everyday life. Pray today, by name, for your head of state, your local leaders, and one public figure you find hard to like. Pray for their good and their salvation, and thank God for one specific good thing that has come through them.

For worship. The Lord who rules the kings of the earth is never threatened by them. He turned the heart of Cyrus, humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and used a Roman census to bring his Son to Bethlehem. And his church, praying for Nero in a house in Ephesus, was not a frightened minority pleading for its life. It was a royal priesthood interceding for the world, under a King whose kingdom no emperor could touch.
verseByVerse.note: Christians were to pray for rulers such as Nero, under whom they would later suffer.

parallels.desc: seek the welfare of the city

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good and pleasing. Pray for everyone, because God’s saving concern reaches everyone. The church’s prayers are to be as wide as God’s desire.

Who desires all people to be saved. All people is the same phrase as verse 1. God is not grudging toward sinners; his heart is open to all kinds of people, including kings who persecute and Gentiles whom the false teachers may have excluded. The sentence sits beside the Bible’s equally clear teaching that God chooses and that his purposes do not fail. And he does not merely wish; he saves. Every person who will stand before his throne, from every tribe and language and people and nation, will be there because this God desired it and accomplished it, and gave his Son to make it so.

The knowledge of the truth. Knowledge (epignōsis) is full knowledge; the truth is the gospel (2 Timothy 2:25; Titus 1:1). God saves people by bringing them to know the truth, and he brings them the truth by sending people to tell it, which is why prayer and preaching go together.

The desire with tears in it. To see what God’s desire for the lost looks like, look at his Son. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–42) and said, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The same Lord said that he would lose none of all that the Father had given him (John 6:39). Both are true in one Christ, and those tears show most clearly that God’s call is sincere.

Where Christians differ: if God desires all to be saved, why are not all saved? Arminian Christians argue that God wills to save every individual equally and that his grace enables everyone to believe, so that the difference lies in each person’s free response: God does his part, and each person decides. Universalists argue that, since God desires it, all will eventually be saved. This commentary’s view: Universalism contradicts Scripture’s plain teaching on final judgment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). As for the Arminian view, Scripture distinguishes between what God desires in the sense of what pleases him and what he commands (his revealed will), and what he has decreed will happen (his decretive will). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11) and sincerely calls all to repent; yet he has, for wise and holy reasons, chosen to save some and not all (Romans 9:18; Ephesians 1:4–5). Two further points help. First, all people in context means all kinds of people, including rulers and Gentiles (vv. 1–2, 7), as all often means in Scripture (Titus 2:11; compare Revelation 5:9). Second, God’s desire here is the ground for the church’s universal prayer and preaching: we do not know who the elect are, so we pray for and preach to all, knowing that God is pleased to save through that means. The Reformed view does not make God less loving; it makes him the sovereign author of every salvation. Arminian brothers and sisters hold their view out of a real concern for God’s love and human responsibility, and they preach the same crucified Christ; the difference is serious, but it is a difference within the family.

Two ways of speaking about God’s will. The distinction between what God commands and what he has decreed is not an evasion invented for this verse. The cross was the most wicked act men ever committed, and God’s law forbade it; yet it was exactly what his hand and his plan “had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:27–28). God genuinely takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, genuinely commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30), and has purposed to save a people he will not lose. We cannot see how this fits together in the mind of God. We are asked to believe both, and to pray accordingly.

The pastoral force. Paul is telling a small, harassed congregation that there is nobody they may treat as beyond praying for: not the magistrate who fined them, not the emperor, not the neighbour who reported them.

If God has chosen whom he will save, why should I pray and evangelise? Because God ordains the means as well as the end. He has chosen to save people through the prayers and the preaching of his church, just as he has chosen to grow crops through farmers. Paul believed in election more firmly than anyone, and he was the great missionary of the early church; election was what gave him confidence that his preaching would not be wasted (Acts 18:9–10; 2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who God’s elect are, and you are not meant to. You are meant to pray for everyone and tell everyone, and to trust that God will use it.

How can I be sure the offer includes me? Because it is addressed to you.
