The gospel does not say, “Christ died for the elect; find out if you are one.” It says, “Come, believe, repent,” and “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). You never have to look into God’s secret decree to know whether you may come. You look at his open invitation, and you take him at his word. Everyone who has ever come to Christ has been received, and you will not be the first to be turned away.

In everyday life. Think of the person you have quietly decided will never be saved. You were once as far off yourself, and someone prayed for you. Begin again today, and add one name from a group your church usually forgets.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is one God. This gives the reason for praying for all, and its compact, balanced form suggests a confession the churches used. “One God” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession (Deuteronomy 6:4), and it lands with force in a city whose riot in Acts 19 was a two-hour chant: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Since there is only one God, he is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 3:29–30), of rulers and slaves alike, and so the church must pray for every group.

One mediator. A mediator (mesitēs) is a go-between who brings two estranged parties together: here, a holy God and the sinners separated from him. And “one” excludes every other candidate: not angels, not the intermediary beings the false teachers seem to have been fascinated by, not Mary, not the saints, not a priest, not the church itself. Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). There is a single point of access, and it is a person. The eternal Son took our flesh so that one of us could stand in the gap, and he stood there not to bargain for us but to give himself as the price.

The man Christ Jesus. Not the Son, not the Lord: the man (anthrōpos). To represent humans, the mediator had to be truly human; to bring us to God, he had to be truly God (Hebrews 2:14–17; John 1:1, 14). And Paul does not say the mediator “was” a man. He remains a man now, in heaven, in the risen body that showed Thomas the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). He bears our nature and our name before the Father, and he has never lost a single one of those he bought.

Who gave himself. He was not taken; he handed himself over, with authority both to lay his life down and to take it up again (John 10:18). The ransom was a gift, not a seizure.

A ransom for all. The word is antilytron, not found in any earlier Greek writing that survives: lytron, a ransom price, the word Jesus used of himself (Mark 10:45), with anti, in place of. A ransom price paid in place of another: Jesus did not merely pay for us; he stood where we were standing. It is penal substitution: he bore in our place the penalty God’s holy justice required for our sin, to set us free (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24).

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many hold that Christ died for every individual equally, making salvation possible for all. This commentary’s view: In context all means all kinds of people (vv. 1–2, 7), and Christ’s ransom actually frees those for whom it was paid; yet his death is sufficient for the whole world, and the gospel is offered sincerely to every person, and those who differ preach the same Saviour. (See 2 Corinthians 5:14–15 for the fuller answer.)

At the proper time. At the proper time (kairois idiois) is literally “at its own appointed seasons”. History was not drifting; it was being brought to a particular hour, the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), and now in this age the message is proclaimed (Titus 1:3).

To whom was the ransom of verse 6 paid? Not to the devil, as some early writers suggested, as if God owed Satan anything. The ransom was paid to the justice of God. Our debt was to God’s law, which we had broken, and the penalty was death (Romans 6:23). Christ paid it by bearing that penalty himself, so that God could be both just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The Father did not extract the price from an unwilling Son, and the Son did not buy a reluctant Father’s love. The Father so loved the world that he gave, and the Son gave himself. The whole Trinity planned and paid the ransom.

Can I pray to Mary or the saints to help me? No, and you do not need to. They were sinners saved by the same mediator, and they are not commanded or promised to hear our prayers. Scripture never directs a single prayer to anyone but God. More than that, you need no one to soften Christ toward you, because he is not hard. He is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, and he invites us to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:15–16). Go to him directly. Ask fellow believers to pray for you, as Paul did; but bring your prayers to God through Christ alone.

Is it not arrogant to say there is only one way to God? It would be, if Christians claimed to have found the way by being cleverer or better than others. The claim is the opposite: none of us could find the way, so God opened one himself, at the cost of his Son. Every view of salvation draws a line somewhere; even the belief that all roads lead to God shuts out those who think otherwise. And if there were another way, the cross would have been needless (Galatians 2:21): God did not give up his Son for something that could be had another way. So the gospel is narrow in its door and wide in its welcome. There is one mediator, and anyone at all, of any nation or past, may come through him by faith (Romans 10:13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Preacher and apostle. The ransom was for all kinds of people, Gentiles included, and Paul’s commission is the proof that God meant it. Three titles. A preacher (kēryx) is a herald, who announces a king’s decree in the public square and has no licence to edit. An apostle is an authorised messenger. A teacher explains and instructs over time. Together they describe the whole task.

Appointed. The verb is tithēmi, set or placed. Set that against 1:7, where the troublemakers were “desiring to be teachers of the law”. One man was placed; the others placed themselves. That explains why Paul can insist on his credentials in one breath and call himself the foremost of sinners in the next. He is not defending a position he took for himself.

I am not lying. The solemn assertion (like Romans 9:1) is about what he has just claimed: that the ransom was for all kinds of people and that he is teacher of the Gentiles. These were the fighting words of his ministry; the Jerusalem crowd listened to him until the word “Gentiles”, and then shouted for his death (Acts 22:21–22). Even late in his life this was still the contested ground.

A teacher of the Gentiles. Paul’s special calling was to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9). The persecutor of the church became the teacher of the Gentiles, and a message that began in a corner of Judea has reached the ends of the earth. In faith and truth could mean faithfully and truthfully, or teaching the faith and the truth; either way, not in speculation, which is what the rivals dealt in (1:4).

The herald’s voice is Christ’s. A herald speaks in another’s name. Writing to this same church, Paul said that Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). The Gentiles of Ephesus never saw Jesus in Galilee, yet Christ preached to them, because when his herald announced the ransom, the King himself was speaking (Acts 26:16–18).

What he will fight for. The man who calls himself the foremost of sinners does not much mind what people think of him. He minds a great deal that they believe the Gentiles are genuinely included. And if you are not Jewish, he was fighting for you.

The apostolic office. The apostolic office was unique and foundational: the apostles were witnesses of the risen Christ, sent by him in person (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and the church is built once for all on their foundation (Ephesians 2:20), so the office has not continued.

Does God still call people to preach? Yes, though not as apostles. The church still needs heralds and teachers, and God still gives them (Ephesians 4:11; Romans 10:14–15). A call to preach is not normally a voice or a vision. It is a desire for the work, the gifts and character Scripture requires (3:1–7), and the recognition of the church, which tests a man and sets him apart. If you sense that desire, talk to your elders, ask them to test you, and take every opportunity to serve and learn. And whether or not you are called to preach, you are called to speak of Christ to the people around you.

In everyday life. The gospel reached you along a chain of heralds that runs back to Paul. Give thanks for the last link in that chain, and think of the nations that have come to your own street: the family from overseas, the international student, the colleague from another faith.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Conduct in the gathered church: men praying without anger, women adorned with good works rather than display, and the teaching and governing office kept for qualified men, on grounds Paul takes from creation and the fall. It ends with the hard promise about childbearing (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The key word of verse 12 is authentein, to exercise authority. This commentary reads it as plain authority: Paul restricts the thing itself, not only its abuse. He grounds this in the order of creation (vv. 13–14), an order that concerns role, not worth (Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The braided hair, gold and pearls of verse 9 brought social rank into the assembly; Paul replaces that display with good works, in which no one can outspend anyone.

Now: Whatever a church concludes about who teaches, a restriction on a function is never a verdict on a person.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
I desire then. Desire (boulomai) is not a preference but an apostolic instruction, and “then” draws it out of what he has just said: since there is one mediator, here is how the church is to pray.

That in every place. Every place where the church gathers (1 Corinthians 1:2), with an echo of Malachi’s promise that in every place incense will be offered to God’s name among the nations (Malachi 1:11). Paul is not describing a local Ephesian arrangement but what he expects of the churches everywhere, which matters for how his instructions to men and women are read.

The men should pray. The men (tous andras) are males specifically. Men are to lead the congregation in public prayer; this does not forbid women from praying in church (1 Corinthians 11:5). Paul’s first instruction to Christian men is not to take charge but to pray.

Lifting holy hands. The posture is the ordinary one of the ancient world: standing, hands raised and open (1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 141:2). Nothing here forbids kneeling. The weight falls on holy (hosios): hands lifted to God must be clean. God told Israel that when they spread out their hands he would hide his eyes, because their hands were full of blood (Isaiah 1:15).

Without anger or quarreling. What makes the hands unholy here is the state of the man’s relationships. Anger (orgē) is settled resentment; quarrelling (dialogismos) is disputing, or the inner turmoil of a man going over his case against someone. The false teaching had stirred up controversy (1:4; 6:4–5), and men were apparently carrying it into worship. Raised hands do not make up for grievances carried against a brother.

The same track. Scripture always joins the two. “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24); husbands are to live with their wives in an understanding way, “so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Peter 3:7). Worship and the way you treat people run on the same track. If a man’s praying feels obstructed, the first place to look is not his technique but whether there is somebody he is angry with.

The one who can ascend the hill. “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?” asks Psalm 24, and answers: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). Only one man has fully answered that description, our high priest, “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26). Men can lift their hands in every place not because they have qualified themselves, but because the one mediator has opened the way. Because his hands were pierced, ours are washed, and we may lift them to the Father in his name. Holy hands are not hands that never sinned. They are hands cleansed by him and no longer clenched against a brother.

May women pray aloud in church? Yes. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the gatherings at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:5), and in Acts the women were praying with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). What this verse does is lay a particular duty on the men: to lead in prayer, and to do it with clean hands. A church where only women pray has not obeyed this verse, and a church where women are silenced from praying has misread it.

What if I want to be reconciled and the other person refuses? Then do what lies with you, and leave the rest with God. Paul’s own limit is realistic: as far as it depends on you, be at peace (Romans 12:18). Go to them, admit your part honestly without excusing it, forgive them from the heart whether or not they ask, and refuse to nurse the grievance or talk about it to others. If they still will not be reconciled, your hands can be holy even though the relationship is broken, because what defiles them is your anger, not their refusal. Keep praying for them. And if the conflict involves abuse or danger, reconciliation does not mean putting yourself back in harm’s way; forgiveness and safety can go together.
verseByVerse.note: Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer.

parallels.desc: the lifting up of my hands

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women should adorn themselves. “Likewise” ties this to verse 8: as the men have their particular temptation in the assembly, anger, so the women have theirs, display. Adorn (kosmeō, from which comes cosmetic) is to make beautiful. Paul is not against beauty; he directs it.

With modesty and self-control. Respectable (kosmios) is orderly, from the same root as adorn. Modesty (aidōs) is reserve, the instinct not to draw improper attention. Self-control (sōphrosynē) is the settled self-mastery prized in Greek moral thought. Both are inner qualities expressed outwardly.

Braided hair and gold. Elaborately braided hair threaded with gold and pearls required slaves and hours to produce, and it existed to announce wealth and rank (compare 1 Peter 3:3–4).

Ranking in the assembly. So the issue is that social rank was being carried into the church’s gathering. A poor woman, perhaps a slave, entering a room where wealth was being advertised knew exactly where she stood. James addresses the same problem (James 2:1–4), and so does Paul at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:21–22).

With good works. This is the point of the paragraph. A woman who claims to worship God should be known for her good works: kindness, hospitality, service, like Dorcas, who was full of good works and acts of charity (Acts 9:36–39). Paul does not tell them to look poor but to change what they are adorned with, and that is a levelling standard: a wealthy woman can outspend a poor one on pearls, but nobody can outspend anybody on kindness. Paul has replaced the currency of the room with one everybody can trade in.

Adorning the Saviour’s teaching. Paul uses this verb in Titus, where slaves are to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour (Titus 2:10). Good works decorate the gospel, making the beauty of Christ visible in a city that knew only the beauty of money; and the works are his gift, for we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). The Saviour who had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2) is still shown to the world in the plain kindnesses of his people.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all braiding, jewellery, or nice clothes; Rebekah received gold jewellery as a sign of God’s blessing (Genesis 24:22). The issue is extravagant display, status-seeking, and immodesty.

How do I decide what is modest and appropriate? Ask three questions, of any outfit. What is it saying? If the honest answer is “look how wealthy I am”, or “look at my body”, it is saying the wrong thing in the house of God. Whom does it serve? Clothing that makes a poorer sister feel shabby, or that pulls attention away from worship, does not serve the church. And what does it cost, in money and in time? If your appearance absorbs more of both than your good works do, the balance is wrong. Within those questions there is freedom, and cultures differ. Do not judge other women by your own preferences, and do not make rules Scripture has not made.

Does this make women responsible for men’s lust? No. Every man is responsible for his own eyes and his own heart; Jesus put the guilt of the lustful look on the man who looks (Matthew 5:28), and Job made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). A woman is never to blame for a man’s sin against her, and no one may ever excuse harassment or abuse by pointing at what a woman wore. Paul’s concern here is different: that a Christian woman’s aim should not be to draw attention to herself, whether by wealth or by immodesty, but to adorn the gospel with a godly life. Modesty is a woman’s gift to God and to the church, not a fence she must build around men.

For worship. God himself is the great adorner. He clothed Adam and Eve after their shame, and he has clothed his people with the robe of Christ’s righteousness. The church is being made ready as a bride, and her fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). A woman adorned with good works is wearing, already, the clothes of the wedding.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. These two verses are among the most contested in the New Testament, and should be read with the actual words in front of us, and with care for the many Christian women who read them with a lump in the throat. Paul is still setting the gathered church in order: who learns and who teaches when the church meets. Verses 13–14 give his reasons, and chapter 3 goes on to describe the men who are to hold the teaching office (3:1–7).

Let a woman learn. Begin with what is easily missed. Learn (manthanō, be a disciple) is a command, not a grudging permission, and in the first century a generous one: women were often not taught the law at all, and some rabbis spoke with contempt of teaching it to a woman. Whatever else this passage does, it puts women in the class rather than outside the door, as Jesus did when Mary sat at his feet and he said she had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:38–42).

Quietly. In quietness (en hēsychia), the same root as the quiet life of verse 2: not absolute silence but a receptive, peaceable attitude.

With all submissiveness. Submissiveness (hypotagē) is ordering oneself under, the posture of any learner under teaching: submission to the teaching and to the church’s order under the elders. Not submission of every woman to every man.

I do not permit a woman to teach. Permit is present tense: as my settled practice. Teach (didaskō) in the Pastoral Letters is the authoritative teaching of doctrine in the church, the work of elders (3:2; 5:17; 2 Timothy 2:2). Paul is forbidding women to hold the teaching office in the gathered church.

To exercise authority. The key word is authenteō, a rare word found only here in the New Testament. Some argue it carries a negative shade, to domineer or usurp, so that Paul forbids only overbearing authority. That is a serious reading held by serious Christians. But two things weigh against it. Much of the wider evidence for the word in that period, on many scholars’ reading, points to plain authority, though the evidence is debated. And in sentences built like this one, the two activities joined by “or” are normally either both good or both bad, and to teach is a good thing throughout these letters; so Paul is restricting the thing itself, not an abuse of it. The two activities together describe the eldership: teaching and governing (3:2, 5; 5:17).

Where Christians differ: may women be pastors and elders? Egalitarians (Christians who hold that every church office is open to women and men alike) argue that this verse addressed a temporary situation in Ephesus (uneducated women spreading false teaching), so that once women are educated, they may teach and lead equally. They also point to Galatians 3:28, to the women who prophesied and laboured beside Paul, and to the debated meaning of authenteō, and many hold their view precisely because they want to honour both Scripture and the gifts God gives to women. This commentary’s view: The complementarian view is the natural reading. Paul grounds the restriction not in local culture or women’s lack of education but in the order of creation (v. 13) and the account of the fall (v. 14), which apply to all times and places. The same principle appears elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11:3; 14:33–35; Ephesians 5:22–33), and the qualifications for elders assume men (3:2; Titus 1:6). This does not mean women are inferior: men and women are equally made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), equally heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), and equally gifted for ministry. Women may teach other women (Titus 2:3–5) and children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), share the gospel, explain Scripture privately (Acts 18:26), serve as deaconesses or in a diaconal role, and exercise a vast range of gifts. The restriction concerns the office of elder: authoritative teaching and governing of the whole church. Egalitarian brothers and sisters are not enemies of the Bible; this commentary simply judges that Paul’s appeal to creation reaches beyond Ephesus.

The scope. The scope is narrower than it is often made: the gathered assembly (v. 8) and two functions, authoritative teaching and governing. Paul is not saying women may not speak (1 Corinthians 11:5), nor teach anyone at all, nor that they are more easily deceived by nature, or that every woman must submit to every man.

Every disciple sits at one Teacher’s feet. Jesus told his disciples they have one teacher, and they are all brothers (Matthew 23:8). An elder teaches not his own word but Christ’s, as an under-shepherd answerable to the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:1–4). The woman who learns and the man who teaches are both disciples of the same Lord, and the authority Paul restricts is a stewardship, never a possession to boast of.

So may women be pastors or elders? The more likely reading is no. Paul grounds the restriction in creation, “Adam was formed first, then Eve” (v. 13), not in the culture of Ephesus, and in the next chapter an overseer must be the husband of one wife (3:2). The office of elder, with its authoritative teaching and governing of the church, belongs to qualified men. Egalitarian Christians read the verse as a temporary restriction on uneducated women in Ephesus; but Paul does not argue from their lack of education.

What of a woman teaching a Sunday school class, leading a Bible study or reporting on mission? Complementarians draw the line at the authoritative teaching of the gathered church and the office of elder, and churches apply it with some differences. Women may teach women and children (Titus 2:3–4), share their testimony, and explain the faith in many settings, as Priscilla did privately with her husband (Acts 18:26). Many churches also welcome women to teach mixed groups under the elders’ oversight, as long as they are not exercising the elder’s authority. The aim is to honour both the gifts God gives women and the order he has set.

Doesn’t this make women second-class Christians? No, and a church where it feels that way has misunderstood it. A restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person. In the work of salvation the Son willingly submits to the Father, and he is not less God, equal with the Father in nature and glory (1 Corinthians 11:3; 15:28; Philippians 2:6); within the church, the members submit to their elders, and they are not lesser Christians (Hebrews 13:17). The New Testament is full of women honoured for their faith and service: the women who stayed at the cross when most of the men fled, and were first at the empty tomb; Lydia, whose home became the church at Philippi; Phoebe, servant of the church at Cenchreae and bearer of the letter to the Romans; Priscilla, often named before her husband; the women who laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel (Philippians 4:3). Eldership is one calling. The church depends on a thousand others, and on the women who fill them.

What about Deborah, Phoebe and Junia? Deborah was a prophetess and judge in Israel at a time when, as the story itself notes, the men were failing to lead (Judges 4:4–9); she is honoured, but the priesthood of Israel remained male, and her story is not about the office of elder in the church. Phoebe was a servant (diakonos) of her church, likely a deaconess, and Paul commends her warmly (Romans 16:1–2); serving in that way is not the teaching and governing office of elder. Junia (Romans 16:7) is described as well known to the apostles, or well known among them; even if she is called an apostle, the word is used there in the broader sense of a sent messenger or missionary, not one of the Twelve or Paul. None of them overturns the reason Paul gives, which is rooted in creation.

What if a man uses these verses to control or abuse? Then he is defying them. Paul has just told men to lift holy hands without anger; he will require elders to be gentle, not violent and not quarrelsome (3:3); he tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). Headship in Scripture is self-giving love and responsibility, never domination. This passage concerns the office of elder in the church; it does not put every woman under every man. Abuse is never tolerated: a woman being harmed should seek safety and tell the authorities and her church leaders, and a church that protects an abuser or tells his victim to submit to him has betrayed Christ.

In everyday life. If you are a woman, use your gifts in every way Scripture opens to you. If you are a man in leadership, train women to serve, ask their counsel, and honour them publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Adam was formed first, then Eve. The word to watch is “for”: Paul is giving his grounds for verse 12, and they determine how far it reaches. He does not appeal to Ephesian culture or the education available to women. He goes to Genesis. Formed (plassō) is moulded, as a potter shapes clay (Genesis 2:7). God made Adam first and then Eve from him and for him as his helper (Genesis 2:18–23; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). This reason comes from before the fall: it is part of God’s good design, not a result of sin or culture.

Order, not worth. It is about ordering, not worth. Both are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and in Christ “there is no male and female” (Galatians 3:28). And “helper”, which Genesis uses of Eve, is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself (Psalm 33:20; 121:1–2): not the title of a servant but of one who brings what is lacking.

Adam was not deceived. Paul uses deceived (apataō) of Adam and a stronger form (exapataō, thoroughly deceived) of Eve. His second reason comes from the fall (Genesis 3:1–6, 13). It should not be read as a claim that women are more gullible: Paul nowhere says that, men are deceived all the time (2 Timothy 3:13), and elsewhere he lays the fall squarely at Adam’s door (Romans 5:12–19; 1 Corinthians 15:22).

What happened in the garden. The serpent went around the order God had established, approaching Eve and bypassing Adam’s headship, and she was deceived. Adam was with her (Genesis 3:6), said nothing, and sinned with his eyes open, which made his sin, if anything, worse. In the fall, God’s order was reversed, and both parties failed in it. The church should not repeat that reversal.

The man who did not stand by. Paul calls Adam “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14): a pattern, in advance, of Christ. The first man stood silent while his wife listened to the serpent; the last Adam stepped between his bride and the enemy and took the blow himself. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The first man hid among the trees; the second was lifted up on a tree in her place. That is headship done perfectly: not passivity and not domination, but a husband who protects at the cost of his life.

Isn’t the appeal to creation just Paul’s culture talking? That is exactly what Paul rules out by going to Genesis. When Jesus was asked about divorce, he did the same thing: “from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:4–8). Going back to creation is the Bible’s way of saying, “This is not a custom of our time, but how God made things.” If Paul had argued from Ephesian conditions, we could set his instruction aside when the conditions changed. He did not. He argued from the way God made the first man and the first woman, and that has not changed.

How can there be order without inferiority? Look at the Trinity, and at Christ. The Son is equal with the Father in every way, God from God, and yet he delights to do the Father’s will: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). He is not less for obeying. On earth he submitted to Joseph and Mary as a boy (Luke 2:51), and he was not less than them. Order is the way love arranges itself in a family. The world assumes that whoever leads is worth more, and whoever follows is worth less; the gospel has overturned that way of reckoning. “The greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 23:11).

In everyday life. Men, see in Genesis 3 where Adam was standing while his wife was being deceived. Godly headship is not control; it is the courage to protect, to speak and to take responsibility. Ask where you have been silent when you should have spoken. Where you have failed, the last Adam did not: his perfect obedience is counted as yours, and his Spirit gives the courage you lack.

For worship. The Son of God met the same serpent, not in a garden but in a wilderness, and was not deceived. Where Eve was talked out of trusting God’s word, he answered every lie with what is written; where Adam said nothing, he spoke the truth and kept it. The serpent’s first lie was that God was holding back something good. At the cross God held back nothing, not even his own Son (Romans 8:32), and the transgression that began with a lie believed was carried away by the one who is the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet she will be saved. This is one of the genuinely difficult verses in the New Testament, and the first duty is to say what it cannot mean. It cannot mean that women are saved by having babies: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and there is one mediator (1:15; 2:5). “Saved” is the normal word for salvation in Paul. “She” at first refers to Eve, and through her to women generally; the change to “they” shows he means Christian women.

Through childbearing. Childbearing (teknogonia) has three main readings: (1) women will be kept safe physically through childbirth, though saved is normally spiritual, and many godly women have died in childbirth, which no reading of this verse may treat as a sign of God’s displeasure; (2) women will be saved through “the childbearing”, the birth of the Messiah, the offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15, which reads beautifully against verses 13–14, though the Greek “the” need not carry that weight; (3) women will work out their salvation and show its genuineness by embracing their God-given role, of which motherhood is a central example, rather than seeking the role of elder. The third reading fits the context best: the curse on Eve touched childbearing (Genesis 3:16), and the false teachers were apparently forbidding marriage (4:3). A woman is not saved by escaping her circumstances but within them. Reading 2 can be combined with it: the Child born of a woman reversed the curse, and in him women’s ordinary calling is redeemed. Either way, the work of bearing and raising children can be offered to Christ as service (Colossians 3:23).

If they continue. The condition is the sentence’s real anchor: not “if they bear children”, but “if they continue” (menō, abide) in faith. Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9), so these are not payments. Faith, love, holiness (hagiasmos, sanctification, the Spirit’s slow remaking of someone already forgiven, 2 Corinthians 3:18) and self-control are what a saved life goes on showing. Perseverance in these is the evidence of genuine salvation (Colossians 1:22–23), exactly what Paul has asked from everybody in this letter.

What is clear. This verse is not fully clear and good readers differ. What is clear is enough: no woman is saved by anything other than the one mediator.

Where does this leave me if I am single or cannot have children? Exactly where it leaves every believer: saved by Christ, and called to continue in faith, love and holiness. Motherhood is a central example of a woman’s calling, not a condition of salvation. Some of the most fruitful women in the church’s history were unmarried, and Paul himself commended singleness as a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Many childless women are spiritual mothers to dozens. If your childlessness is a grief, it is a real one, and Scripture does not dismiss it: Hannah wept before the Lord, and he heard her. But you are not less in his eyes, and your calling is just as real.

Does if they continue mean I could lose my salvation? No. The condition describes what true faith does, not a test it might fail. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). But he brings it to completion through our continuing, and warnings like this are one of the means he uses to keep us. The person who is anxious to continue in faith is the person God is keeping. The one who should fear is the one who has stopped caring.

In everyday life. If you are a mother, see your work as holy service to God: the meals, the patient answers to the same question, the prayers at the bedside are where your faith is being worked out. And thank a mother in your church this week, especially one who is weary.

For worship. The woman who was deceived was given a promise in the same breath as her sentence: her offspring would crush the serpent’s head. Through the long line of mothers from Eve to Mary, the Saviour came, born of a woman, carried and nursed and raised by a woman. He has redeemed the curse at its root, and every woman who trusts him will be brought safely home, not through her own labour but through his.
verseByVerse.note: One of the harder verses in Paul. Suggested readings include: kept safe through childbirth; saved through the Childbirth, the birth of Christ; or saved while fulfilling her calling. It cannot mean earning salvation.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,<sup>2</sup>for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.<sup>3</sup>This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,<sup>4</sup>who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.<sup>5</sup>For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.<sup>7</sup>For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.<sup>8</sup>I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;<sup>9</sup>likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire,<sup>10</sup>but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.<sup>11</sup>Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness.<sup>12</sup>I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.<sup>13</sup>For Adam was formed first, then Eve;<sup>14</sup>and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.<sup>15</sup>Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Paul sets out who may lead God’s household. Overseers (elders) must be men of proven character, at home, in the church and among outsiders. Only one requirement is a skill: “able to teach”. Deacons, who serve rather than teach, meet the same standard and are tested first.

Then Paul says why it matters. The church is the household of the living God, the pillar that holds up the truth for the world to see. And the truth it holds up is Christ himself, sung in an early hymn: “manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit … taken up in glory.” The rules about wine and money exist so that the pillar stands straight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wanting to be an overseer, or elder, is a good aim, and Paul lists what such a man must be: almost all of it character, tested at home, over time, and in the eyes of outsiders.
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Of some fifteen requirements only one, ‘able to teach’, is a skill; everything else concerns what a man is, and the vices named are the kind a congregation cannot see for years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Overseer’ and ‘elder’ name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7).

Now: Verse 7 gives outsiders a say: what would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 3 sets out who may lead the church, at a time when false teachers had arisen, probably including some of the elders themselves (Acts 20:30). The overseer (vv. 1–7) does a noble work but needs proven character, and only one requirement is a skill. Deacons (vv. 8–13) serve the church’s practical needs under the same standard, tested first. Then Paul says why it matters (vv. 14–16): the church is God’s household, the pillar and support of the truth, and that truth is sung in an early hymn about Christ. The chapter that begins with job descriptions ends with a song, because the ordinary machinery of a church exists to hold up one glorious person where the world can see him.

The setting. In the New Testament, overseer (episkopos, from which comes bishop) and elder (presbyteros, from which comes presbyter) appear to be two names for one office: Paul tells the elders of Ephesus that the Spirit has made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5–7 moves between the two words. Elder stresses maturity; overseer stresses watching over the flock. Churches were led by a plurality of elders (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1). The system of one bishop over several churches developed in the second century.

The saying is trustworthy. The second of the five trustworthy sayings in these letters (1:15; 4:9), most likely introducing what follows, though some take it back to 2:15.

If anyone aspires. Two verbs, both positive. Aspires (oregō) means to stretch toward something. Paul does not treat the wish as suspicious, as though the only safe candidate were the man who has to be dragged to it. It is not pride to want to serve as an elder, provided the motive is to serve Christ and his people.

A noble task. The second verb, desires (epithymeō), is to set one’s heart on, to long for. The task is a work, not a title or a rank. Eldership is hard labour (5:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12), not honour for its own sake. Everything that follows in this chapter is about character rather than ability precisely because the job is not a platform but a labour. And in a culture where church leadership could bring danger rather than prestige, the desire was a mark of devotion: when persecution came, leaders were often the first to suffer, as James was in Jerusalem (Acts 12:1–2).

A flock bought with blood. Why is the work noble? Because of whose flock it is. Paul told the elders of this very church “to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). The overseer watches over people for whom Christ died, and that makes the job both splendid and frightening. The office itself is a gift of the risen Lord: when he ascended on high, he gave shepherds and teachers to equip his people (Ephesians 4:8, 11). A man who desires to be an overseer is asking to become one of Christ’s gifts to his church, which is a noble thing to want, and a humbling one. Christ is the chief Shepherd and the true Overseer of our souls (1 Peter 2:25). He did not merely desire the noble task; he laid down his life to do it, and he still watches over every sheep the Father gave him.

Keeping the office. Ephesus was full of men who wanted the standing of a teacher (1:7). Paul does not respond by abolishing the position. He keeps the office, affirms the desire, and raises the bar, which is a better answer to the abuse of authority than pretending authority should not exist. On leadership in the home, the church, work and the state, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Where Christians differ: how should the church be governed? Episcopal churches have bishops over priests and deacons (three orders); congregational churches vest final authority in the members; presbyterian churches govern through elders in local sessions and wider courts. Each reads the New Testament honestly, and each has produced faithful churches. This commentary’s view: The New Testament knows two ongoing offices in the local church: elders (overseers), who shepherd, teach and govern, and deacons, who serve practical needs (Philippians 1:1). Each church should be led by a plurality of qualified elders, men who meet these qualifications (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5). Apostles were a unique, foundational office that has ceased. Within this, churches differ charitably on how much authority the congregation holds and how churches relate to one another.

What does an elder actually do? He shepherds the flock: knowing the people, praying for them, visiting the sick, warning the wandering, comforting the grieving (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2–3). He teaches, in public and in private, and guards the church from error (Titus 1:9). He leads, with his fellow elders, in the decisions that shape the church’s life (5:17). And he will give an account for the souls in his care (Hebrews 13:17). That is why the work is noble and why it is heavy. An elder is not a board member who attends meetings; he is an under-shepherd of Christ’s sheep.

How do I know whether I should aspire to this? Begin with the desire, and examine it: do you want to care for people and feed them God’s Word, or do you want to be recognised? Then hold your life up against the list that follows, honestly, and ask others who know you well to do the same. Look at what you already do. Men who will make good elders are usually already doing elders’ work without the title: opening their homes, teaching a group, visiting the lonely, praying for the flock. Tell your elders of the desire, ask them to watch and test you, and be content to wait. The call is confirmed by the church, not by the man alone.

In everyday life. Pray for your elders by name today. Their work is noble and hard, and much of it is invisible: the hospital visit at night, the conversation with a couple in crisis, the hours over a passage that you will hear in forty minutes on Sunday. Send one of them a note this week to say you are praying for him, and name one specific thing he has done that has helped you.
verseByVerse.note: “Overseer” and “elder” appear to be two names for the same office.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above reproach. This first requirement is the heading over all the rest. Must (dei): these are requirements, not ideals. Above reproach (anepilēmptos) means there is nothing in his life an accuser could take hold of. Not sinless, which would empty every pulpit, but with no glaring, ongoing pattern of sin that could be fairly charged against him.

Character, not performance. Nearly all of the list concerns character; the single skill is “able to teach”. Any church that chooses leaders for their gifts or their following has turned Paul’s priorities upside down. After the confident, empty teachers of chapter 1, the emphasis is deliberate.

A life the flock can follow. An elder shepherds Christ’s flock as an example to it (1 Peter 5:3), and the sheep learn their Shepherd partly by watching his under-shepherds (1 Corinthians 11:1). His marriage, his table, his temper and his teaching are meant to show, in small and imperfect measure, what Christ is like. There has been one man in whom every one of these qualities was perfect. He was faithful to his one bride, the church, and gave himself up for her; he was clear-headed in the wilderness, self-controlled under every provocation, and hospitable to sinners at his table. A gifted man of poor character teaches one thing with his mouth and another with his life, and the flock usually believes the life.

The husband of one wife. Literally a one-woman man (mias gynaikos andra), the most argued-over phrase in the list. Proposed meanings: (1) not a polygamist; (2) not remarried after divorce or the death of his wife; (3) married; (4) sexually faithful to his wife, devoted to one woman. The fourth fits best. Polygamy was rare in the Greek world, so the first is unlikely; Paul encourages younger widows to remarry (5:14), against the second; and he himself was apparently unmarried and commends singleness (1 Corinthians 7:8), against the third. The phrase concerns present character rather than an audit of a man’s history: a marriage in which nobody can point to unfaithfulness. And the qualifications assume that elders are men, which agrees with 2:12.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced and remarried man be an elder? Some churches forbid it absolutely; others ignore the question. This commentary’s view: The phrase concerns present faithfulness and character, not merely marital history. A man who was divorced on biblical grounds (adultery or desertion by the other spouse, Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15) and has since lived faithfully may be considered. But a man whose divorce was sinful, especially recent, or whose marriage history brings reproach, would not be above reproach. Each case requires wise judgment by the church.

A widower and the past. A widower who remarried is plainly not excluded, and a man divorced long ago, before he came to Christ, may qualify if his past is not a present scandal; the church must not pretend that a man’s history is irrelevant or that it is unforgivable.

Sober-minded. Temperate, clear-headed (nēphalios). A shepherd who is not awake cannot see the wolf. Self-controlled: of sound judgment (2:9; Titus 1:8), not driven by moods or appetites. Respectable: orderly, the same word as 2:9; his days, finances and commitments are in order, and people can rely on him.

Hospitable. Literally a lover of strangers (philoxenos). Inns had a bad name, and travelling Christians depended on households opening to them (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), which means an elder’s family bore the cost of his office. An elder whose home is closed cannot shepherd a flock, because the flock is mostly shepherded around tables.

Able to teach. The one gift-based qualification, which distinguishes elders from deacons: able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). Not every elder must be a gifted preacher, but every elder must be able to teach, whether to a congregation or a troubled man across a kitchen table.

What it does not mean. It does not require that elders be married or have children; it describes how they behave if they are. And these qualities are expected of every Christian; elders must model them.

Does a terrible past before conversion disqualify a man? Not in itself. Paul, a former persecutor, wrote these words, and he had been the foremost of sinners. Above reproach describes the man’s present life and reputation, not a record with nothing in it. What matters is whether he has been changed, whether that change has been tested over time, and whether his past still brings reproach on the church: some offences, such as the abuse of children, rightly bar a man from office permanently, because the trust the office needs cannot be restored and the vulnerable must be protected. The church must judge with both grace and wisdom.

Does this list mean the church is to be led by the respectable? No. It describes a man in whom grace has done visible work, not a man who never needed grace. The respectable man who trusts his own record is not what Paul means, because a heart proud of its goodness is rarely gentle, teachable or safe with other people’s failures (vv. 3, 6). The man who wrote this list called himself the foremost of sinners (1:15). And the list is for office, not for belonging: no one is welcomed into the church by meeting it, because everyone enters the same way, as a sinner received through Christ. Elders must show what that grace produces, so that the flock can see it is real.

In everyday life. Use this list as a mirror. You will not meet it perfectly; Christ has, in your place, and the Spirit who joins you to him is growing these qualities in you. Which is he growing now? If hospitality, invite someone to eat with you this week whom you would not normally invite.

verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a drunkard. Four more, describing how a man behaves under pressure. Drunkard (paroinos) is literally “beside wine”: one who lingers over it. The Bible does not forbid wine; this letter tells Timothy to take a little (5:23). What is in view is the man whose relationship with drink governs his evenings.

Not violent but gentle. Violent (plēktēs) is a striker, a bully. Against it Paul sets epieikēs (Philippians 4:5): gracious, forbearing, the man who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed. An elder deals with people patiently, not domineering over those in his charge (2 Timothy 2:24–25; 1 Peter 5:3).

The gentleness of Christ. Paul appealed to the Corinthians by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1), using the noun from this same word. Gentleness is the character of the Lord elders serve: he would not quench a smouldering wick, a faith barely alight (Matthew 12:20), and he restored Peter with questions by a charcoal fire rather than a rebuke (John 21:15–17). An elder is to be gentle because the church already has a Shepherd who is.

Not quarrelsome. Not a fighter, here with words. Ephesus was full of vain discussion (6:4–5), and it would be easy to conclude that the church needed a leader who could out-argue the talkers. Paul says the opposite: a man who enjoys the fight is disqualified, however right he happens to be. An elder must still refute error (Titus 1:9); the difference is between a contentious spirit and a faithful defence.

Not a lover of money. Money runs through this letter: godliness as a means of gain (6:5), the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils (6:10). Elders may be paid (5:17–18), but they must not be in it for money. A man who loves money will eventually be bought, and everyone will find out what the price was.

What they have in common. Drink, violence, arguing, money: each is a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until it is far too late. You can assess a man’s preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see. Ask his wife, his children and the people who have disagreed with him.

What if my pastor is harsh, controlling or a bully? Then he is failing one of the plainest requirements of his office, and it should not be excused as strong leadership. Elders are not to domineer over the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and a man who manipulates, intimidates, shames people from the pulpit or punishes disagreement is not gentle. If it is a single incident, speak to him privately and humbly. If it is a pattern, take it to the other elders, or to whatever wider body your church answers to. If you have been harmed, you are not being disloyal by speaking up, and abuse of any kind, spiritual, emotional or physical, must never be covered up to protect a leader’s reputation. The flock belongs to Christ, not to the shepherd.

Should Christians drink alcohol at all? Scripture permits it and warns against its abuse. Jesus made wine at a wedding, and the Psalms praise wine that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15). But drunkenness is sin (Ephesians 5:18), and wisdom may call for abstinence: if you have a history of addiction, if drink runs in your family as a destroyer, if you are with someone who is struggling, or simply for the sake of a weaker brother (Romans 14:21). Many godly Christians choose not to drink, and many godly Christians drink moderately. Neither should judge the other, and both should watch that the thing never becomes their master.

For worship. The Lord of glory came gentle and lowly in heart. He would not quarrel or cry aloud in the streets; when he was reviled he did not revile in return. And the one man who never loved silver was sold for thirty pieces of it by a man who did. His gentleness is the strength of a King who has nothing to prove, and it is how he shepherds us still.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must manage his own household well. Manage (proistēmi) is to lead, to care for, the word used of elders who rule well (5:17). The household included family, servants and property, and a man’s leadership at home is a testing ground for leadership in the church.

With all dignity. With all dignity probably describes the father’s manner: he maintains order in a dignified way, not by shouting or force. A house kept in line by fear would meet the letter of this requirement and fail its spirit, and Paul has already ruled out the violent man (v. 3). This concerns children still at home.

For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? Then the reason, put as a question that answers itself. The argument runs from lesser to greater, and it assumes something the modern church often does not: that home and congregation are the same kind of thing. Both are households, and Paul will call the church the household of God ten verses later (v. 15).

Care for. The verb changes at the crucial moment. Paul does not ask how a man will manage God’s church but how he will care for it (epimeleomai), the word used of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:34–35). Church leadership is not corporate management but tender care.

The Son over the house. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). An elder is never the master of the church, only a steward in a house that belongs to the Son, and he must first have learned at his own table what faithful, gentle care looks like.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must have perfect children, or that he is disqualified because an adult child has chosen to rebel. Children have their own wills, and Scripture nowhere promises that a good father’s children will all believe. It means a pattern of godly, loving leadership.

The place where character is known. The principle reaches past elders to everyone. Public competence is easy to manufacture for a few hours a week; nobody sustains a performance in front of the people who see him tired. Ask how a man’s children speak of him when he is not in the room.

Have I failed if my child has walked away from the faith? Not necessarily, and you must not assume it. Every parent fails in many ways, and it is right to confess those failures to God and, where it helps, to your child. But a child’s faith is not manufactured by parenting; it is the gift of God, who calls whom he wills. Adam and Eve had a perfect Father and walked away. Keep loving your child, keep the door open, keep praying without ceasing, and do not turn every conversation into a sermon. Many prodigals have come home years later, remembering a father or mother who never stopped loving them. Leave the outcome with God, who loves your child more than you do.

In everyday life. Fathers: is your leadership at home marked by dignity and care, or by harshness or neglect? Lead out of the Father’s patience with you, not fear of failing; his Spirit gives what you lack. This week, apologise to one of your children for something you got wrong. Children learn what God the Father is like by watching their fathers.

For worship. God is the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He rules his household with perfect dignity and perfect tenderness, never harsh, never neglectful, disciplining his children for their good and running to meet the prodigal on the road. The church is his household, and he has never once mismanaged it. Every earthly father, and every elder, is learning to do in small what he does perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be a recent convert. The last two requirements are each guarded by a warning about the devil. Recent convert (neophytos) is newly planted, our neophyte: however gifted, not yet tested. The church at Ephesus was about ten years old; in Crete, where the churches were all new and every believer a recent convert, Paul omits this requirement (Titus 1:5–9).

Puffed up with conceit. Puffed up (typhoō, related to a word for smoke) means swollen larger than the substance warrants. Give a new believer standing quickly, and you may not be honouring him but endangering him.

The condemnation of the devil. Either the condemnation the devil received or the accusation he brings; most take the first. The sin that ruined the devil was pride, and a man promoted before he is ready is being walked along the same road. Yet because the Son humbled himself, the devil’s condemnation will never touch those who are hidden in him.

Thirty quiet years. The church has a better example of patience than any rule. The Son of God, sinless from the cradle, spent some thirty years in a carpenter’s home before he began his public ministry (Luke 3:23), increasing in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52). Even then, the Spirit first led him into the wilderness, where the devil offered him every shortcut to glory and he refused them all (Luke 4:1–13). If the Lord of the church was content to wait for his Father’s hour, his under-shepherds can wait for theirs.

Well thought of by outsiders. The most surprising qualification. Paul makes the opinion of non-Christians, who see the man when he is not being religious, a formal qualification for office. Not that they must approve of his beliefs; the gospel will always offend. But they must not be able to say he is dishonest, or cruel, or unreliable.

A snare of the devil. Snare (pagis) is a bird-snare (2 Timothy 2:26). A leader with a bad reputation outside the church is already caught: everything he says about Christ is discounted by those who know what he is like.

In the flow. The enemy has already appeared in this letter (1:20; 2:14) and will be named again in 4:1. The qualifications are part of the good warfare of 1:18, and an unready or disreputable leader is a gap in the wall.

How long is a recent convert? Scripture gives no number of years, and wisely, because people mature at different speeds. The question is whether a man’s faith has been tested by time and trouble, whether his character has been seen under pressure, and whether he has shown humility when corrected. In an established church that will usually mean years, not months. Paul himself, after his conversion, spent years in relative obscurity before his great missionary work began (Galatians 1:17–18; 2:1).

Should a famous convert be put on the platform straight away? No, and churches do great harm when they do it. A celebrity, an athlete or a public figure who comes to Christ is a cause for joy, and his testimony may be told. But to give him a pulpit, a book contract or a leadership role before his roots have grown is to do exactly what this verse forbids, and many such men have fallen publicly, to the gospel’s shame and their own harm. Love him by letting him be an ordinary church member for a good long while: learning, serving, being known.

In everyday life. What would your neighbours and colleagues say about you if the subject came up? Be the one who pays on time, keeps his word, and treats the cleaner with the same respect as the director.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons serve rather than teach, but their character is held to the same standard and tested first, as are the women of verse 11; those who serve well gain great confidence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

The gynaikas of verse 11 may be deacons’ wives (so the ESV) or women serving as deacons (compare Phoebe, Romans 16:1). The passage does not settle it; the standard of character is the same either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Missing from the deacons’ list is ‘able to teach’: they serve rather than teach, under standards just as demanding.

Now: Test first, then appoint (v. 10): the order churches reverse to their cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deacons likewise. Same seriousness, different function. Deacons (diakonoi) are servants. The office is often traced to Acts 6:1–6, where seven men handled the distribution to widows so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the word. Deacons care for practical needs, freeing elders to shepherd and teach.

What is missing. There is no “able to teach”: the deacon serves rather than teaches. Everything else is just as demanding. Every deacon who carries a meal or keeps an honest ledger is following the steps of a Servant-King, who emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and whom God has highly exalted.

Not double-tongued. Dignified: serious, worthy of respect. Not double-tongued: literally two-worded (dilogos), saying one thing in one house and another in the next, a real danger for men who move between households hearing everybody’s business.

Not greedy for dishonest gain. Deacons handled the church’s money and gifts to the poor, often with no one checking the accounts. The disciples once had a treasurer, Judas, who helped himself to what was put into the bag (John 12:6).

The mystery of the faith. Mystery (mystērion) is a truth once hidden, now revealed. Deacons need not expound the faith, but they must hold it, with a clean conscience, the letter’s steady link between belief and behaviour (1:5, 19). A man may distribute bread faultlessly while hiding a sin he has not dealt with, and Paul will not have it.

The mystery is a person. Paul names the mystery at the end of the chapter, and it is a hymn about Christ (3:16): not a secret doctrine for insiders but the open secret of the Son of God made man, crucified, raised and reigning. A deacon who holds this faith is holding on to Christ himself, even while he carries bread to a widow.

Tested first. Tested (dokimazō) is the assayer’s word for testing metal: not necessarily a formal probation, but an observed track record. Blameless (anenklētos) is unaccused. Paul’s order is: observe the man, then appoint him. The reverse order has brought many churches to grief.

What do deacons do in a church today? Whatever practical service frees the elders to pray, teach and shepherd. In many churches deacons care for the poor and those in need, manage the church’s finances and buildings, organise care for the sick and the elderly, welcome newcomers, run the practical side of the Lord’s Supper and baptisms, and coordinate the many volunteers who keep a church running. The details vary, and Scripture leaves room for that. What does not vary is the spirit: deacons serve, and they serve so that the Word can run and no one in need is forgotten, as in Acts 6, where the widows were being overlooked.

Is serving less spiritual than teaching? No. The word deacon means servant, and the Lord of the church took that title for himself: I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:27). The seven in Acts 6 were required to be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to wait on tables. Carrying meals to a widow, fixing a leaking roof, counting the offering honestly and driving an old man to church are as much the work of Christ as preaching, and they are often how the gospel becomes visible to a watching world.

In everyday life. Deacons serve quietly. Look for one practical need in your church that nobody has noticed, and meet it without telling anyone.
verseByVerse.note: Deacons (“servants”) cared for the church’s practical needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their wives likewise. The Greek simply says women (gynaikas), which can mean either wives or women; the language does not distinguish, and there is no word for “their” in the Greek. So the verse is genuinely ambiguous, and the choice matters. Two readings are held by serious Christians: (1) the wives of deacons, who would assist their husbands in ministry; or (2) women deacons, often called deaconesses. In favour of the second: “likewise” introduces a new group, as with deacons in verse 8, as though a third category is being named; the qualities listed match the deacons’ own point for point; no qualifications are given for elders’ wives, which would be odd if deacons’ wives needed them; and Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1). In favour of the first: the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph, and verse 12 returns to male deacons as husbands of one wife, suggesting the women of verse 11 belong to them. The ESV reads “their wives”, with a note that the word can mean “women”. Both views are held by faithful complementarians, since the diaconate is not an office of teaching or governing authority over men.

Not slanderers. Slanderers (diaboloi) is the word used of the devil, whose name means accuser. Careless talk about people is given the devil’s own title, which should sober anyone who has ever enjoyed passing something on.

Faithful in all things. The woman to whom you could give the keys, the money and the secret, and sleep well.

Husband of one wife. The same requirements as elders (vv. 2, 4).

A good standing. A promise rather than a requirement: a good step (bathmon kalon), good ground to stand on, respect in the church.

Great confidence. Confidence (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech, the word used of Peter and John before the council (Acts 4:13). Faithful service grows assurance before God and boldness in speaking to others. Paul does not promise deacons promotion; he promises them this. A man or woman who has carried food to widows for years, quietly and honestly, ends up with a settledness in the faith that no amount of study produces on its own.

Boldness that rests on Christ. The confidence lies in the faith that is in Christ Jesus (compare Ephesians 3:12). A faithful deacon grows bold not by admiring his record but because, year after year, he has watched Christ keep his promises in the homes of the poor and the sick.

Where Christians differ: may women serve as deacons? Some say the diaconate is for men only; others allow women deacons. This commentary’s view: Either reading of verse 11 is within faithful bounds. Since deacons do not hold the authority to teach and govern the church (2:12), women may serve in a diaconal capacity, as Phoebe did. Churches should decide wisely and charitably, without treating the question as a test of orthodoxy.

So may my church have women deacons? It may, and many faithful churches do; others keep the office for men and have women serve alongside in diaconal work without the title. Paul calls Phoebe a servant of the church and asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, for she has been a patron of many (Romans 16:1–2). Whatever your church decides, the work matters more than the title. Within a few generations the church had women formally serving in this way, caring for women in need, visiting the sick and assisting at the baptism of women. If your church is divided on the question, do not let it become a cause of quarrelling; Paul has just said that a quarrelsome man is unfit to lead.

How do I share a prayer need without gossiping? Ask three questions before you speak. Is it mine to tell? If it was told you in confidence, it is not, and asking for prayer does not change that. Would they be glad to hear me telling it? If not, keep it between you and God. And what is my aim: that this person be helped, or that I be the one who knows? Often the best prayer request is the vaguest: “Please pray for a friend going through a hard time.” Gossip disguised as concern is still gossip, and the devil’s name is on it.

For worship. The accuser’s name is slanderer, and his work is to spread what will wound. Christ’s name is Advocate, and his work is to speak for us before the Father, covering our sins rather than exposing them. He knows every secret of every household in his church, and he has never once betrayed a confidence or brought up again a sin he has forgiven. He is faithful in all things, and the accuser’s whispers fall silent before the one who has answered every charge against his people with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: “Their wives” may also be translated “women,” that is, women deacons; the Greek can mean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter’s statement of purpose: how to behave in the household of God, the church that holds up the truth. And the truth it holds up is Christ, in an early hymn that runs from his coming in the flesh to his being taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress

The church does not create the truth; it holds it up where it can be seen (v. 15). And the hymn of verse 16 is six passive lines, God doing all of it, from ‘manifested in the flesh’ to ‘taken up in glory’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a city proud of Artemis’s hundred-odd columns, house churches are called the pillar of the truth.

Now: The question to ask of a church is not whether it is impressive but whether it is holding up Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing these things. The letter’s own statement of purpose. Paul intends to come, but he may not, and the letter stands in for his presence, now for the whole church in every generation.

The household of God. This verse is the key to the whole letter. Everything in chapter 3 has been building here. The overseer must manage his own household because the church is one; the deacons serve in it; and now the whole is named. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body, kin, servants, dependants, with an order to it and a head. The church is that, and it is God’s: God as Father, believers as brothers and sisters, elders as stewards (Titus 1:7).

The church of the living God. “Living” has a sharp edge in Ephesus, whose great temple housed an image that could not move, and whose craftsmen made a living selling silver shrines of it (Acts 19:23–41). The Ephesians boasted that their image had fallen from the sky (Acts 19:35). The true God is alive and present among his people, and the Thessalonians turned to him from idols, “to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). And a living God is a holy one. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31), which is why Paul cares so much how people behave in his house: it is not a club with rules but the dwelling of the Holy One.

A pillar and buttress of the truth. A pillar (stylos) holds a thing up where it can be seen; a buttress (hedraiōma) is a support that keeps it from shifting. The temple of Artemis, according to Pliny, had 127 columns, each sixty feet high. Paul takes the vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to a congregation meeting in houses.

The right way round. The relation between church and truth is often turned upside down. The church does not create the truth or make it true. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own, and the church’s task is to hold it visibly in place, which is exactly what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do.

A temple with a cornerstone. Paul had already told the Ephesians what this temple stands on: the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–22). The living God of this verse does not live in a marble shrine; he lives among a people joined to his Son. And the truth the pillar holds up is not finally a system but that same Son, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). A congregation is not primarily a service provider, a campaign or a community centre. It is a pillar of the truth to the degree that it lifts Christ up where the town can see him.

Where Christians differ: does the church stand above Scripture? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse to argue that the church, through its teaching office, is the infallible guardian and interpreter of truth, and that Scripture and tradition together form the rule of faith. This commentary’s view: The church supports the truth; it does not create it or stand over it. The truth is God’s Word, which the church receives, guards, and proclaims (2 Timothy 1:13–14; Jude 3). When a church departs from Scripture, it ceases to be a pillar of truth, as the false teachers in Ephesus showed. Scripture alone is the final authority over the church (sola Scriptura, by Scripture alone). Roman Catholic Christians who see it otherwise often love the church’s long history deeply, and that love is right; the question is only whether the church is the roof or the pillar.

Why do I need to belong to a local church? Because this is what God has made for you to live in. You cannot be a member of a household by yourself. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who believe privately and belong nowhere: every letter is written to a gathered church or its leaders, and every command about loving one another, bearing burdens, submitting to elders, using gifts and sharing the Lord’s Supper assumes you are in one. Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you when you are ill, correct you when you wander or need your gifts. Find a church where the Bible is taught faithfully, join it, and commit yourself to its people.

What if my church is a poor pillar? Every church is imperfect, and Timothy’s church was troubled by false teachers when Paul wrote this. Do not leave over preferences, disappointments or ordinary weakness; pray, serve, and be part of the remedy. But if a church has abandoned the gospel itself, denying the truths about Christ that the church has always confessed, or refusing to submit to Scripture, it has stopped being a pillar of the truth, and you should find one that still is. The question is not whether the church is impressive but whether it is holding up Christ.

In everyday life. Think of your local church as it really is, with its weak points and its awkward people. Christ has built you into this house; are you bearing weight in it, or watching from the forecourt?

For worship. The living God has a house, and it is not made of marble. It is made of forgiven people, gathered in his Son’s name. The temple of Artemis lies in ruins, a single reconstructed column standing in a marsh; the household of the living God still stands in every nation, holding up the truth about Jesus, because the one it rests on is alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness. We confess (homologoumenōs) means by common confession, undeniably. Mystery is a truth once hidden and now revealed; “of godliness” means that this truth produces godliness. And the opening may be a deliberate contrast with the two-hour cry in the theatre at Ephesus: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19:28, 34).
