The mob shouted the greatness of a goddess who could not hear them. The church confesses the greatness of a Saviour who came.

A hymn. What follows is almost certainly an early Christian hymn or creed: six lines, each beginning with a verb in the same form, perhaps in three pairs contrasting earth and heaven, from his coming as a man to his being raised to glory. Every verb is passive: Christ is the subject throughout, and God is doing all of it.

He was manifested in the flesh. The truth at the centre of godliness is a person. “He” (hos) is literally “who”. Manifested is made visible, which means he existed before he appeared; and in the flesh, true human nature, not a costume (John 1:14). The line rules out the two errors the early church had to fight: that he was not truly divine, and that he was not truly human.

Vindicated by the Spirit. Vindicated (dikaioō) is declared righteous, shown to be in the right. Condemned by a Jewish council and a Roman court, he was “declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4): God’s higher court overturned their verdict.

Seen by angels. Angels appear at every turning point of his life, from the announcement to the empty tomb and the ascension (Acts 1:10–11), and the salvation they watched is something they long to look into even now (1 Peter 1:12).

Proclaimed among the nations. The message went to the whole world; Paul himself had been appointed its herald to the Gentiles (2:7).

Believed on in the world. Not merely proclaimed but believed, and this is the least likely thing on the list. The other lines are about him; these two are about what happened next. A crucified provincial was announced to the empire, and people believed it. Nothing in the world’s self-interest explains that. There was no army, no money and no prestige behind the message, only witnesses who said they had seen him alive and held to it under threat of death (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), and the Spirit opening hearts to believe them. Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true, and every believer reading it today is more evidence of the same.

Taken up in glory. The word used of the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11). The hymn ends where he now is, reigning at the Father’s right hand, from where he will come again.

Textual note. Many later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read “God was manifest in the flesh” (theos) instead of “He who was manifested” (hos). In ancient manuscripts, the abbreviation for God (ΘΣ) looked very like “who” (ΟΣ) with a small line added. The earliest and best manuscripts read “who”, and this is the more likely original. The deity of Christ does not depend on this verse; it is clearly taught elsewhere (John 1:1; Romans 9:5; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8), and the hymn itself assumes his pre-existence.

What it is all for. Paul has spent a chapter on the unglamorous machinery of a working church, and then says: this is what it is all for. The rules about drink and quarrelling exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

What is godliness, and how does a hymn about Christ produce it? Godliness (eusebeia) is a life turned toward God in reverence, love and obedience: the whole person living before his face. Paul calls this hymn the mystery of godliness because godliness grows from it and from nothing else. You do not become godly by trying harder to be religious, as the false teachers taught; you become godly by beholding Christ. As we see the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The incarnate, risen, ascended Christ is not only the object of your faith but the pattern and the power of your new life.

In everyday life. When you are weary of the meetings, the rotas and the disagreements about small things, read the six lines aloud slowly, and take one line a day this week into your prayers.
verseByVerse.note: Probably an early Christian hymn or creed, with six lines in three pairs. “He” is literally “Who” in Greek; some manuscripts read “God,” others “Which” (ESV note).

3.text: <sup>1</sup>The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.<sup>2</sup>Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,<sup>3</sup>not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.<sup>4</sup>He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive,<sup>5</sup>for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?<sup>6</sup>He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.<sup>8</sup>Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain.<sup>9</sup>They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.<sup>10</sup>And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.<sup>11</sup>Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.<sup>12</sup>Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.<sup>13</sup>For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that,<sup>15</sup>if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.<sup>16</sup>Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
The Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, following seared consciences that forbid marriage and foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good and to be received with thanks, made holy by God’s word and prayer.

Then he turns to Timothy: the kind of minister who trains for godliness, sets an example, puts the reading of Scripture first, and watches his life and his doctrine, the means by which God will bring him and his hearers safely home.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lie behind the Ephesian error, and the answer to it: what God made is good, and is to be received with thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic: it made holiness a matter of giving things up, and impressed by how much it gave up. Paul answers it not by negotiating but with Genesis 1: everything God made is good, created to be received with thanksgiving (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conscience is seared one small step at a time, each time a man overrules it and says what he knows to be untrue (v. 2).

Now: Giving thanks at the table sets an ordinary meal apart for God (v. 5): neither refuse the gift nor grab it, but take it and say thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 4 moves from the truth the church upholds (3:15–16) to the lies that attack it, and then to the kind of minister Timothy must be. Chapter 3 ended with a hymn to Christ; chapter 4 opens with the voice of spirits that deceive, forbidding marriage and foods, and Paul answers that everything God created is good (vv. 1–5). Then Timothy’s own ministry (vv. 6–16): fed on sound doctrine, trained for godliness, an example to the believers, devoted to the public reading of Scripture, watching his life and doctrine. The chapter that begins with demons ends with a young man reading the Bible aloud to a congregation, and that is the whole strategy of God against the lie.

The setting. The false teaching had an ascetic strand: it treated the material world, marriage and certain foods as spiritually dangerous, perhaps mixing Jewish food laws with Greek ideas that matter is inferior to spirit. The teachers may also have believed the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), so that believers should already live like angels, who do not marry (Luke 20:35–36).

The Spirit expressly says. The word is rhētōs: explicitly, in plain terms, as the Spirit had said through Jesus himself (Mark 13:22) and through Paul’s own warnings (Acts 20:29–30). And there is comfort in that. The church has never been taken by surprise by apostasy. Its Lord saw it coming and told his people in advance, so that when it happens it is not evidence that he has lost control but evidence that he spoke the truth. Some depart, but none whom the Father gave to the Son is lost.

That in later times. Not some distant final period. The New Testament treats the whole stretch between Christ’s two comings as the last days (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and the prophecy was being fulfilled in the room where the letter was read, as it has been in some room in every generation since.

Depart from the faith. The verb (aphistēmi) gives us our word apostasy: a standing away, a deserting of the faith once professed. These are not pagans who never believed, but people who had professed the faith, sat in the meetings, perhaps taught in them, and then walked away from it.

Deceitful spirits. Paul does not treat false teaching as merely a clever man reasoning badly. The men in Ephesus were church people with opinions about genealogies and diet, and Paul says there is something else in the room: deceiving spirits at work behind the teachers (2 Corinthians 11:13–15; 1 John 4:1–3). Satan’s great weapon has always been the lie: he is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44).

The insincerity of liars. The demonic works through ordinary channels: no possession, no darkened room. Insincerity (hypokrisis) is the actor behind a mask: men saying what they know to be untrue, in a normal voice, wearing the face of piety. The devil rarely appears with horns. He far prefers a pulpit.

Consciences are seared. The verb (kaustēriazō) is used of a hot iron, and there are two pictures in it. A slave was branded, marked as belonging to someone; and a wound was cauterised, burned until the flesh no longer felt. These men have gone against their consciences so often that the nerve has died. It is what 1:19 described: first the conscience is pushed aside, then the faith is wrecked. It is done one small overruling at a time, and the frightening part is that by the end it does not hurt.

The same Spirit who vindicated him. The chapter break hides a link. The Spirit who vindicated Christ manifested in the flesh (3:16) now warns against a teaching that despises the flesh. If matter were unclean, the Son of God could not have taken a body, eaten at tables, or been raised bodily from the tomb. Teaching that despises the body is, at bottom, embarrassed by the incarnation.

Can a genuine Christian be deceived like this? A true believer can be confused, misled for a season, and drawn into error on secondary matters; the Galatians were bewitched for a while (Galatians 3:1), and Peter himself had to be corrected (Galatians 2:11–14). What Christ promises is that his sheep will not finally be snatched from his hand (John 10:27–29). The elect cannot be finally deceived (Mark 13:22): the false Christs would lead them astray if that were possible, and it is not. So the right response to this verse is not anxiety about whether you will fall, but watchfulness: stay close to Scripture, stay in a faithful church, and keep your conscience soft. Those are the very means by which God keeps his own.

How can I tell if a teaching comes from deceitful spirits? Not by how spiritual it sounds or how sincere the teacher seems, because hypocrisy is exactly the disguise Paul names. Ask three questions. What does it say about Jesus Christ: does it confess him come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, the only Saviour (1 John 4:2–3)? What does it do with Scripture: does it submit to the Bible, or add to it, subtract from it, or claim a secret key to it? And what does it do to grace: does it rest everything on what Christ has done, or quietly move the weight onto what you must do or avoid? Teaching that makes Christ smaller, the Bible thinner, or grace conditional is not from the Spirit of truth.

Is talk of demons not just an old way of describing bad ideas? No, though the question is understandable. Jesus himself spoke of the devil as a real person who lies and murders (John 8:44), and he cast out demons as a sign that the kingdom of God had come (Luke 11:20). Paul is not being superstitious here; notice how undramatic his demons are. They work through sermons, opinions and diets, not through séances. That is the claim: behind ordinary persuasion there can be a will set against God. If we wave the idea away, we have not become wiser than Jesus; we have only made ourselves easier to deceive. And the remedy is not fear but Christ, who disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

In everyday life. Keep your conscience tender by confessing sin quickly. Notice the small things you have learned to overrule: the unkind remark, the figure rounded in your favour, the thing you watch that you would not watch with your pastor in the room. Go to God about them while they still sting, because the sting is a mercy.

For worship. Against the father of lies stands the God who cannot lie, and against every seared conscience stands the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). It does what no surgeon can, and makes a dead conscience feel again.

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who forbid marriage. We assume false teaching will be permissive; this kind impresses by how much it gives up. These men taught that marriage was unspiritual, which flatly contradicts God’s design: it was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18–24), and who calls the marriage bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4).

Abstinence from foods. Probably specific foods were treated as impure, and behind it lay an old and durable idea, that the material world is the problem. Marriage and food are the two most bodily things there are, so both had to go (compare Colossians 2:21). And it has a pull on the heart that is easy to miss. A religion of rules you can keep gives you something to measure and something to be proud of: it puts holiness within your own control. That is why it impresses, and why it is a do-it-yourself salvation. It looks wise, but it has no power to hold back our sinful desires (Colossians 2:23).

Received with thanksgiving. Paul’s answer is not a compromise about how much asceticism is appropriate. He goes straight to the doctrine of creation. God made food (ktizō, created; Genesis 1:29–31; 9:3), and that single clause dismantles the whole system. If the world is God’s and he made these things deliberately, then refusing them is not superior spirituality; it is an insult to the Giver. And note the purpose he names: God created them to be received (metalēmpsis, a sharing, a partaking). Declining a gift is not humility when the gift was made on purpose for you. The proper response to God’s gifts is gratitude, meta eucharistias, with thanksgiving: the word from which we get Eucharist, an old name for the Lord’s Supper, as though every meal were meant to be a small thanksgiving service.

Those who know the truth. Believers know that Christ has declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). And more: an unbeliever can eat and marry with great pleasure, but he cannot receive them as gifts, because he does not know there is anyone to thank. The Christian alone can taste the bread and see the hand that gave it.

What marriage and bread were made to show. The false teachers banned the two things God has used most plainly to picture his Son. Marriage was made from the beginning with Christ in view: Paul says the union of husband and wife is a profound mystery that refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). And bread is the sign Christ chose for his own body given for us (Luke 22:19). To forbid marriage and food as unspiritual is to tear down the pictures God set up of his Son’s love and his Son’s sacrifice. The Lord himself came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34), and he gave his church a meal to remember him by. A religion of refusal cannot follow a Saviour who gives.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier than marriage? Some traditions require celibacy of clergy, or have treated virginity as a higher spiritual state. This commentary’s view: Celibacy is a gift for some, and can free a person for undistracted service (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35; Matthew 19:12). But marriage is equally honourable and holy (Hebrews 13:4). Forbidding marriage to ministers contradicts both this passage and 3:2, where an elder may plainly be a married man. Neither state is more meritorious before God. The Reformers applied this verse directly to compulsory clerical celibacy, and they were right to: a calling to singleness freely chosen for the kingdom is good; a rule forbidding ministers to marry is not.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid voluntary fasting or personal abstinence for health, conscience, or love for a weaker brother (Romans 14:21). The error is making abstinence a rule that defines holiness.

I am single, and not by choice. Is this verse saying I am missing out on God’s best? No. Paul is attacking teachers who forbade marriage as unholy; he is not saying every Christian must marry or that the unmarried are second class. Your singleness is not a spiritual failure, and neither is your longing for marriage, which is the desire for a good thing God made. Jesus was unmarried, and so, at least in his ministry, was Paul. Bring the longing to God honestly; it is not unspiritual. Meanwhile your life is not on hold: the single believer has real freedom to serve (1 Corinthians 7:32–35), a family in the church (Mark 10:29–30), and the same full inheritance in Christ as any married saint. God’s best for you is himself, and that is not rationed by marital status.

Are there modern versions of this error? Yes, and they rarely use religious language. Any teaching that makes a diet, a regime of abstinence, or a renunciation the mark of the truly spiritual is walking this road: the Christian circle where what you do not eat, drink or own becomes the badge of seriousness; the subtle suggestion that married people are less devoted; the wellness gospel that treats certain foods as defiling rather than merely unhelpful. Self-denial for love of Christ and neighbour is good. Self-denial as a ladder to holiness, or a way to look down on others, is the Ephesian error in modern dress (Colossians 2:20–23).

For worship. Here is the generosity of the Creator against the stinginess of every false religion. The demons forbid; God gives. When Adam and Eve took the one tree, he did not withdraw the rest. And on the night he was betrayed, the Son through whom every grain of wheat was made took bread into his hands and gave thanks for it, and then gave himself, so that the hungry might eat and live for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everything created by God is good. Paul echoes Genesis 1, where God pronounces what he made good, and then very good (Genesis 1:31), a verdict never withdrawn. The fall brought a curse on creation (Romans 8:20), but the curse spoiled how the world works and how we use it. It did not change who made it. A religion that treats the physical as unspiritual is at odds with the first page of the Bible, and with the last, where the new creation has rivers and fruit and a city, and with the middle, where the Son of God took a body and kept it.

Nothing is to be rejected. No food is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14), but the condition is not a formality: “if it is received with thanksgiving”. The same meal eaten with gratitude and eaten greedily are two different acts. Paul does not divide foods into clean and unclean; he divides the ways of receiving them, with thanks or without.

Made holy. Sanctified, set apart for God’s use, by two ordinary instruments: the word of God, perhaps the Genesis verdict just cited, and prayer, thanks before eating. So saying grace, the habit children learn first and adults do without thinking, is a holy act: it sets an ordinary meal apart for God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

The harder way. Paul’s alternative to asceticism is neither to refuse God’s gifts nor to grab them, but to take them and say thank you, which requires you to think about God at the moment you are most likely to forget him. It is easy to remember God in a hospital. It takes grace to remember him at a feast.

Good because it is his. All things were created through the Son and for him (Colossians 1:16), so the goodness of bread, wine, marriage and morning light is Christ’s own workmanship. Before he fed the five thousand he said a blessing over five loaves (Mark 6:41), and every Christian grace at a table follows him. He is not the reluctant God of the ascetics, grudging every pleasure, but the overflowing Father who invented taste and colour, friendship and marriage, bread and wine, and gave them away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anything is acceptable if we say grace over it; sin cannot be sanctified by prayer. Nor does it override love (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Does this cover things like alcohol, or food I struggle with? It covers what God made, received rightly. Wine is among God’s gifts (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11), so total abstinence cannot be made a test of holiness. But receiving it with thanksgiving rules out drunkenness, which Scripture forbids (Ephesians 5:18), and the same goes for gluttony with food. If something has become a master to you, it is not being received as a gift, and the loving and wise thing may be to put it down altogether (1 Corinthians 6:12). That is not asceticism; it is freedom. A believer who abstains for that reason, or for a weaker brother, is obeying this passage, as long as he does not turn his choice into a rule for everyone else.

Is saying grace just a habit, or does it really matter? It really matters, and this verse is the reason. Thanksgiving at a meal is not a superstition that makes food safe, and God does not need the words. But by it you confess before him, and before whoever is at the table, that this came from his hand and not merely from the shop or your wages. You are setting apart an ordinary act as worship. If grace has become mechanical, do not stop; change it. Name one thing on the table, or one mercy of the day. Let children hear you thank God for specific gifts, and they will learn that the whole world is his.

In everyday life. Take one ordinary pleasure today, the first cup of coffee, a walk in the light, an evening with your wife or husband, and receive it deliberately from God. A gift received tastes different from a thing merely taken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good servant of Christ Jesus: fed on sound doctrine, training for godliness, an example, given to Scripture, and watching his life and teaching to the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

Godliness is trained for like a body, by repetition (v. 7), and unlike bodily training its results survive the body, with value for this life as well as the next (v. 8). God is Saviour of all as their preserver, and especially of believers (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Public reading of Scripture came first (v. 13) in a church where few could read: read, explain, apply.

Now: A young leader earns respect by being an example where nobody is watching (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put before the brothers. The verb (hypotithēmi) is gentle: to set before, as a host sets food on the table. These things are the truths of verses 1–5. Timothy’s task is not to innovate, but to serve up what he has been given. Christ sets the truth before us still, by his Spirit and through his servants, and the bread he gives is himself.

A good servant. Servant (diakonos) here means minister. What makes a servant good is not brilliance or a large following, but faithfulness in setting the truth before God’s people: a standard any minister can meet and none can exceed.

Being trained. The word (entrephomenos) is a feeding word, and its form means going on being fed: Timothy is to keep feeding on the truth while he feeds others. A minister who has stopped being fed will shortly have nothing to serve.

That you have followed. Followed closely, the word Luke uses of his own research (Luke 1:3). Timothy had kept close to sound doctrine since childhood (2 Timothy 3:14–15). He was not chasing novelty.

Irreverent, silly myths. Irreverent (bebēlos) is profane, without any sense of the holy; silly (graōdeis) is literally old-womanish, tales told by the fire to keep children quiet. Paul does not even stop to argue with these teachings. Some error should be answered carefully; some should simply be refused a hearing, because it only gains weight when people treat it as worth arguing about. Timothy is told to walk past them. They treat holy things as common, and leave a person less in awe of God than they found him.

Train yourself for godliness. The verb is gymnaze, the gymnasium word, and it means the disciplined, repetitive, unglamorous work of an athlete in training. Paul does not merely tell Timothy to avoid a distraction; he gives him somewhere to spend the effort. The false teachers had their own rigorous training, the training of abstinence; Paul calls Timothy to the right kind: Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship and obedience. Godliness, on this account, is not a temperament some people are born with. It is trained for, the way a body is, by doing the same unremarkable things repeatedly, long past the point where they feel interesting. What, then, is godliness? It is reverence for God that reaches into everything: a life that takes God seriously at the breakfast table and at work as much as in church, because it knows he is there (Proverbs 3:6).

The mystery of godliness has a name. Paul has just named “the mystery of godliness”, and his next words were about Christ (3:16). The secret of godliness is a person. The athlete trains towards a standard; the Christian trains towards a Saviour. That is why the myths must go: they offer spiritual exercise with Christ left out, and it builds nothing that lasts.

If grace trains me, why do I have to train myself? Because God’s grace does not bypass your will; it works through it. The athlete’s strength is a gift: he did not create his muscles or his lungs. But he still has to run. In the same way, it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and that is exactly why you are told to work out your salvation (Philippians 2:12–13). Effort is not the opposite of grace; earning is. You do not train in order to be accepted by God; you train because you already are, and because the Spirit has given you the desire. A Christian who waits to feel holy before he prays will wait a long time. One who prays in obedience finds, slowly, that the Spirit meets him there.

What does training for godliness actually look like? Ordinary things, done regularly. Reading the Bible daily, even briefly, with a plan rather than at random. Praying at a set time and place, using the Lord’s Prayer or the Psalms when your own words dry up. Being in church every Lord’s Day, under the preached Word and at the Lord’s Table, not when convenient but as a fixed point. Memorising Scripture. Keeping close company with other believers who will ask how you are really doing. Practising obedience in the small things: the honest word, the kind act, the temptation refused. None of it is dramatic. That is the point. Athletes do not train by waiting for big races; they train on wet Tuesdays.

In everyday life. Choose one discipline and practise it this week, small enough to keep and specific enough to check: ten minutes in the Gospel of Mark before breakfast, not a vague intention to read more.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bodily training. Read the comparison carefully, because it is not the dismissal it is often taken for. Bodily training, prized in Ephesus with its great gymnasium, is of some value (pros oligon ōphelimos, profitable for a little, or for a little while): a genuine concession from a man who has just defended food and marriage against people who despised the physical. It may also glance at the false teachers’ ascetic regimen, which was its own kind of bodily training.

Of value in every way. The comparison is one of scope: godliness profits the whole person, in every sphere and for all time.

Promise for both lives. Holds promise means it has a promise attached, like a deed. Every athlete knows that whatever he builds will eventually be taken from him; even the strongest body on earth will weaken and die. Training for godliness is the only regime whose results survive the body it was performed in. But do not miss the first half: godliness holds promise for the present life, not only the next. A life ordered toward God is better now: peace with God, contentment (6:6), wisdom, love and purpose, in the plain sense that self-control beats being ruled by appetite, that a clear conscience sleeps better, that love makes richer company than resentment. And it holds promise for eternity: the life to come, the inheritance, the crown (2 Timothy 4:8). Not that godliness earns eternal life, but that eternal life is promised to those whom grace makes godly.

The promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus. Paul uses that phrase at the start of his next letter (2 Timothy 1:1). The promise attached to godliness is life in Christ, already begun and not yet complete. For now, we live joined to him as branches to a vine (John 15:5); in the life to come, we shall be with him in the place he has gone to prepare (John 14:2–3). All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). His own body was broken and laid in a tomb, and on the third day it rose, never to tire or age or die again; because he lives, godliness is not a gamble but an investment with a promise attached, signed in his blood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean godliness guarantees health, wealth and comfort in this life; Paul himself suffered greatly (2 Timothy 3:12), and he will guard the promise against those who imagined godliness was a means of gain (6:5).

Should a Christian exercise, then? Yes, and with a good conscience. Your body is God’s creation and the Spirit’s temple, and caring for it is stewardship, not vanity. Exercise can give you energy to serve, clarity to think, and years to love your family and your church. What Paul guards against is the inversion: when fitness, appearance or performance becomes the thing you are really living for, and the hours at the gym are guarded jealously while prayer and worship are fitted around them. The question is not whether to train the body but which training is getting the best of you. Keep the body in its place: valued, cared for, and second.

In everyday life. Read your diary for a normal week as a training log, and see which part of you gets the best hours. The soul, like the body, answers not to inspiration but to small and steady change: one block of time moved, and kept for a month, will tell.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy. The third of the five trustworthy sayings (1:15; 3:1), most likely pointing back to verse 8. It is a seal: this can bear your whole weight.

We toil and strive. Toil (kopiaō) is labour to the point of weariness; strive (agōnizomai) is the athletic word for contending in the arena. Paul puts himself in the gymnasium with a plural we. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read suffer reproach (oneidizometha); the earliest read strive, and most modern Bibles follow them.

Hope set on the living God. The fuel is hope rather than duty. Hope set is perfect tense: we fixed our hope, and it remains fixed. A man will work himself to exhaustion for godliness because he expects something, from a God who is alive, unlike the image in the temple of Artemis down the road, which could neither see nor hear nor save.

The Savior of all people. A phrase that has caused genuine difficulty. “Savior” and “especially” (malista, which means most of all, or perhaps “that is” or “namely”) must be read together. It cannot mean everyone is finally saved; this chapter has just spoken of men departing from the faith, and the New Testament everywhere assumes a real division. Nor does “especially” mean that believers simply get a better version of the same thing. There are two main explanations. First, God is the preserver and benefactor of all people, giving life, breath, rain and food to all (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; 17:25), and he is the Saviour in the full, eternal sense of believers. The word saviour in Scripture covers rescue and preservation as well as eternal salvation. Second, malista may mean “namely”, so that the last phrase defines which people God saves: all people, that is, all who believe. Read the first way, the verse fits its context exactly. Paul has been defending the goodness of creation against men who despised it. The God who feeds and sustains everybody is the same God who saves believers, and it is the same generosity, going far deeper for those who believe.

The living God has shown his face. This letter has already said how this God saves: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), the one mediator (2:5). He sent his Son and raised him from the dead, and the resurrection is the decisive proof that he is alive. That is why the toil is not wasted.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach universal salvation? Universalists cite this verse to argue that God will finally save everyone. This commentary’s view: The verse itself distinguishes between all people and those who believe, which would make no sense if all were saved in the same way. Scripture plainly teaches that unbelievers will face eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 3:36; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). God is the Saviour of all in that he preserves all, shows kindness to all, and offers the gospel freely to all; he is the Saviour of believers in that he actually rescues them from sin and death forever.

How does this fit with God choosing his people? Comfortably. Scripture teaches both that God chose a people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4) and that he is truly kind to all and sincerely offers Christ to all (Matthew 11:28; 2 Peter 3:9). He gives sun and rain to his enemies; he commands all people everywhere to repent; and he effectually draws those he has chosen, so that they believe (John 6:37, 44). The general goodness is real goodness, not a trick, and it is meant to lead people to repentance (Romans 2:4). Election does not shrink God’s kindness to the world. It guarantees that his saving purpose will not fail, and it is why Paul could toil so hard: he knew the living God would certainly save those who believe. Election is God’s choosing, before time began, of particular people to be saved in Christ, out of his own love and not for anything in them (Ephesians 1:4–5).

In everyday life. If your effort is running on duty alone, it will run out; lift your eyes to the living God and let hope do what willpower cannot. And every good thing in your unbelieving neighbour’s life is the kindness of the God who also offers him eternal life in Christ. Tell him whose kindness it is.

For worship. He feeds the sparrows and the ungrateful, the farmer who curses him and the child who has never heard his name, because it is his nature to give. Every loaf on an unbeliever’s table is a kindness from his hand. And to those who believe he gives what no harvest can grow: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope and an inheritance that cannot fade, bought with the blood of his Son. The God who sends rain on the fields of his enemies sent his Son to die for enemies, and made them his friends (Romans 5:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Command and teach these things. The first verb (parangellō) is to give orders with authority, and the form of both verbs means keep on commanding and teaching. Timothy speaks as Paul’s delegate, and Paul as Christ’s apostle, so the instructions are Christ’s and not Timothy’s own.

Let no one despise you. To despise (kataphroneō) is to look down on someone and count him as not worth listening to. Youth is relative: in the ancient world a man under forty could be called young. Timothy was probably in his thirties, which in a culture that gave authority to age was young for the job he had, and the congregation contained older men, some of whom he had to correct, and some of whom fancied themselves teachers of the law (1:7). Paul does not tell Timothy to assert himself, or to remind people of his commission, or to be tougher. Nor does he tell the church to respect him. He tells Timothy to be so obviously worth following that contempt has nothing to feed on. Christ was the young man despised by the elders of his own nation, and he never once answered contempt with self-assertion.

An example. The word is typos, the stamp that leaves its impression (2 Thessalonians 3:9). Authority in this letter is not claimed; it is displayed. Timothy’s life would win the authority his age could not.

Five areas. Their order repays attention. Speech: what comes out of his mouth and how it is said, the most public thing about him (Ephesians 4:29; Colossians 4:6). Conduct: the whole visible manner of life. Love: the goal of all instruction named back at 1:5. Faith: his actual trust in God, and with it his trustworthiness. And purity (hagneia): chastity, moral and sexual purity, especially important for a young man ministering to women (5:2). Purity is the private one, and the last, and the foundation of the other four. They run from the most visible to the least, and the least visible is where a man’s real character is decided. A young minister cannot make a congregation respect him, but he can earn it where nobody is watching.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “in spirit” after “in love.” The earliest manuscripts lack it.

A copy of the true pattern. Paul received mercy so that Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example (1:16). The example Paul set was Christ’s mercy on show in a forgiven man, and Timothy’s is to be the same. What Ephesus is meant to see in his speech and purity is the work of the Saviour who has laid hold of him, which is what makes the standard bearable.

In everyday life. Take purity seriously where only God sees: the screen at midnight, the private thought life, the friendship that is drifting somewhere it should not. That is where an example is actually made.

In the flow. Verse 12 turns from Timothy’s message to Timothy himself, and the rest of the chapter stays there. In the household of God (3:15) the truth is never carried apart from a life that matches it.

Is this only for pastors? It was written to a pastor, but the pattern is for every believer. Every Christian is watched by someone: children watch parents, colleagues watch the one they know goes to church, younger believers watch older ones. And the five areas are the same for all of us. The particular word to the young applies widely: a teenager can be an example to his parents’ friends, a new Christian to someone who has been in church for decades. You do not need a title to be a typos. You need a life that has been stamped by Christ, so that it leaves his impression on others.

What if people still look down on me, however I live? Then you are in good company. Some despised Jesus, who was without sin. Paul’s instruction is not a technique guaranteeing respect; it is a way of making sure that if you are despised, it is not for good reason (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Keep living faithfully, do not retaliate, and do not try to win standing by louder claims or harsher words. Leave your reputation with God. Over time, a consistent life usually earns trust, but even when it does not, it pleases the One whose opinion finally matters.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was probably in his thirties, young for a church leader in that culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I come. Paul expected to come (3:14), but meanwhile the church had what it needed: the Scriptures and a man to read them.

The public reading of Scripture. Devote yourself (prosechō) is the same word used of the false teachers absorbed in myths (1:4) and devoted to deceitful spirits (4:1). Everyone is absorbed in something; Timothy is to be absorbed in Scripture instead. Public reading (anagnōsis) is reading aloud, and it tells us something easily lost. Many, perhaps most, Christians could not read, and copies of the Scriptures were expensive and scarce. For a congregation, hearing the Bible meant one literate person standing up and reading it aloud to everybody, and that is what Paul puts first. Before explanation, before application: the text itself, read out. This is the synagogue pattern carried into the church: Scripture read aloud and then explained (Acts 13:15). Early churches read the Old Testament and the apostles’ letters (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). A church’s primary act of teaching is letting the Bible be heard.

Exhortation and teaching. Exhortation (paraklēsis) is urging, applying, calling the hearers to respond; teaching explains what the Scripture means. Read, explain, apply: the shape of Christian ministry in three words, unchanged in two thousand years.

Do not neglect the gift. Neglect (ameleō) is to let something lie unused. Timothy’s gift (charisma) for preaching and leading can be possessed and yet wasted, like something left in a drawer; elsewhere Paul says to fan it into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

The council of elders. Two things had happened at that commissioning: something was spoken over him (dia prophēteias, through or accompanied by prophecy; the prophecies of 1:18 had identified his gift and calling), and a group of men put their hands on him. The council of elders (presbyterion, the body of elders, the presbytery) did it together, with Paul (2 Timothy 1:6). The laying on of hands was the Old Testament gesture of commissioning, identification and blessing (Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 6:6; 13:3), and here it is the church’s public act of setting a man apart. The gift came from God; the laying on of hands publicly recognised and confirmed it. Timothy did not appoint himself, and he was not appointed by one man alone. A body of men had publicly identified themselves with him, which is exactly the thing to remember when the job is going badly and a man wonders whether he was ever meant to be doing it.

The reader in the synagogue at Nazareth. The pattern Paul commands has a famous scene behind it. Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, read it aloud, sat down, and said that this Scripture had been fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:16–21). The sermon on that public reading was preached by the One the reading was about. After his resurrection he opened all the Scriptures to his disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, and showed them the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). So when Timothy stands up to read, he is not reciting religious literature. He is reading the book whose subject is Christ, and the reading, the exhortation and the teaching all exist to set him before the church. When the Word is read, the Shepherd is calling his sheep.

Where Christians differ: does ordination convey grace? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches regard ordination as a sacrament that confers an indelible spiritual character and power, and they treat it with a reverence that is right in itself. This commentary’s view: Ordination is the church’s solemn recognition of a man’s gifts and calling, and its commissioning of him to office, with prayer. The gift is from God; the church recognises it. The laying on of hands is a fitting sign, not a channel that transmits grace by the act itself. Scripture names only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

What it does not mean. The role of prophecy here does not mean new revelation continues today; prophecy belonged to the foundational era of the church (Ephesians 2:20). Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers expect prophecy now, and they are brothers and sisters to be heard with respect; this commentary holds that revelation of that kind ended because Scripture is complete.

How do I know what my gift is, and am I neglecting it? Look for where three things meet: what you are able to do that builds others up, what you find yourself drawn to serve in, and what mature believers around you recognise and confirm. That last is the lesson of this verse: Timothy’s gift was recognised by the elders, not merely self-diagnosed. Gifts are discovered mostly by serving, not by questionnaires: say yes to needs in your church and see where God blesses the work. You are neglecting a gift if you know you have been given something useful to others and have quietly stopped using it, through fear, busyness or resentment. Ask an elder or a trusted friend where they see God using you, and start there.

Why does public Bible reading matter if everyone has a Bible now? Because hearing God’s Word together is different from reading it alone. In public reading the whole church sits under the same word at the same moment, the young and the old, the scholar and the child, and God addresses his people as a people. It also guards the church: when Scripture is read at length, the sermon is held accountable to the text everyone has just heard. Many churches now read only a few verses before a long sermon. Paul put the reading first. Listen to it as God speaking, not as a preliminary, and read it well if you are asked to.

In everyday life. Before Sunday, read the passage that will be read in church, and pray for the one who will read and the one who will preach. If there is a gift Christ gave you that you have let slide, pick it up again this week.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Practice these things. Practise (meletaō) is cultivate; immerse yourself is literally be in these things, live there. Godliness is not a weekend interest.

Your progress. The word is prokopē, progress, and Paul expects it to be visible: the congregation should be able to see that Timothy is a better man than he was five years ago. A minister does not need to appear perfect; he needs to be visibly growing. A leader who cannot be seen to be growing is teaching his people that growth stops somewhere.

Watch yourself and the teaching. Two objects, in that order, and the order is the point. His own life first, his character and walk with God; then his doctrine, what he teaches. A man may guard his theology with great care while his character quietly comes apart, and this letter has already shown where that ends: the conscience goes, and the doctrine follows it down (1:19). But Paul will not let either one stand in for the other. A sound teacher with an unholy life will destroy his message; a holy man with false doctrine will mislead. Both must be watched closely, and for life. Paul said the same to the Ephesian elders at Miletus: pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock (Acts 20:28).

Persist in this. Many begin well. The crown is for those who finish.

Save yourself and your hearers. Save here means salvation in the full sense, so it needs stating carefully: there is one mediator (2:5), and no minister saves anybody. Timothy’s perseverance in godliness and sound doctrine is the means by which God will bring him and his hearers through to final salvation; those whom God has chosen persevere, because he preserves them through these means (Philippians 1:6; 2:12–13). Timothy is one of the instruments, and the instruction is to stay usable.

Progress towards a person. The progress Paul wants is growth into him who is the head, into Christ (Ephesians 4:15). A minister’s visible growth is Christ becoming more visible in him: more of the Lord’s patience in his answers, more of his humility in his authority. He watches his life so that it looks like Christ, and his teaching so that it tells of Christ.

In the flow. The chapter began with men who departed from the faith (4:1); it ends with a man told to give himself wholly to the right things and persist in them. Watch yourself and the teaching is the cure for both diseases this letter has diagnosed, a ruined conscience and a ruined faith (1:19), and only a man who watches himself first can safely correct anyone else (chapter 5).

If God guarantees that his people persevere, why warn them to persist? Because the warning is one of the ways he guarantees it. God does not keep his people like parcels in a vault, but like a father keeping a child on a mountain path: he holds the hand, and he also says watch your step. The promise and the command are not rivals. The elect will certainly persevere (John 10:28–29), and they will do so by heeding exactly these exhortations. So if you hear the warning and it makes you watch yourself more closely, that is not a sign you are unsafe. It is the Shepherd’s voice doing what it is meant to do in you.

What does watching my life and doctrine look like for someone who is not a pastor? For your life: a regular, honest look at yourself before God, asking where you are drifting, what you are hiding and whom you are not loving, and confessing it quickly. For your doctrine: knowing what you believe and why, from Scripture, and not absorbing every idea that comes through a feed or a friend. Read a good catechism or confession. Ask questions of your pastor. Belong to a church where both are taught. And do it with others: watching yourself is hard alone, because the log is in your own eye. Give one or two mature believers permission to tell you the truth.

In everyday life. Ask yourself the progress question: what can people see in me now that they could not see five years ago? If the answer is nothing, do not despair: your standing rests on Christ’s perfect watch, not yours, and his Spirit has not stopped working. Begin again today, with the Word and prayer.

For worship. The God who saves is the God who uses means. He could have saved us by lightning; he chose a Book read aloud, a man who keeps watch over himself, and a people who keep listening. And behind every faithful pastor stands the Chief Shepherd, who kept perfect watch over his life and teaching and persisted to the end, and saved, not himself, for he would not come down from the cross, but all his hearers who believe.
