5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
The church is a family, and Paul tells Timothy how to treat its members: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Then widows: families care for their own first (a Christian who neglects his relatives “has denied the faith”), the church supports those truly alone, and younger widows should remarry rather than take a vow they may not keep.

Elders: those who lead well, especially in preaching, should be paid generously (with a saying of Jesus quoted as Scripture); accusations need two or three witnesses, but those who persist in sin are rebuked publicly. Appoint slowly, judge without favouritism, and remember that both hidden sins and hidden goodness will come to light.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church is God’s household, so Timothy is to treat its members as family, in all purity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

The church is God’s household (3:15), and here Paul puts that into practice: treat people as what they actually are, fathers, brothers, mothers, sisters. That rules out both harshness and a timid respect that never corrects anyone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young leader not taken seriously is tempted to be harsher than the case requires (4:12).

Now: ‘As sisters, in all purity’ gives a relationship rather than a rulebook as the safeguard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 5 applies the truth that the church is God’s household (3:15) to its ordinary relationships: treat the church as family (vv. 1–2); support widows who are truly alone, while families care for their own (vv. 3–16); honour, protect, correct and appoint elders with care (vv. 17–25). It is a chapter about welfare lists, salaries and procedure, and it is full of God: the protector of widows, the Lord who sees in secret, the Judge before whom the angels stand. Church administration, in Paul’s hands, is theology with its sleeves rolled up.

Do not rebuke an older man. The verb (epiplēssō) means to strike at, to upbraid harshly, found only here in the New Testament. Older men may need correcting, but this is not how it is done. A young man in authority who is not being taken seriously (4:12) is tempted to compensate, to be harder than the case requires, and Paul takes the option away: you shall stand up before the grey head and honour the face of an old man (Leviticus 19:32).

Encourage him as a father. A gentle appeal, as a son would speak to his father. You do correct your father, but carefully, and never in public.

Brothers and mothers. All four groups are to be treated as family: this is the household of God (3:15) put into practice. Younger men as brothers, with frankness and affection, not lording it over them; older women as mothers, with honour. It rules out both mistakes a young leader can make: the harshness that treats the congregation as subordinates, and the deference that never says anything at all.

In all purity. The phrase is added to one category only, and purity is the same word as 4:12. Paul is a realist. A young minister, possibly unmarried, doing pastoral work with young women is in a situation that has destroyed a great many ministries, and he says so without fuss or embarrassment. His dealings with younger women must be utterly free of any impropriety, in thought, word and action, and of anything that could give rise to suspicion. The safeguard he gives is not distance but a relationship: as sisters, which is better than a rulebook. A man does not have to invent boundaries with his sister; he already knows what is and is not thinkable. Paul asks Timothy to bring that instinct into the church, with a brother’s protective love, which protects the women, protects him, and does not require him to treat half his congregation as a hazard.

The family Jesus named. These words, mothers, brothers and sisters, were first given to the church by Jesus. When his relatives came to take him home, he looked at those sitting around him and said that whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:31–35). Paul’s instruction is that saying put into practice in Ephesus. The church is a family because it gathers round him, and every relationship in it is shaped by his: no believer is a stranger to another, because each has been made a brother or sister of the Son. The eternal Son is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11); the Father has adopted us and given us his Spirit, by whom we cry, Abba. Those who had no family have been given mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold in his house. That is also why purity is not negotiable. No one may treat a woman as anything less than what she is, a sister of Christ.

What practical safeguards does purity call for? The family instinct comes first, but wisdom adds sensible habits, especially for anyone in pastoral care. Avoid situations that would be private and unaccountable: meet in an open office or a public place, keep a door ajar, let someone else know where you are. Do not let pastoral conversations drift into emotional dependence; if they do, involve a wise older woman or your wife and step back. Never send messages you would not want read aloud. These are not signs of suspicion but of love: they protect the vulnerable from harm and the church from scandal, and they make sure that a sister is always treated as a sister.

What if an older person in the church really is in the wrong? Then he must be told, but as a son would tell his father. Go privately, not in front of others. Speak with respect: begin by honouring what is good in him, and put the matter as a concern rather than a verdict. Appeal rather than command: ask him to consider it before God. Be ready to listen, because age often sees what youth misses. Respect for age never means silence about sin, and it never means tolerating harm to others; if the wrong is serious, or the person is unwilling to listen, involve the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). The gentleness is in the manner, not in the content.

In everyday life. Picture your church as the family it is: the widower is your father, the teenager your younger brother, the woman who has been missing for weeks your mother. Phone her.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Widows: families care for their own first, the church supports those who have no one, and Paul sets out who may be enrolled and why younger widows should rather remarry.
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

To neglect one’s own relatives is to deny the faith and fall below the decency of unbelievers (v. 8); caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser duty but where godliness is practised (v. 4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The widows on the church’s list prayed for others night and day (v. 5), and what qualified them was a lifetime of service nobody had recorded (v. 10).

Now: Paul’s remedy for idleness and gossip (vv. 11–13) is not more rules but ordinary life: marriage, children, a home to run (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the ancient world, widows were often destitute. There were no pensions, and a widow without family could face starvation or be forced into prostitution. God himself executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18), a father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5), and the early church continued his care (Acts 6:1; James 1:27). But resources were limited and some were abusing the system. Paul is not inventing a policy; he is protecting one.

Truly widows. Honour (timaō) here clearly includes financial support, as in Matthew 15:4–6 and the double honour of verse 17. Truly widows are those genuinely alone (v. 5).

Godliness at home. The family, not the church, is the first line of support. Caring for an ageing mother is not a lesser, secular duty; it is where godliness is practised, the fifth commandment in practice (Exodus 20:12), the opposite of the excuse Jesus condemned, when people declared their money Corban, given to God, so as not to support their parents (Mark 7:9–13).

Make some return. The language of repaying a debt: parents cared for us when we were helpless; we should care for them when they are. Even the pagan world recognised it.

Pleasing to God. The same word as 2:3. The changed sheets and the hospital visits and the patient repetition of the same conversation are seen, and welcomed, in heaven.

Godliness at the foot of the cross. The Son of God kept this command himself. As a boy he went down to Nazareth and was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). And when he hung on the cross, bearing the sins of the world, he looked down at his mother and gave her into the care of the beloved disciple, who took her to his own home from that hour (John 19:26–27). In the hour of his agony he did what Paul asks of every child and grandchild: he made some return to his mother. The One who fulfilled all righteousness fulfilled the fifth commandment too, and his obedience is counted to believers who have often failed in it. Caring for an ageing parent is walking where he walked.

Does this mean I must have my elderly parent live with me? Not necessarily. The command is to honour and provide, and what that requires depends on the parent’s needs, your own circumstances, and other responsibilities God has given you, including to your spouse and children. For some families, a parent moving in is the loving choice. For others, good professional care is the wise and loving choice, especially where medical needs are beyond what a family can safely give. What Scripture forbids is not using a care home; it is abandonment: leaving a parent unvisited, unfunded, unknown. Whatever the arrangement, stay involved, contribute what you can, visit often, and make sure they know they are loved.

What if my parent was abusive or neglectful? Honour does not require you to put yourself back under harm, to pretend the past did not happen, or to submit to further abuse. You may need distance and boundaries for your own safety and your family’s, and that is not sin. But even then, the gospel may call you, in ways that are wise and safe, to make sure your parent’s basic needs are met, perhaps through others, and to pray for them. Seek counsel from a wise pastor. God sees the debt you never received, and he is a Father who does not fail (Psalm 27:10). Honouring a parent who did not honour you is costly, and it is one of the places where the grace of Christ shows most clearly.

In everyday life. Ask your parents or grandparents what they need this week, and listen to the answer. If they have died, honour them by caring for someone else’s parent in your church who has no one nearby.

For worship. The God of this paragraph is the God who notices widows. He made laws in Israel so that she would find grain left at the edges of the fields, sent Elijah to a widow of Zarephath, and sent his Son to the gate of Nain, where he had compassion on a widow and gave her only son back to her (Luke 7:11–15).

verseByVerse.quote: She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Left all alone. Two kinds of widow now, starkly contrasted. The verb (memonōmenē), from the root that gives us our word monk, means left alone and remaining alone, with nobody to turn to.

Set her hope on God. The verb has the same form as in 4:10: she has fixed her hope and keeps it fixed. Every human prop was taken away, and she found she was standing on the Rock.

Night and day. Night and day is what Paul says of his own prayers (2 Timothy 1:3) and what Luke says of Anna (Luke 2:37). The church is not merely dispensing charity; it is supporting a body of intercessors, praying while everyone else sleeps. A congregation that supports its widows gains far more from their prayers than it gives in money.

Dead even while she lives. The word (spatalōsa) is strong: living luxuriously, pleasure-seeking, given over to indulgence, with a note of wantonness. Some commentators think a few were even selling their bodies to support themselves. Paul is describing a widow with freedom and no dependants who has turned her freedom into indulgence, and the church should not support such a lifestyle. Dead even while she lives is one of the most arresting phrases in the letter. Not dying, not spiritually endangered: dead, present tense, while the body carries on. It is the same verdict Jesus passes on the church at Sardis: you have the reputation of being alive, and you are dead (Revelation 3:1). Her diary is full, but toward God there is no prayer, no hunger for him, no love: like cut flowers in a vase, still bright for a while, but already severed from the root.

Two widows. Both have lost a husband; both have time on their hands. One spends it praying and is alive. The other spends it on herself and is a corpse that has not noticed. The same question is worth asking of every retirement, every empty evening, every free Saturday: on whom is this time being spent?

What Anna’s prayers were waiting for. The widow Paul describes has a portrait in Luke. Anna had been a widow for many years and did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day, and her hope was answered in a person. When the infant Jesus was carried into the temple, she came up at that very hour, gave thanks to God and spoke of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36–38). That is what a hope set on God looks like in the New Testament: it is fixed on the God who has kept his word in Christ. And the woman who is dead while she lives has the remedy every sinner has: God, rich in mercy, makes the dead alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5).

I am widowed and lonely. How can I set my hope on God when it hurts this much? Grief is not a lack of faith. The widow in this verse is not someone who has stopped feeling her loss; she is someone who has taken her loss to God, again and again, night and day. Setting your hope on him does not mean pretending; it means telling him the truth and asking him for help, as the psalmists do. Begin there, even with a few words. Let the church carry you: accept the meals, the visits, the invitations, even when it is hard. And know that your prayers matter. A widow who prays is not on the edge of the church’s life but at the centre of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without reproach. The word used of overseers in 3:2. No one should be able to accuse widows or their families of neglect or self-indulgence; Paul is protecting the reputation of Christian households in a watching city.

Provide for his relatives. One of the fiercest sentences Paul ever wrote. Provide (pronoeō) means plan for: not crisis rescue but forethought, and the closer the relationship, the greater the duty. That is how God provides. He provided for Adam before Adam knew he needed anything; he fed Israel with bread from heaven for forty years; he clothes the lilies and numbers the hairs on our heads. He thought ahead for us before the foundation of the world, and in the fullness of time he sent his Son.

He has denied the faith. Denied (arneomai) is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard (Mark 14:68), a denial not in words but in deeds (Titus 1:16). A man may recite the creed accurately and, by leaving his mother destitute, have denied every word of it.

Worse than an unbeliever. Pagans looked after their own; family obligation was a recognised virtue across the ancient world. A Christian who neglects his relatives has fallen below the ordinary decency of people with no faith at all. Spirituality here is measured not by devotion or ministry activity but by whether the people related to you have what they need.

The Provider of his own household. Neglect denies the faith because the faith is about a Saviour who provides. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, and he nourishes and cherishes her as a man does his own body (Ephesians 5:25, 29). He has never received his people and then left them to fend for themselves. A believer who leaves his own family in want is telling a story about Christ that is not true. A believer who plans and provides for them is preaching without a word the faithfulness of the Son, who is faithful over God’s house (Hebrews 3:6). The family table is one of the places where the gospel is either confirmed or contradicted.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a person unable to provide, through illness, poverty or circumstance, has denied the faith; the point is unwillingness. Nor does it mean only men provide (v. 16). Some families are estranged for grave reasons, and some carers are already at the end of their strength. Paul is writing about people who could and do not, and who have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

Does this apply to a husband who will not work or support his family? Yes, directly. A man who is able to work and support his wife and children and refuses, or who spends on himself what his family needs, is the person this verse describes. Scripture expects able-bodied people to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). A wife and children left in want by such a man are not obliged to pretend all is well, and the church should not pretend either: the elders should lovingly confront him and, if he persists, treat it as a matter of discipline, while making sure his family is cared for. Financial neglect can also be part of a pattern of control or abuse; where it is, the church must protect the vulnerable, not the abuser.

How do I balance providing for my family with giving to the church and the poor? Begin with the order Paul gives: your own household is your first earthly responsibility, and neglecting it is not generosity but disobedience. But provision is not the same as luxury, and the Bible also commands generous giving to God’s work and to the poor (2 Corinthians 9:6–8; Galatians 6:10). Most of us have more room for both than we think, once wants are separated from needs. Plan ahead, as the word provide implies: budget, save for your family’s future, and give first rather than from what is left. Then trust the God who feeds the sparrows to keep his promises to those who honour him.

In everyday life. Christ has never left you to fend for yourself. Is there an ageing parent whose needs you have not planned for, a sibling quietly struggling, a will you have not written? Provision is forethought. Do one piece of it today.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a widow be enrolled. Now the criteria for an actual roll of names: widows supported by the church who in return devoted themselves to prayer and service (v. 5), something like the recognised group of widows we read of in the early church after the apostles.

Not less than sixty. Past the age of likely remarriage and of earning a living: Paul draws the line where genuine long-term dependence begins, and where she would probably not want to leave the role to remarry (vv. 11–12).

The wife of one husband. Literally a one-man woman, the counterpart of the one-woman man of 3:2, and best read the same way: faithful in her marriage. It cannot bar a woman who was widowed, married again and was widowed a second time, since Paul tells younger widows to marry in verse 14.

A reputation for good works. Well attested: a track record known to all, and it is a list of unglamorous things. Bringing up children, her own or perhaps orphans she took in; hospitality, opening her house, as the overseer must (3:2).

Washed the feet of the saints. The lowest job in the household, given to the least slave, and the one Jesus did in the upper room. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he rose from supper, tied a towel round himself and washed his disciples’ feet, and then told them that they also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:3–5, 14; compare Luke 7:44). The widow on Paul’s list has simply done what her Lord said and did: the Lord of glory set the pattern with a basin, and she has spent a lifetime following it. The phrase stands for every kind of humble service, and it is the plainest proof that a woman has learned Christ.

Cared for the afflicted. Those in distress: the sick, the poor, the persecuted. Before she needed help she gave it, which is precisely why the church now owes her.

Every good work. Not one item is public, spectacular or recorded anywhere. A woman is put on the roll because of a lifetime of things nobody wrote down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should refuse help to widows under sixty or without this record; these are criteria for the enrolled list, not for emergency help (Galatians 6:10).

Should churches keep a list of widows today? Churches today rarely keep a formal roll, and nothing here requires one. Much of what the list did is now partly met by pensions and state provision. But the principle remains: real need, met first by family and then by the church, with care to support those who are genuinely alone, and wisdom to make support a blessing rather than a trap. Many churches meet this through deacons, who know the widows and the needy by name and make sure no one is overlooked (Acts 6:1–6). And the honour remains: older women who have given a lifetime of quiet service should be valued, visited and drawn on for their wisdom and prayer, not left at the edge.

In everyday life. The Lord who knelt with a basin for you is at work in you by his Spirit; begin the kind of record this list describes: a meal taken round, a guest welcomed, a sick friend sat with. Do one this week, and tell no one.

For worship. Heaven’s list of honour is not the world’s. God does not record the speeches and the titles; he records the cup of cold water, the guest made welcome, the night by a sickbed. Nothing done for his people is forgotten by him (Hebrews 6:10). On the last day the King himself will read the list aloud, and to women whose names were never written anywhere but in his book he will say that what they did for the least of his brothers they did for him (Matthew 25:40). The Lord who served will honour those who served, and their reward will be himself.
verseByVerse.note: There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in turn served it.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refuse younger widows. These three verses are the difficult ones. Refuse is the verb used of the silly myths in 4:7. Paul uses it here not because younger widows are less worthy, but for their own good.

Passions draw them away. The verb (katastrēniasōsin) means to grow restless against something. The desire for marriage is not wrong (v. 14), but here it pulls them away from a commitment made to Christ.

Their former faith. That sounds at first like a condemnation of remarriage, until verse 14, where Paul tells these same younger widows to marry. So he plainly is not against it. Something else is going on, and the phrase former faith (tēn prōtēn pistin, their first pledge) is the clue. Most likely, enrolled widows made a pledge to devote themselves to Christ and the church’s service for the rest of their lives, without remarrying. A young woman who makes that commitment and later finds she cannot keep it has broken a promise. The problem is the broken pledge, not the marriage: it brings condemnation (here meaning God’s censure) because the pledge was a vow made to God (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). A vow is spoken to the holy God, who is in heaven while we are on earth (Ecclesiastes 5:2), and he does not treat our words as lightly as we do. Paul is being realistic here, not harsh. He judges that a woman in her twenties or thirties should not be asked to bind herself for life, because many will not manage it and the failure will damage them. The kindest policy is not to let them make the vow.

They learn to be idlers. The verb is learn: the arrangement itself teaches them idleness. Put a young woman on a stipend with no dependants, no work and no structure, and she will fill the days somehow: going from house to house, perhaps under the guise of ministry, the route the false teachers also used (2 Timothy 3:6).

Gossips and busybodies. Busybodies (periergoi) are meddlers, the word Paul used of idle men at Thessalonica: not busy, but busybodies (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Saying what they should not may mean spreading the false teaching, or private matters learned in visiting homes. The diagnosis is not really about women: idleness is never neutral. Remove a person’s proper work and the energy goes into other people’s affairs, and Paul’s remedy is correspondingly practical: give them something real to do.

The pledge Christ never breaks. Our promises to Christ are fragile; his to us are not. God swore by himself to Abraham, and he has never once broken his word. Having loved his own, he loved them to the end (John 13:1); if we are faithless, he remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:13). So a woman who had broken her pledge was not beyond hope: the Lord she failed is the Lord who restored Peter after three denials.

What it does not mean. It does not mean younger widows are worse people. Nor does condemnation mean loss of salvation; it is the censure due to a broken vow.

How do I know if I am gossiping? Ask three questions before you speak about someone who is not present. Is it true, and do I actually know it, or am I passing on what I heard? Is it mine to tell, or was it shared in confidence, or is it simply none of my business? And would I say it the same way if the person were standing here? Gossip often wears the clothes of concern: let me tell you so you can pray. If you genuinely need help with a situation, go to someone who can help, such as an elder, not to someone who will merely enjoy knowing. And when someone brings gossip to you, you can kindly stop it: ask whether they have spoken to the person directly.

Does this teach that Christians should not make lifelong vows? No. Marriage is a lifelong vow, and so is the covenant made in church membership. What Paul warns against is binding people, especially the young, to vows they are unlikely to keep and that Scripture does not require, such as lifelong celibacy. He is wary of the very thing the false teachers promoted in 4:3. Vows to God are serious and must be kept (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5), which is exactly why they should not be made lightly. Jesus warns against rash oaths (Matthew 5:33–37). Make the promises God asks of you, keep them by his grace, and do not add others that he has not asked for.

In everyday life. If you have unstructured time, give it somewhere good to go before it finds somewhere bad.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Younger widows marry. I would have is a word of direction (2:8): Paul prefers remarriage. Against the false teachers who forbade marriage (4:3), his answer to a pastoral risk is not more restriction but ordinary life: a husband, children, a household to run. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is lawful (Romans 7:2–3), provided it is in the Lord, that is, to a fellow believer (1 Corinthians 7:39).

Bear children, manage their households. Manage their households (oikodespotein) is a strong word: to rule the house (Proverbs 31:10–31). A modern reader may hear this as small; Paul does not. Running a household is a calling from God with real authority in it, and a far better use of a life than drifting from house to house.

No occasion for slander. Occasion (aphormē) began as a military word for a base of operations. The church is watched, by human enemies or by Satan, and its arrangements can hand them ammunition (3:7).

Strayed after Satan. This is not hypothetical: some younger widows had already turned aside (1:6), perhaps to immorality, perhaps to the false teachers (4:1).

A believing woman. The duty of verse 8 is not the men’s alone. Care for is the word of verse 10: what the widow once did, others now do for her.

Let the church not be burdened. Every family that supports its own frees the church’s resources for the women who have nobody. This is not meanness; it is the arithmetic of love. A congregation that carries people whose families could carry them will run out before it reaches the destitute.

Homes that carry the Saviour’s name. Paul gives Titus the same concern about young wives: that the word of God may not be reviled, and that believers may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:5, 10). A Christian household is a public sign of what the gospel does. The street that never reads Paul can read a home: a widow given a new start, children raised in love, a house run with order and kindness. When such homes collapse into idleness and scandal, it is Christ’s name that is mocked. When they flourish, the watching city sees in ordinary kitchens what the Saviour does with lives he has taken in hand.

What it does not mean. It does not command every younger widow to remarry; singleness remains honourable (1 Corinthians 7:8, 40).

How does this apply today? Families first, then the church, for members in real need who have no family to help (v. 8). (See James 1:26–27 for the fuller answer.)

Is it disloyal to my late husband or wife to remarry? No. Marriage is for this life; death ends the bond (Romans 7:2), and Jesus taught that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30). Paul here actively encourages remarriage for younger widows, and it was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone. Love for a spouse who has died is not betrayed by a new marriage; many find that a good first marriage prepared them to love again. Take time, grieve honestly, seek counsel, and marry only in the Lord. And be patient with children or friends who find it hard; their grief may move at a different pace.

In everyday life. Is there a widow in your family or church you could help this week? Ask her what would actually help: a lift to the shops, help with paperwork, an evening of company.

For worship. God is the great Householder who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6). He does not despise ordinary life; he fills it with his presence, so that a kitchen and a nursery can be as holy as a temple. And over every widow stands the Bridegroom whose Bride will never be widowed, because he died and rose, and is coming back for her.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elders: how to pay, protect, rebuke and appoint them, with a word about Timothy’s health, and the assurance that neither sins nor good works stay hidden.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 introduces both Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus recorded at Luke 10:7 with ‘the Scripture says’; on the most natural reading, this is among the earliest signs that the written words of Jesus were already counted as Scripture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An elder is protected from loose accusations (v. 19), but not from open rebuke if he persists in sin (v. 20); a church needs both verses.

Now: Verse 23 shows Paul correcting a good man who was being stricter with himself than God required, and verse 25 promises that unrecorded goodness cannot stay hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders who rule well. Elders hold the office of 3:1–7. Rule (proistēmi) is the household word of 3:4, with a father’s care in it. Not all lead equally well; those who do deserve recognition.

Double honor. Honour is the word of verse 3, where it included money, and the two quotations that follow are both about paying workers, which settles it. Double probably means ample, or honour in two forms, respect and pay: support that is generous and not grudging.

Preaching and teaching. Labour is kopiaō, work to exhaustion. Whatever pulpit work looks like from a pew, it is not restful. All elders must be able to teach (3:2), but “especially” implies that some give themselves particularly to the word, and these deserve support.

Do not muzzle an ox. The first quotation is from the law (Deuteronomy 25:4): oxen threshing grain must be free to eat as they worked. As in 1 Corinthians 9:9–11, if God cares that an ox is fed from its labour, how much more those who labour in the gospel.

The laborer deserves his wages. The second is not from the Old Testament at all. These are the words of Jesus as recorded in Luke 10:7 (compare Matthew 10:10). On the most natural reading, “the Scripture says” covers both quotations, so Paul places a saying of Jesus, apparently in its written form in Luke, alongside Deuteronomy and calls both Scripture. Some scholars take the second line as a well-known saying simply added on, and those who date the letter after Paul’s death read it differently. But if Paul wrote it, as this commentary holds, it is one of the earliest signs that the words of Jesus were already received as Scripture alongside the Old Testament, stated without argument, as something his readers would accept. Peter does the same with Paul’s letters (2 Peter 3:16). The Law of Moses and the sayings of Jesus are bound together by the one Spirit into one Scripture, so that the voice from Sinai and the voice of the Lord Jesus are the voice of the same God.

The Lord of the harvest pays his workers. The saying Paul quotes was spoken as Jesus sent out the seventy-two (seventy in some manuscripts and the KJV) ahead of him. He told them to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers, and then to eat what the houses that received them provided, for the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:2, 7). The workers were his, the harvest was his, and their bread was to come from the people they served. So a church that supports its preachers is not hiring staff or doing them a kindness. The risen Lord is feeding the men he sent, through the people he sent them to, and he himself called it wages.

In the flow. The word honour joins the elders (vv. 17–25) to the widows of verse 3. Chapter 3 said what an elder must be; this passage says how the church treats one, supported and accountable.

Where does the idea of teaching and ruling elders come from? From the especially of this verse, which implies that some elders laboured in preaching and teaching and some did not, or not to the same degree. Presbyterian churches speak of teaching elders (ministers) and ruling elders; many Baptist and independent churches speak simply of elders, some of whom are set apart and paid to preach. Both read this verse honestly, and both agree on the essentials: there is one office of elder, all must be able to teach, and some give themselves especially to the ministry of the word and should be supported to do it. Faithful churches differ on the details of government, and this text does not settle them all.

How much should a church pay its pastor? Scripture gives no figure, but it gives a spirit: double honour, ample and not grudging. A good test is whether the pastor can live without distraction at a level comparable to the people he serves, provide for his family (5:8), offer hospitality (3:2) and buy books, without either luxury or anxiety. A church that keeps its minister poor to keep him humble has misread this verse, and so has a minister who demands more than his people can bear. Many churches set the salary in relation to the average income of the congregation. And remember that honour includes more than money: respect, prayer, encouragement and a willingness to be taught.

In everyday life. Write your pastor a note naming one specific way God has used his preaching in your life. A single sentence of specific thanks can carry a tired man for a month.
verseByVerse.note: The two sayings come from Deuteronomy and from Jesus’ words as recorded in Luke, a sign that the Gospels were already being received as Scripture.

parallels.desc: You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A charge against an elder. A man in public office is a target, and accusations cost the accuser nothing and can end a ministry before anything is established. Timothy is not to open proceedings on the word of one person.

Two or three witnesses. The rule comes from the law (Deuteronomy 19:15), applied by Jesus to church discipline (Matthew 18:16) and by Paul (2 Corinthians 13:1). It is not indifference to wrongdoing but the ordinary requirement of justice; a church that ignores it will destroy good men on rumour.

Those who persist in sin. But the protection is not a shelter for sin. The form of the verb means those who keep on sinning after being dealt with, most likely elders, though perhaps any member. This is not a first response.

In the presence of all. Rebuke (elenchō) means expose, convict, reprove. In the presence of all means publicly, before the church, or possibly before the other elders. Leaders sin publicly in the sense that their sin affects the whole church; the correction must be equally public. That reverses a common instinct, which is to protect the institution: settle it quietly, move the man on, tell nobody. Is that not humiliating? It is meant to be sobering, not cruel. It comes only after private warnings have been refused, and its aim is the man’s repentance and the flock’s safety, not his ruin (Galatians 6:1).

That the rest may stand in fear. A healthy fear of sinning: leaders are accountable (James 3:1). Hold the two verses together: an elder is hard to accuse, and his office is no place to hide. A church that keeps only verse 19 makes leaders untouchable; one that keeps only verse 20 lets any grievance ruin a man.

The trial where the rule was broken. The law Paul cites was broken once in a way that changed history. At the trial of Jesus the chief priests sought testimony against him and found none; many bore false witness against him, and their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:55–59). No two witnesses could be found to agree, and the one wholly innocent man was condemned in the end for his own confession that he is the Christ (Mark 14:61–64). So a church that refuses to condemn on rumour is honouring its Lord, who knows from the inside what a false accusation is. And a church that openly rebukes persistent sin honours him too, because he is the holy Head of the church, and its leaders carry his name.

What it does not mean. It does not mean elders are above correction; the opposite. Nor does it mean that a victim’s report of abuse should be dismissed for lack of witnesses; corroborating evidence, patterns of behaviour and the testimony of multiple victims can serve as witnesses, and civil authorities must be involved in criminal matters (Romans 13:1–4). The principle is careful justice, protecting both the accused and the vulnerable.

I have been harmed by a church leader and there were no other witnesses. Will I be believed? You should be heard, carefully and seriously, and this verse must never be used to silence you. The two or three witnesses rule concerns what is needed to establish a charge, not whether a report may be made or investigated. Abuse usually happens in private, and Scripture’s own standard allows for evidence beyond eyewitnesses: patterns of behaviour, other people who come forward, messages, records. If the matter involves a crime, report it to the police; the church must not handle criminal abuse internally, and should help you do so. Speak to another elder or a trusted leader outside the situation. God is the defender of the oppressed, and a church that protects an abuser to protect its reputation has abandoned this very passage.

What should I do if I hear an accusation against my pastor? Do not repeat it. If someone brings it to you, ask whether they have spoken to the person directly or to the other elders, and encourage them to do so, or to go to the authorities if it is criminal. If you yourself have a concern, take it to the elders, not to the congregation or social media. Then pray, and wait for a fair process. Being slow to believe an accusation is not the same as refusing to believe it; it means letting the truth be established before you act on it, as you would want done for yourself.

For worship. God is perfectly just. He never condemns the innocent and never clears the guilty, and his courtroom has no favourites and no cover-ups. He hears the cry of the wronged when no human witness stood with them. And the Son who was falsely accused was also openly shamed: stripped, mocked and lifted up in the presence of all, as if he were the one who had persisted in sin. He bore that public rebuke for the hidden and the open sins of his people, so that those who come to him may stand before God without fear, and need never hide again.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the presence of God. This is one of the two most solemn sentences in the letter (the other is 6:13), and the solemnity is the point. It is an oath-like formula (2 Timothy 4:1). Paul swears Timothy in, as a witness is sworn before testifying, and he names three parties watching: God, Christ Jesus, and the elect angels. The angels are the surprising item. The elect angels are the angels who did not fall with Satan, kept by God’s choice (contrast 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Paul mentions them elsewhere as observers of church life (1 Corinthians 4:9; 11:10; Ephesians 3:10), and they will accompany Christ at the judgment (Matthew 25:31). The picture is of a courtroom with an unseen gallery: what Timothy does about a difficult elder is done in front of a congregation that includes more than he can see. They watch the little church in Ephesus, and the little church you belong to, because there the manifold wisdom of God is on display.

Keep these rules. Charge (diamartyromai) is solemnly testify. Why such weight for church administration? Because of what Paul is guarding against.

Without prejudging. Prejudging (prokrima) is having decided in advance; partiality (prosklisis) is literally leaning toward, favouritism. Do not favour friends, the wealthy, the influential, or those you like. God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11; James 2:1–9; Deuteronomy 1:17). Timothy will like some of these elders and find others difficult. When a charge comes in, he will know before he hears it which way he wants it to go, and that is exactly what Paul puts him under oath about. Rules for discipline are easy to write and easy to keep when the accused is a stranger. The test is the case where you already know whose side you are on, and Paul’s answer is not a better procedure but a reminder of who is watching.

Before Christ Jesus, the Judge without favourites. Paul uses the same oath in his last letter, and there he adds who Christ Jesus is: the one who is to judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4:1). Timothy must judge without partiality because the Lord watching him has none. Even his enemies admitted it. Meaning to trap him, they told him that he was true, did not care about anyone’s opinion, and was not swayed by appearances (Mark 12:14). It was flattery, and it was exactly right. He welcomed a despised tax collector and let a rich man walk away sorrowful, and in each case he looked at the heart. A church leader who refuses favouritism is copying his Lord.

What does it mean that angels are elect? It means God chose and kept some angels so that they did not fall when Satan and others rebelled. Their standing, like ours, rests on God’s sovereign choice, not on their own strength. That is a quiet confirmation of the doctrine of election: even in heaven, those who stand, stand by grace. But there is a difference. The elect angels never fell and so needed no Saviour; elect sinners fell and were redeemed by Christ, who became man, not angel, to save us. That is why the angels look on with wonder at the church (Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12). They have seen God’s power and holiness from the beginning; in us they see his mercy.

How do I avoid partiality when someone I love is involved? Admit the bias first; you cannot correct what you will not name. Then put distance between your feelings and the decision: hear both sides fully before you form a view, ask what you would conclude if the names were reversed, and involve others who do not share your attachment. In church matters, a leader with a close relationship to someone involved should often step back from the decision altogether. And remember, as Paul tells Timothy, who is watching. Fairness is not coldness; it is loving everyone involved, including the person who is not your friend, enough to give them the same justice.

In everyday life. Look today for where you have already decided before you have heard, about a colleague, a family member, someone in church you find difficult, and go and hear the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be hasty. The laying on of hands is, in context, ordination: the public act by which the church sets a man apart, as the elders did over Timothy himself (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). Some have thought it refers to restoring repentant sinners, but the context of elders favours ordination. This picks up 3:6, where a recent convert must not be made an overseer lest he be puffed up and fall, and 3:10, where deacons must first be tested. Take time to observe a man’s life before appointing him. Ephesus needed leaders; the church was under pressure and its existing teachers were part of the problem. The temptation to fill posts fast would have been considerable, and Paul says no. The pressure is usually a matter of the heart before it is a practical one. A church that wants to look successful, or a leader who wants to be rid of a burden quickly, will see gifts and overlook character, because gifts can be put to work at once.

The sins of others. Take part (koinōneō) means be a partner: a man who ordains hastily is implicated in what the ordained man does, because he put him there (2 John 11). He cannot later say he could not have known; with proper testing (3:10) he often could, and haste is itself the fault.

Keep yourself pure. Pure (hagnos): free from complicity in others’ sins, and personally holy. A man who appoints carelessly does not stay clean. Personal holiness is often kept or lost in decisions that look like mere procedure.

The Lord who chose after a night of prayer. Before he chose the twelve, Jesus spent the whole night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12–13). He knew all hearts and still did not appoint in a hurry; the church, which knows far less, has more reason to wait. Elders who ordain act as servants of the ascended Christ, who gives shepherds to his church (Ephesians 4:11), and haste presumes to know his choice before he has shown it. And this is our comfort: the Head of the church is never deceived. Men may be hasty, but he is not, and he keeps his church even through our mistakes.

What it does not mean. A church that acted with care is not guilty of the sin of a man who later fell. Nor does it mean we must keep away from sinners; Jesus ate with them (Luke 15:1–2).

How long should a church take before appointing someone? Scripture sets no fixed period, but it sets a principle: long enough for the man’s character to be genuinely known (3:2–7, 10). That usually means years of observed faithfulness, not months of enthusiasm. A gifted speaker can impress quickly; the qualities Paul lists, self-control, a well-ordered home, a good reputation with outsiders, gentleness, can only be seen over time. Talk to his wife, his colleagues, those he has served under. Watch how he handles disappointment and correction. The greater the responsibility, the longer the testing. And the same applies, in proportion, to youth leaders, small group leaders and anyone entrusted with the vulnerable.

In everyday life. Before you recommend someone, for a church post, a job or a reference, take time to know them well: your endorsement is a responsibility.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drink only water. It is one of the strangest verses in the New Testament: a piece of medical advice dropped into a passage about elders and discipline. The word (hydropotei) means be a water-drinker. Timothy apparently abstained from wine entirely. Probably he did it on principle. Paul has just told him to keep himself pure (v. 22), and this letter’s opponents were ascetics who forbade marriage and food (4:3). A conscientious young minister in that environment, wanting to be above reproach and not a drunkard like the men excluded in 3:3, might well have gone teetotal to be safe, at some cost to a body that was already often unwell. Paul’s next words show that purity does not require asceticism.

A little wine. Water was often contaminated, and wine was used medicinally (Luke 10:34). Paul does not argue theology; he says take a little, for your stomach. Paul is careful in both directions. “A little” gives no licence for heavy drinking, and he makes no rule that everyone must drink: those who abstain are not wrong (Romans 14:21).

Frequent ailments. Timothy was often sick, and Paul answers with an ordinary remedy (compare Philippians 2:25–27).

A window into a friendship. The verse also says something about the man who wrote it. Paul has been dictating solemn instructions about elders, witnesses and the elect angels, and in the middle of it he remembers that his friend is unwell and stops to say so. It is the same apostle who asked for his cloak and his parchments (2 Timothy 4:13). Great theology and ordinary care for a person’s body sit in the same paragraph without embarrassment. And there is a lesson for those whose conscience is stricter than God’s word. Timothy’s mistake was a good man’s mistake: trying to be blameless and overshooting into something that damaged him. Paul does not praise the strictness. He tells him to stop.

A high priest who knows weakness. The Son of God had a body that hungered (Matthew 4:2), slept exhausted in a boat (Mark 4:38) and thirsted on the cross (John 19:28). We have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and the word there is Paul’s word for Timothy’s ailments. Timothy’s stomach was not beneath Christ’s notice, and neither was the humble remedy (Psalm 104:15).

For worship. The God of all glory cares about a young man’s stomach. The Spirit who inspired the mystery of godliness also inspired a sentence about indigestion, so that we would never imagine our bodies are beneath his notice. The Lord who touched lepers and took a fevered woman by the hand has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, and one day he will raise these weak and ailing bodies in power, with no more frequent ailments, no more pain, and no more death.

Why did Paul not simply heal Timothy? Even the apostle who had done extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) did not heal at will, and here he prescribes a remedy for his closest friend. He left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God does not always heal miraculously, illness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith, and using medicine is no lack of trust. The miracles of the apostles were signs confirming the message in the founding era (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Christians differ on whether gifts of healing like the apostles’ continue; this commentary holds that those signs belonged to the founding era, while honouring brothers who expect them now. Today we pray for the sick, and God often answers, sometimes beyond what doctors expect (James 5:14–15); but we also take the medicine, and both are ways of looking to him.

I am often unwell, like Timothy. Does it mean God is displeased with me, or that I am less useful? No. Timothy was one of the most trusted men in the apostolic church, and he was frequently ill. Paul himself served with a thorn in the flesh that God would not remove, because his power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Illness can limit what you do, and that is a real grief, but it does not lower your standing before God or your worth to his church. Use the means: rest, see the doctor, take what helps. Bring the weakness to God honestly. And serve in the ways your strength allows; prayer offered from a sickbed is not second-class ministry.

In everyday life. If you have been putting off a doctor’s appointment out of a sense that it is unspiritual to worry about yourself, make it. And if a rule you have taken on is quietly harming you, ask a wise friend whether it is godliness or needless strictness.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sins that are conspicuous. These verses return to choosing elders (v. 22). Conspicuous (prodēlos) means obvious beforehand: some people’s sins walk ahead of them like heralds, reaching the court before the accused does, and no examination is needed.

Sins that appear later. Other people’s sins follow behind and catch up eventually. Paul has laid down a careful procedure, and now admits it will not catch everything. He does not respond by tightening the rules. He offers the assurance that no procedure can give: nothing stays hidden, if not in this life then at the judgment. That is why haste is unnecessary as well as unwise.

Cannot remain hidden. Then verse 25 turns it round. Some goodness is visible; much is not, and it cannot stay hidden either (Matthew 6:4). Timothy should not overlook a modest, faithful man because his virtues are not on display. Think of the widow of verse 10 with her lifetime of unrecorded work. It is not lost. Hold on to that if your faithfulness has gone unnoticed and someone else got the credit. Both records are being kept, the sins and the good works, and both will be read out.

Brought to light by Christ Jesus. Paul knows who will do the revealing. God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus (Romans 2:16), and the Lord, when he comes, will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness (1 Corinthians 4:5). The eyes that will finally read both records are the eyes of the risen Christ, which John saw like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14; 2:23). That is sobering for the hypocrite, who has hidden his sins from every church committee but not from him. And it is deep comfort for the faithful whom nobody noticed, because the Judge is the same Lord who watched a widow put two small coins into the offering box and said she had put in more than all the rest (Mark 12:41–44).

If all my sins will come to light, should I be afraid of the judgment? Not if you are in Christ. For the believer, the sins that will be exposed have already been judged, at the cross, and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). The light of that day will show what grace forgave, not a debt still owing. That is why the best thing to do with hidden sin is to bring it into the light now: confess it to God, and where it is wise and fitting, to a trusted believer (James 5:16; 1 John 1:7–9). Hidden sin festers; confessed sin is cleansed. What should alarm us is not the light but the hope that we can keep anything from it.

In everyday life. Is there something you are hoping will never come out? Bring it to the God who has already covered it in Christ, and if it involves someone you have wronged, begin to put it right.

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
The last chapter ties the letter together. Slaves are to honour their masters, so that God’s name is not slandered. Then the root of the false teaching is exposed: these men thought godliness was a way to make money. Paul answers that “godliness with contentment is great gain”, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

Timothy, the man of God, must flee all this and fight the good fight until Christ appears, the King of kings who dwells in unapproachable light. The rich are not told to give everything away, but to hope in God, who gives richly for enjoyment, and to be rich in good works. Finally: guard the deposit, and grace be with you all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul finishes his household instructions with Christian slaves, whose conduct is to keep God’s name and the teaching from reproach, including those whose masters are fellow believers.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Paul Does and Does Not Say

Paul gives slaves a reason for their conduct that has nothing to do with their masters’ rights: the honour of God’s name (v.1). Read it beside his condemnation of slave-trading (1:10) and his plea for Onesimus as a beloved brother (Philem 16). Paul planted inside slavery a principle, brotherhood in Christ, that would in time dissolve it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Equality in Christ, Paul says, should make a slave serve a believing master better, not worse (v.2).

Now: That change took far too long, and Christians defended slavery with verses like this while ignoring 1:10; yet abolition came largely from people arguing from this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 6 closes the letter by returning to its two great concerns: the false teachers and the kind of man Timothy must be. At the centre of a chapter about slaves, money and quarrels, the letter rises into one of the highest descriptions of God in the Bible. Paul cannot talk about wealth for long without being carried up to the only One who is truly rich.

The setting. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world; on some estimates as much as a third of the population of a city like Ephesus were slaves, though the figures are uncertain. It was not based on race, and many slaves were educated and skilled, could own property and could hope for freedom; but they were legally their masters’ property and could be cruelly treated. The church contained both slaves and masters, as brothers in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16), and some slaves, as verse 2 shows, were owned by fellow Christians. Some may have thought that their new equality in Christ freed them from duty to their masters, perhaps encouraged by the false teachers. A movement calling for immediate abolition would very likely have been crushed as rebellion, as the slave revolt under Spartacus had been, and the gospel heard as a call to arms rather than as good news about Christ.

Under a yoke. “Under a yoke” (hypo zygon) is a picture of servitude and burden (Leviticus 26:13), and “bondservants” (douloi) are slaves. Paul does not pretend the condition is light; he names it a yoke. And it is the word for the yoke God himself broke when he brought Israel out of Egypt, breaking the bars of their yoke and making them walk upright.

Worthy of all honor. “Masters” (despotai) are owners, lords; our word despot comes from it. “All honor” (pasēs timēs) is full respect, owed even to unbelieving masters.

Not be reviled. “Reviled” (blasphēmeō) means slandered, blasphemed. If Christian slaves were rebellious or lazy, outsiders would say that Christianity destroys social order. The gospel’s reputation was at stake (Titus 2:9–10). The slave is not told to obey because his owner deserves it or because the arrangement is just. His reason has nothing to do with his master’s rights. The reputation of God is, astonishingly, in the hands of a slave. The man with the least standing in Ephesus is entrusted with the honour of the highest name in the universe.

Not be disrespectful. “Disrespectful” (kataphroneō) means despise, look down on. Some had reasoned, quite understandably, that equality in Christ meant the old arrangement no longer bound them. The thought was: he is my brother, so I need not work hard for him. Paul’s answer is not to deny the equality. He affirms it in the same breath, calling the master a brother, believing and beloved. Spiritual equality does not cancel earthly responsibilities.

Serve all the better. “Serve all the better” (mallon douleuetōsan) means serve them even more; “benefit” (antilambanomai) means take part in, receive. And there is a quiet revolution in the word beloved. The slave is told to see his owner as one whom God loves; the owner, reading the same letter aloud in the same room, is being told that his slave is his brother.

Serving the Lord Christ. In his letters to Colossae and Ephesus Paul gives slaves the deepest reason of all: work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward, for you are serving the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23–24; Ephesians 6:5–8). It is an astonishing thing to say to people who by law could inherit nothing. Their earthly owner was not their final master, and their work was not finally done for him. That is why a slave could serve wholeheartedly without grovelling, and why his faithfulness could adorn the gospel: every honest day’s work was offered to a Lord who sees it and will reward it.

In the flow. These verses finish the household instructions of chapter 5, tied by one word: widows honoured (5:3), elders worthy of double honour (5:17), masters worthy of all honour (6:1), and in every relationship the question of what will keep the gospel from reproach.

Where Christians differ: does the New Testament approve of slavery? Critics have accused the Bible of endorsing slavery, and slaveholders once used such texts to defend it. This commentary’s view: The New Testament regulates an institution it did not create and could not abolish by decree, while planting the principles that would undermine it. It condemns slave-trading (1:10), tells slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21, on the most likely reading), commands masters to treat slaves justly and remember that they too have a Master (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1), and declares slave and free one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by Scripture’s own law (Exodus 21:16). Christians who fought for abolition, like William Wilberforce, did so from these principles. That is the strategy: not a revolt that would have been drowned in blood, but a principle planted inside the institution that would eventually dissolve it. It took far too long, and Christians defended slavery for centuries by quoting verses like this one while ignoring 1:10 and Philemon. That is a grief and a shame to the church. But when abolition finally came, much of its moral force came from people arguing from this book.

Does this mean I must put up with an abusive boss? No. An employee today is not a slave: you are free to leave, to complain through proper channels, and to seek justice, and you should when you are mistreated (1 Corinthians 7:21 shows Paul valued freedom where it was available). What carries over is the attitude: honest work, respect for those in authority, no sulking, cutting corners or badmouthing behind their backs, so that your conduct commends Christ. But respect is not complicity. You must never do what is sinful because you are told to (Acts 5:29), and harassment, abuse or illegal practice should be reported, not endured in silence. Working well and standing up for what is right are both ways of keeping God’s name from being reviled.

What about slavery and trafficking today? Christians must oppose it with all their strength. Modern slavery, forced labour, debt bondage and sex trafficking are exactly the kidnapping that God’s law punished with death (Exodus 21:16) and the slave-trading that Paul condemns in this very letter (1:10). Nothing in these verses gives them any cover. In practice that means praying, supporting organisations that rescue and restore victims, asking where the goods you buy come from, and refusing to look away when something seems wrong in your community. The gospel that made Onesimus a beloved brother still sets captives free.

In everyday life. You already serve the Lord Christ, who bought you and sees what no manager sees; work today for him. The moment to watch is when you are tempted to do less because no one will check, or because your manager is a Christian and will understand. Do the job well, speak well of the people above you, and let your work be the sermon your colleagues actually hear.

For worship. The Lord of glory took the form of a doulos. He who owned the universe was sold for the price of a slave, thirty pieces of silver, and he washed feet. He is the Master in heaven who shows no partiality, and the Redeemer who buys slaves to set them free. In his house there are no slaves, only sons and daughters, and the slave who reveres his name in a Roman kitchen will sit at the marriage supper of the Lamb beside kings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul traces the false teaching to its root, the love of money, and sets against it the real gain of godliness with contentment. The warning that follows falls on the desire to be rich, which has led some away from the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Root Beneath the Quarrels

The men behind the Ephesian error were making money from religion: they thought “godliness is a means of gain” (v.5). What their teaching produced was envy, quarrels and suspicion between people (v.4). The love of money is “a root of all kinds of evils” (v.10): there is hardly a sin it cannot lead to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul takes the false teachers’ word “gain” and says where it is really found: in godliness with contentment (v.6).

Now: Verse 9 warns those who desire to be rich, and a person can desire that on any income.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A different doctrine. Paul returns to the false teachers one last time, and traces their error to a root that turns out not to be a matter of ideas at all. “Teaches a different doctrine” (heterodidaskalei) is the word of 1:3, so the letter ends where it began.

The sound words. “Agree with” (proserchomai) means adhere to. “Sound” (hygiainousi) is the medical word again: healthy. “The words of our Lord Jesus Christ” are either the teachings of Jesus himself, or the apostolic gospel about him, which carries his authority. True doctrine produces spiritual health.

Accords with godliness. Teaching is measured by what kind of life it produces. That has been the letter’s yardstick since 1:5.

Puffed up with conceit. “Puffed up” (typhoō) is the inflation word again (3:6): swollen with air, or blinded by smoke. The pairing is deliberate: he thinks the most of himself and understands the least.

An unhealthy craving. “Unhealthy craving” (nosōn) is literally being sick, the opposite of the sound teaching just named: an appetite that is itself a sickness. He does not merely tolerate argument, he needs it. “Controversy” (zētēseis) means speculative questions, as in 1:4, and “quarrels about words” (logomachias) are word-battles over technicalities, not substance (2 Timothy 2:14).

Envy, dissension, slander. Five words, and not one is a doctrinal error. They are all relational damage. “Envy” (phthonos) is jealousy. “Dissension” (eris) is strife, rivalry. “Slander” (blasphēmiai) is abusive speech. “Evil suspicions” (hyponoiai ponērai) are malicious suspicions, assuming the worst. “Constant friction” (diaparatribai) is mutual irritation, people rubbing against each other until the skin is raw. Paul judges the teaching by its wreckage: a congregation where people suspect each other and cannot stop arguing has a teaching problem, whatever is on its statement of faith.

Depraved in mind. “Depraved” (diephtharmenōn) means thoroughly corrupted; “deprived” (apestermenōn) means robbed. They once had access to the truth, but have been robbed of it, or have turned from it.

A means of gain. Then the root. “Means of gain” (porismos) is a source of profit, a money-making scheme. Beneath the genealogies and the quarrels about words was a business. These men had discovered that religion pays: that a reputation for spiritual insight brings money, standing and a following. Like the teachers Paul warns Titus about, they taught for shameful gain (Titus 1:11). And the danger reaches closer to home than Ephesus. Religion can be used for gain without any fee: for a reputation, for a sense of being better than others, or for a quiet bargain that if I am good, God owes me a good life. That too treats godliness as a means of gain, and the gospel ends it, because Christ is not a means to something else but the treasure himself (Philippians 3:8).

The words that make peace. The standard is not Paul’s own teaching but the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, carried by the men he sent, so that to hear them was to hear him (Luke 10:16). Set those words beside the five that verse 4 lists. Jesus blessed the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), washed his disciples’ feet, commanded them to love one another as he had loved them (John 13:34), and prayed that they would be one (John 17:21). A teaching that leaves envy, suspicion and friction behind it has wandered far from the One whose words make peace. He never once argued for the pleasure of winning, though he silenced every opponent; and his truth does not puff up, it bows the proud and lifts the humble, and it will be standing when every quarrel about words has fallen silent.

How can I tell the difference between defending the truth and loving controversy? Look at three things. The subject: is it something Scripture treats as central, such as the person of Christ, the gospel, the authority of the Bible, or is it a speculation Scripture does not settle? The manner: are you gentle, patient and willing to listen, or do you enjoy winning and look for the next fight (2 Timothy 2:24–25)? And the fruit: does the conversation leave people closer to Christ and to each other, or does it leave envy, suspicion and friction? A healthy defender of the faith would rather not argue, and does so for the sake of others. A lover of controversy argues for the pleasure of it, and would be lost without an opponent.

How do I recognise a teacher who is using religion for gain? Watch the money and the message together. Be wary when giving is tied to promised returns, when a teacher’s lifestyle is lavish and unaccountable, when pressure is applied to give more, or when the message flatters the wealthy and fits suspiciously well with what the teacher needs. Ask whether there is real accountability: elders, published finances, a church that can correct him. Gain need not be money; it can be fame, a platform or power over people. A faithful teacher can be paid (5:17–18), but he is not driven by it, and his teaching makes you want Christ, not him.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great gain. Paul takes their phrase and turns it inside out. They imagined godliness was a means of financial gain; Paul says godliness is great gain, but only with contentment. “Contentment” (autarkeia) is a word the Stoic philosophers loved (compare Philippians 4:11), and Paul gives it a new meaning. For the Stoic it meant self-sufficiency through inner strength, needing nothing outside yourself. For Paul it means having enough because of who supplies you: sufficiency in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13; 2 Corinthians 9:8).

We brought nothing. Paul gives two arguments, and the first is unanswerable (Job 1:21; Ecclesiastes 5:15). It is not a religious claim but an observation anybody can verify. We arrive naked and leave naked, and whatever a person accumulates is held for the middle stretch only. Why stake your life on what you cannot keep?

Food and clothing. Then the second argument: two items. Not comfort, not security: food and covering (skepasmata, which can include shelter). When we have these, we have enough to be content (Matthew 6:25–33). Paul has set the bar at survival. He is not saying it is wrong to have more; he will tell the rich in verse 17 that God gives us everything to enjoy, which rules out asceticism. He is saying that everything above food and clothing is surplus, and that a Christian should know it is surplus. And contentment is not a matter of income: anyone can name a figure at which they would be content, but the honest question is whether contentment arrived when the last increase did.

The Lord who came and left with nothing. The Son of God kept these two verses more completely than anyone. He came into the world with nothing, laid in a manger (Luke 2:7), and he left it with nothing, while soldiers divided his clothing among them (John 19:23–24). In between he said that his food was to do the will of the One who sent him (John 4:34). He is the proof that a life with little more than food and covering can be the richest life ever lived, and he is the secret Paul learned: I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:12–13). Godliness with contentment is great gain, because the godly have God.

How do I actually learn contentment? Paul says he learned it (Philippians 4:11–12); it is not a temperament but a trained habit of the heart, and its secret is Christ, through whom he could do all things. Practise gratitude daily, naming specific gifts, because thanksgiving and discontent cannot live long in the same heart. Notice what feeds your wanting, the adverts, the scrolling, the comparisons with friends, and starve it. Give generously, because giving loosens the grip of things. Remember verse 7: you will leave with nothing. And above all, feed on what does satisfy: the God who has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, which is the very reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5).

Is it wrong to want a better job, a pay rise or a nicer home? Not necessarily. Wanting to provide better for your family, to use your gifts more fully, or to have room for hospitality can be good desires. Paul assumes people may improve their situation. The question is what the wanting is doing to you. Ask: am I anxious, envious or restless about it? Would I be at peace with God if it never came? Am I prepared to sacrifice integrity, family or church to get it? If you can want it with open hands, pray for it and work for it. If it has become the thing you cannot be happy without, it has become an idol, and contentment means laying it down.

In everyday life. Contentment rarely arrives as a feeling; it usually arrives as noticing. The meal in front of you, the coat on the hook, the bed you will sleep in tonight: food and covering, and more besides. Often the thing we could not live without last year is the thing we now barely notice.
