verseByVerse.quote: But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who desire to be rich. The warning is not for the rich: Paul will address them separately in verse 17. “Desire” (boulomenoi) means set their will on: those whose goal in life is wealth. The danger is in the desiring, and a poor man can desire riches as fiercely as a rich one.

Into a snare. The verbs describe a descent. They fall (empiptō), as into a pit, into temptation and a snare (pagis), the bird-trap word from 3:7, something that closes on you before you have seen it: dishonesty, neglect of family, idolatry, oppression.

Senseless and harmful desires. Many desires, senseless (anoētous) and harmful (blaberas), which arrive in company, because wanting one thing teaches you to want others, and none of them satisfy.

Ruin and destruction. Finally these plunge people (bythizō), a verb used of a ship going down. “Ruin” (olethros) and “destruction” (apōleia) together describe total, final ruin, in this life and the next (Matthew 16:26).

The love of money. The line is famously misquoted. It is not money but the love of it (philargyria, love of silver, avarice); money is a tool and Paul is about to tell wealthy Christians what to do with theirs. It is not the root but a root (rhiza: the Greek has no word for “the” here, and most translators rightly render it a root); Paul is not claiming every sin traces here, and pride and lust do fine without it. And it produces all kinds of evils (pantōn tōn kakōn) rather than every single evil; the point is the variety. There is almost no wickedness that money-love cannot eventually produce. And at bottom it is idolatry (Colossians 3:5; Matthew 6:24). You cannot serve God and money.

Wandered away. “Craving” (oregomenoi) is reaching out for, stretching toward. “Wandered away” (apeplanēthēsan) means been led astray, not renounced. Nobody sets out to leave Christ for money. The word suggests drifting off the path while looking at something else, which is exactly how it happens. The love of money has led some to abandon the faith, perhaps including the false teachers: like Judas, who sold his Master for silver (Matthew 26:14–16), and Demas, who loved this present world (2 Timothy 4:10).

Pierced themselves. The verb (peripeirō) is violent: impaled, as on a spit. And the sting is in the word “themselves”: nobody did this to them. “Pangs” (odynais) are griefs: anxiety, guilt, broken relationships, regret. The griefs money-love produces are self-inflicted, and they come to the person who got what he wanted.

The temptation he refused. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and offered them for one act of worship (Matthew 4:8–10). It was the desire to be rich in its purest form, the whole world as the price of a divided heart, and he refused it with Scripture: worship the Lord your God and serve him only. Where others reach for wealth and are dragged under, the Son of God turned down everything and kept his Father. The love of money is not overcome by a stronger grip on ourselves but by a greater love. The One who refused the world is worth more than all of it.

Where Christians differ: does God promise wealth to the faithful? The prosperity gospel teaches that God wants every believer to be rich, and that faith, giving or positive confession will produce wealth. This commentary’s view: This passage directly refutes it. Paul warns that the desire to be rich is a trap that leads to destruction. Jesus warned against storing up treasure on earth (Matthew 6:19–21) and said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25). God promises to provide what we need (Philippians 4:19), not wealth. Teachers who promise wealth are precisely those who think godliness is a means of gain (v. 5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean money itself is evil, or that providing for one’s family is wrong (5:8). Nor does “wandered from the faith” mean that a true believer can be finally lost (see on 6:21). If you see a drift towards money in yourself and it grieves you, that grief is the mark of the Spirit at work, and the way back is open (1 John 1:9).

How do I know if I love money? Love shows itself in what you think about, what you fear losing, and what you will sacrifice for. Ask: Do I think about money more than about God? Am I anxious when it is short, proud when it is plentiful? Do I resent giving, or give only what I will not miss? Would I bend the truth, cut a corner or neglect my family to get more? Do I envy those who have more? Does the prospect of losing it terrify me more than the prospect of losing fellowship with Christ? Nobody answers all of these well. The cure is not guilt but a better love: look at Christ, who though he was rich became poor for you, and give something away today as an act of worship.

Is it wrong to save, invest or have a pension? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the wise who plan ahead (Proverbs 21:20), and providing for your family includes thinking about the future (5:8). Saving becomes sin when it is driven by fear rather than faith, when it becomes the place your security truly rests, or when it crowds out generosity. The rich fool’s problem was not that he had barns but that he built bigger ones for himself alone and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). Save wisely, give generously, and hold it all loosely, remembering whose it is.

For worship. We pierce ourselves with griefs we chose; the Son of God was pierced with griefs that were never his, wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5). Money leaves its lovers sinking; Christ is the Lord who reached out his hand to Peter sinking in the waves (Matthew 14:31), and that hand still lifts the drowning and holds them fast. Money promised Judas everything and left him with a field of blood; Christ, who had no silver, gives himself to all who come to him with empty hands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against the false teachers stands the man of God, charged to flee, pursue and fight until Christ appears; and the thought of that appearing carries Paul into a hymn of praise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Titles Thrown at Idols

“Only Sovereign”, “King of kings and Lord of lords”, “who alone has immortality” (vv.15–16): Ephesus gave such honours to Artemis and to the emperor, and Paul says they belong to God alone. And the God who dwells in unapproachable light is reached only through the one mediator (2:5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy confessed Christ among friends; Jesus confessed before Pilate, who could kill him (vv.12–13).

Now: Flee and pursue (v.11): some temptations must simply be run from, and a man who only runs away, without chasing something better, will eventually be caught.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O man of God. The contrast is emphatic (sy de, but you): against the men who imagine godliness is gain stands one person, addressed directly. “Man of God” (anthrōpe theou) is the Old Testament’s title for prophets and leaders such as Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1) and Elijah (1 Kings 17:18), men who stood for God against a drifting people. Paul gives that title to a young minister in Ephesus who has been having a difficult time of it, and in 2 Timothy 3:17 he uses it of anyone whom Scripture equips for every good work, which many read as every believer.

Flee these things. Then two verbs, and the Christian life is in both. “Flee” (pheugō) has the form that means keep fleeing: keep fleeing the love of money, pride, controversy and greed (vv. 3–10). It is what Joseph did, leaving his garment in her hand rather than staying to argue with Potiphar’s wife (Genesis 39:12). Some temptations are not to be engaged, reasoned with or managed. Distance is often the only reliable tactic, and a man who stays to test his own strength has usually already decided to give in (2 Timothy 2:22).

Pursue righteousness. “Pursue” (diōkō) is the word used of hunting: chase it down. Fleeing alone leaves a vacuum, and a man who is only avoiding things will eventually be caught by one of them. Six virtues, in three pairs. Righteousness and godliness: right living toward people and toward God. Faith and love: the inner life of a believer, the two that have run through this letter since 1:5. Then steadfastness (hypomonē, the staying power that does not buckle) and gentleness (praupathia, mildness of temper). A man dealing with quarrelsome teachers and constant friction needs to be immovable and unaggravated at the same time: to hold the ground without becoming like the people pushing him.

Running towards a person. Elsewhere Paul shows what lies at the centre of this fleeing and pursuing. In Romans he tells believers to cast off the works of darkness and then, instead of a list, gives a name: put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:12–14). The six virtues here are not a self-improvement programme. Each is a feature of his character, and to pursue them is to pursue likeness to him. The man of God is not left to his own strength: the One he is running towards has already run the course, and lives in him by his Spirit.

What does fleeing look like in practice? It means arranging your life so that the temptation has less access to you. For money: unsubscribe from the shopping emails, stop browsing what you cannot afford, avoid the friendships built around getting and spending. For sexual sin: filters and accountability, no being alone where you know you are weak, leaving the room or switching off at once. For controversy: closing the thread, not reading the comments. Fleeing is not cowardice; it is wisdom about your own weakness. And it is always paired with pursuing: put something good in the space you have cleared, or the old thing will come back with friends (Matthew 12:43–45).
verseByVerse.note: “Man of God” is an Old Testament title for prophets such as Moses, Samuel and Elijah.

verseByVerse.quote: Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good fight. The verb (agōnizou) comes from the arena: contend, struggle, strain, the root of our word agonise, and its form means keep fighting. Note the word “the”: “the good fight of the faith”. Not any struggle a Christian happens to be in, but the one contest that matters, waged over the faith itself, the deposit he will name in verse 20. Paul uses the same words of his own life at its end: I have fought the good fight (2 Timothy 4:7).

Take hold. The verb (epilabou) means seize, grasp. That sounds odd applied to eternal life, which Timothy already has as a gift (John 5:24). But this is Paul’s regular pattern: what God gives, you are then told to lay hold of; work out your salvation because God works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). The gift is secure, and Timothy is still commanded to grip it.

To which you were called. “Called” (eklēthēs) is God’s effectual call, the call that creates the response it asks for (Romans 8:30; John 6:44). Timothy did not wander into eternal life; he was summoned into it by the voice that raises the dead. The call came from God before the confession came from Timothy: he spoke Timothy’s name before Timothy spoke his.

The good confession. “Confession” (homologia) is a public declaration. The good confession was probably made at Timothy’s baptism, when he confessed Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9–10), or perhaps at his ordination, before the congregation as “many witnesses”. When a man is flagging, Paul sends him back to what was said over him and by him at the beginning (1:18; 4:14). That is a practical kindness. Feelings about ministry come and go; the fact that you stood up in front of witnesses and confessed Christ does not, and on the days when nothing else is steady it is a fixed point you can put your weight on.

Laying hold of the One who laid hold of you. Eternal life is not a thing apart from Christ: this life is in his Son (1 John 5:11; John 17:3). So to take hold of eternal life is to take hold of Christ. And Paul knew which grip comes first. He pressed on to make it his own, he said, because Christ Jesus had made him his own (Philippians 3:12). Timothy’s grasp is weak and must be renewed every day. The hand that holds him is not weak, and it does not let go.

What is the fight, for an ordinary Christian? It is the daily contest to keep believing and living the gospel against everything that pulls the other way. Inwardly, it is the fight against unbelief, doubt and the sins that would choke faith. Outwardly, it is holding to the truth when the world, or even a church, drifts from it, and speaking of Christ when it costs you. Its weapons are those God supplies: the Word, prayer, the fellowship of the church, the Lord’s Supper (Ephesians 6:10–18). It is not fought by aggression toward people; Paul has just told Timothy to pursue gentleness. And it is a good fight: one that ends in victory, because the Captain has already won it.

Why does it matter that I made a public confession? Because faith in Christ is not meant to be private. Jesus said that whoever confesses him before men, he will confess before his Father (Matthew 10:32). For a believer, baptism is the appointed place for that first public confession, made before witnesses who can later remind you of it and hold you to it. If you are a believer and have never been baptised, this verse is an invitation: speak to your pastor. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, because the baptisms of the New Testament follow hearing and believing (Acts 2:41; 8:12); many godly Christians who were baptised as infants, and whose churches see baptism as the covenant sign given to believers’ children, would point instead to the day they publicly owned their faith, and both agree that faith in Christ must be confessed openly. If you have been, look back on it when faith feels weak. You did not imagine it. You stood before God and his people and said Jesus is Lord, and the God who called you then has not changed his mind.
verseByVerse.note: The “good confession” was probably made at Timothy’s baptism or ordination.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the presence of God. The second solemn charge in God’s sight in the letter (compare 5:21). “Gives life” (zōogoneō) means preserves alive, which is what a man needs to remember if the charge might cost him his own life: the God who gives life to all things will raise Timothy if he dies for his faith.

Before Pontius Pilate. Before Pilate, Jesus declared that he was a king, whose kingdom is not of this world, and that he came to bear witness to the truth (John 18:33–37). Timothy made his good confession in a room full of friends; Jesus made his before a magistrate who could kill him, and did. Confession before a supportive congregation is real; confession before a hostile authority is the same act with the price attached, and Timothy is being told which one he is signed up to.

Suffered under Pontius Pilate. Pilate is known from Tacitus, Josephus and an inscription found at Caesarea, and the creeds would keep his name. The faith Timothy is charged to keep is not a philosophy but something that happened at a particular hour in front of a particular official.

Keep the commandment. “The commandment” (tēn entolēn) is probably the whole charge Timothy received, the gospel and its demands (1:18), which he will call the deposit in verse 20.

Unstained and free from reproach. “Unstained” (aspilos) means spotless; “free from reproach” (anepilēmptos) means irreproachable, as of elders (3:2). These may describe the commandment or Timothy, and in practice both are true, because a man’s life can put a mark on the message he carries. No minister has ever kept it perfectly. The One who did is Christ, who kept his Father’s charge without a stain and in our place, and his obedience is counted to all who are his (Romans 5:19); so Timothy guards it as a man already accepted, and his failures, confessed, do not undo that.

Until the appearing. “Appearing” (epiphaneia) was used in the Greek world for the appearance of a god or the arrival of an emperor; the Pastoral Letters use it for Christ’s return (2 Timothy 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13). Not until the trouble in Ephesus resolves, but until Christ appears: the assignment has one end date, and it is not in Timothy’s diary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul knew Christ would return within Timothy’s lifetime; he leaves the timing to God, who will bring it about “at the proper time” (v. 15). It means a minister is to keep serving faithfully with his eyes on Christ’s return, whenever it comes.

What will Christ’s appearing be like? Public, visible and glorious. Scripture describes one return of Christ at the end of the age, not a secret coming: he will come on the clouds with power and great glory, every eye will see him, the dead will be raised, and he will judge the living and the dead and make all things new (Matthew 24:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7). Many Christians, especially in churches that teach a rapture, expect Christ to come secretly for his people some years before a later visible return; this commentary reads the coming of 1 Thessalonians 4, with its shout and trumpet, as that same loud and public final return, while gladly owning those who see it otherwise as brothers who love his appearing too. It will be terror to those who rejected him and unspeakable joy to those who love his appearing (2 Timothy 4:8). We do not know the day, and we are not told to calculate it. We are told what Timothy was told: keep faith until then, and live so that you would be glad to be found doing what you are doing.

What if I am afraid to confess Christ before people who could harm me? Look at the One who went first. Christ did not ask Timothy to do anything he had not already done, before a far more dangerous judge. Fear is not itself sin; it is the soil in which courage grows. Pray for boldness, as the apostles did (Acts 4:29). Remember that the Spirit gives words in the hour of need (Matthew 10:19–20). Use wisdom: you are not commanded to court danger needlessly. And if you have failed, as Peter did in the courtyard, remember that the risen Lord restored him and later gave him courage to die for him (John 21:15–19). The God who gives life to all things holds yours.

For worship. He stood bound before the governor of Judea, the true King before a man who thought he held the power of life and death, and he told the truth knowing it meant the cross. Christ did not deny us when we would have denied him. He was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and on the third day he rose again. One day he will appear, and every knee will bow, the governor’s among them.

verseByVerse.quote: which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the proper time. The mention of Christ’s appearing sets Paul off into the letter’s second doxology, a burst of praise to God (compare 1:17), perhaps something the churches already sang. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois) means in his own seasons, as in 2:6. God will bring about Christ’s appearing at the moment he has appointed (Acts 1:7). Nobody hurries it and nobody delays it.

The blessed and only Sovereign. Then the titles, and every one is a stone thrown at an idol. “Blessed” (makarios) is the word from 1:11: perfectly happy. God is not a lonely or needy being who made us to fill an emptiness; he is supremely happy in himself, Father, Son and Spirit, and he creates out of fullness. He needs nothing, and gives everything. “Only Sovereign” (monos dynastēs) is a pointed claim in a city that worshipped both Artemis and the emperor: there is one ruler, and it is neither of them.

King of kings. This was royal vocabulary: Eastern monarchs used the formula of themselves (Ezra 7:12), and the emperor in Rome claimed divine honours. Paul takes the highest title in the political world and says it belongs to someone else (Deuteronomy 10:17), and in Revelation 19:16 it is given to Christ, the Lamb who conquers.

Who alone has immortality. “Immortality” (athanasia) is deathlessness, belonging to God by nature, and to nobody else in that way. God alone has life in himself (John 5:26); all other beings continue because he sustains them. Believers will receive immortality as his gift at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53–54). If the false teachers spun speculations about spiritual beings out of their genealogies (1:4), Paul cuts beneath them all: there is one immortal.

Unapproachable light. God’s holiness and glory are like blinding light that no creature can approach on its own (Exodus 33:20; Isaiah 6:1–5). Light is what makes seeing possible, and here it is what prevents it: not darkness keeping God hidden but excess of brightness.

Whom no one has seen. God as he is in himself is invisible (1:17; John 1:18). We see him only as he reveals himself, supremely in Christ: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). In a letter about false teachers claiming special access, the doxology lands here: nobody has seen him, and no technique will get you nearer. Which makes the line Paul has already written the more astonishing: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (2:5). The unapproachable light came out to meet us, so that one day we, who could not look on him and live, will see his face (Revelation 22:4).

Honor and eternal dominion. “Dominion” (kratos) is might, power, rule. The proper response to such a God is worship, and Paul does not argue for it; he simply gives it. Teaching about God that does not end in praise has not yet understood him.

What it does not mean. “Who alone has immortality” does not mean human souls cease to exist at death. Humans have an immortality given by God; God alone has it by nature. Scripture teaches that the soul lives on consciously between death and the resurrection, and that all people exist for ever (Luke 16:22–26; Matthew 25:46). Nor does “no one can see” contradict the promise that the pure in heart will see God; we will see him as he reveals himself in the glorified Christ.

If God dwells in unapproachable light, how can I pray to him? Through Christ. On your own you could not approach this God for a moment; Isaiah, seeing only the edge of his glory, cried that he was undone. But the One who dwells in that light sent his Son into our darkness, and through his blood we have confidence to enter the holy places by the new and living way he opened (Hebrews 10:19–22). So you come not in your own name but in his, and you are welcomed as a child. Hold both truths together when you pray: the awe of verse 16, which keeps prayer reverent, and the access of the gospel, which makes it bold (Hebrews 4:16).

Why does Paul break into praise in the middle of instructions? Because for Paul doctrine and worship are one thing. He cannot mention Christ’s appearing without being carried up to the God who will bring it about. It is a lesson in how to read the Bible and how to live: every truth about God is meant to end in adoration. If your study of Scripture never moves you to praise, slow down and ask what the passage shows you of God. And it is a comfort in hard places: Timothy, facing false teachers and difficult elders, is reminded that the One he serves is the only Sovereign, and that every throne in Ephesus is beneath his.

Is a God who wants honour not simply vain? No, and the difference matters. When a human being demands praise, he is asking for more than he is worth. When God receives it, he is being given exactly what he is worth, and nothing he lacks, for he is blessed in himself and needs nothing (Acts 17:25). Praise is also how joy completes itself: we naturally praise what we delight in, a view, a piece of music, a person we love, and the praise finishes the enjoyment. So when God calls us to honour him, he is calling us to the one delight big enough to bear the full weight of our love. A God who did not want our worship would be leaving us to worship lesser things.

In everyday life. Pray these two verses back to God phrase by phrase this week: blessed, only Sovereign, King of kings, alone immortal, dwelling in light. When the news makes some earthly ruler seem all-powerful, or the future makes you anxious, remember who sets the proper time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives the wealthy a charge for using what they have, then makes a last plea to Timothy to guard the deposit, and ends with grace for the whole church.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guard the Deposit

The deposit (paratheke) of verse 20 is property left with someone for safekeeping, to be returned exactly as received. So with the gospel: Timothy is not to develop it or make it more interesting, but to guard it against teaching that falsely calls itself knowledge.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul does not tell the rich to give everything away but to hope in God, who gives everything to enjoy (v.17), and to get rich in good works (v.18).

Now: The “you” of the closing grace is plural (v.21): after pages addressed to Timothy, Paul turns to the whole room.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich in this present age. Now Paul turns to the rich in the congregation, those who already are wealthy, as distinct from those who desire to be (v. 9). He does not tell them to give it all away, and he does not treat wealth as a sin requiring repentance. He gives them instructions for handling it. “In this present age”: their riches belong to this passing world only.

Not to be haughty. “Haughty” (hypsēlophronein) means high-minded, and it is the natural drift of money: it quietly persuades a person that he is a different sort of human from the people who do not have it, and that he does not need God (Deuteronomy 8:11–17).

The uncertainty of riches. The phrase is exact: not on uncertain riches but on the uncertainty of them (adēlotēti, unreliability). The thing to know about wealth, if you are tempted to hope in it, is that it may not be there tomorrow. Riches can sprout wings and fly away overnight (Proverbs 23:5).

God, who richly provides. This is a generous sentence, from the man who has just said food and clothing are enough. “Richly” (plousiōs) is a play on the word rich: the truly rich one is God. And the purpose named is enjoyment (eis apolausin), not bare sufficiency. God is not a miser: sunlight and bread, music and friendship, the laughter of children and the taste of fruit are all from his open hand. This is the final answer to the ascetics of chapter 4 who forbade marriage and food: wealth is a gift to be enjoyed with thanks (4:4), not trusted.

Rich in good works. Then four things for the rich to do, each going further than the last. “Do good” (agathoergein) is the general instruction. “Be rich in good works”: and there is the deliberate wordplay. They are rich in one currency, and Paul tells them to get rich in another.

Generous and ready to share. “Generous” (eumetadotous) means open-handed. And “ready to share” (koinōnikous) is a further step, from the fellowship word: not merely willing when asked, but holding what they have as common property with people who need it.

Storing up treasure. The image is Christ’s own: treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy (Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:33; 16:9). And it turns the whole thing round. Giving money away is here described as an investment, the only one whose returns are guaranteed.

Truly life. “Truly life” (tēs ontōs zōēs) is life that is really life; some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read eternal life, but the earliest read truly life. What the rich are currently holding is not, in Paul’s estimate, real life (Luke 12:15). There is a realer thing available, the life of God, now and forever, and the way to lay hold of it is to loosen your grip on possessions.

The rich man who became poor. The truly rich man of the New Testament does not live in Ephesus. Paul reminds the Corinthians of the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, who was rich and for their sake became poor, so that by his poverty they might be made rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is the pattern behind every instruction here. He did not hoard heaven; he shared it, taking our lot so that we might have his. The life that is truly life is a person: whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). The rich lay hold of it the way everyone does, by letting go of what they were trusting and holding on to him.

In the flow. Verses 9–10 warned those who want to be rich; verses 17–19 instruct those who already are. The doxology stands between them for a reason: the blessed and only Sovereign, who richly provides, is the only safe place for a wealthy person to rest his hope.

Does generosity earn heaven? No. Good works are the fruit of saving faith (Ephesians 2:8–10), and the reward is God’s grace. Paul is telling the rich to use their wealth for others because they have something better to hope in. He sets no fixed amount; the measure is a generous heart and a ready hand (v. 18).

Am I rich? Most readers of this probably are, by any global or historical measure. If you have regular meals, a home, clothes beyond what you need and some money left at the end of the month, you are among the rich in this present age, even if you feel stretched compared with those around you. That feeling is itself one of the dangers: we measure ourselves against people who have more, and so never notice we are the ones Paul is addressing. Read verses 17–19 as written to you. Not to make you guilty, but to free you: from pride, from false security, and into the joy of using what God has given for others.

How much is generous? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but it gives a direction and a spirit. Paul’s charge to the rich here is not a figure but a habit: be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (v. 18). Give regularly and in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the church that feeds you (5:17–18; Galatians 6:6), and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point and then grow beyond it; for some on very low incomes, faithful giving will be smaller. The test of verse 18 is not the amount but readiness: a hand that opens quickly, and a heart that enjoys it.

In everyday life. Do both halves of verses 17 and 18 on purpose: give a gift you will notice to someone who needs it, and then sit down to a good meal and thank God for it without guilt. Generosity and enjoyment are not rivals; both say that God is the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Timothy. The letter’s last direct address, and calling him by name gives it the sound of a hand on the shoulder.

Guard the deposit entrusted to you. “Guard” (phylaxon) means keep safe, like a sentry. The deposit (parathēkē) is a term from banking and law: property placed with someone for safekeeping, with the absolute obligation not to invest it, improve it or use it, but to return exactly what he received. That is Paul’s picture of the gospel (2 Timothy 1:12–14) and of Timothy’s job. It was entrusted to Paul (1:11) and now to Timothy, who is not its owner but its guardian, and must hand it on intact (2 Timothy 2:2).

Irreverent babble. “Irreverent” (bebēlous) is profane, as in 4:7; “babble” (kenophōnias) is empty chatter. The false teaching was all noise and no substance.

Falsely called knowledge. “Contradictions” (antitheseis) are counter-claims. “Knowledge” is gnōsis, the word from which the second-century movements now called Gnosticism take their name, with their promise of secret understanding for the spiritual elite. Whether or not developed Gnosticism existed yet, the instinct plainly did, and Paul names it: “falsely called”. Against this, the Christian gospel is public, open to all, and centred on the historical Christ.

The whole letter in one verse. On one side a deposit: fixed, received, handed on, not yours to alter. On the other an endless production of new material that sounds impressive and is empty noise, and the second is always the more exciting of the two. Guarding does not mean aggression: Paul has ruled out the quarrelsome man (3:3). A guard does not chase; he stays where he was posted, and the thing he was given is still there in the morning.

The knowledge that has a name. Against knowledge falsely so called Paul sets a person. In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:2–3), hidden not as a secret for initiates but laid open to everyone who comes to him. At the centre of the deposit is the saying the letter has already given Timothy: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15). Every promise of a deeper knowledge that moves past Christ is moving away from where the treasure is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid learning or scholarship. True knowledge of God is commanded (2 Peter 3:18). The problem is false claims to secret or superior knowledge that contradict the gospel.

I am not a pastor. How do I guard the deposit? Every believer has been entrusted with the gospel, and you guard it first by knowing it: read the Bible whole, learn a sound confession or catechism, and be able to say clearly what the gospel is. Guard it in your home by teaching it to your children. Guard it in your church by supporting faithful preaching, asking questions when something sounds wrong, and being slow to embrace new ideas that cannot be found in Scripture. Guard it in your own life by holding to it when it is unfashionable. And pass it on: tell someone else. The deposit is guarded best not by being buried but by being faithfully handed to the next person (2 Timothy 2:2).

Are there modern forms of falsely called knowledge? Yes. Any teaching that claims a secret key to the Bible, a hidden message only insiders can see, or a spiritual experience that lifts some believers above ordinary Christians follows this pattern. So does the claim that the church misunderstood Jesus until some recent discovery or theory, or the idea that real spirituality lies in techniques beyond the Word, prayer and sacraments. Scripture is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17); it is not a code for an elite but light for all God’s people. When a teaching makes you feel you must get past the plain meaning of the Bible to find the real truth, turn away.

For worship. His truth is not kept for an elite: he revealed these things to little children (Matthew 11:25–26). And the deposit is safe, not finally because Timothy guarded it, but because God does: he is able to guard what has been entrusted until that day (2 Timothy 1:12). The gospel has passed through twenty centuries of hands, many of them weak, and it reaches us whole, because the Lord of the gospel keeps his Word.
verseByVerse.note: “Knowledge” may point to early forms of the teaching later called Gnosticism.

verseByVerse.quote: for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Swerved from the faith. The letter ends where it began. “Swerved” (ēstochēsan) means to miss the mark, the word of 1:6. How it happened: “by professing it” (epangellomenoi, making a show of). The moment a man announced he had this knowledge, he was committed to a position, and the faith had to be adjusted around it. Public claims have a way of taking their maker where he did not intend to go.

Grace be with you. The you is plural (meth’ hymōn); some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read the singular and add Amen, but the earliest have the plural. Much of the letter has addressed Timothy personally, and at the very end Paul turns to the room: the elders, the widows, the rich, the slaves, the would-be teachers. This has been a demanding letter, with qualifications, disciplines and warnings, and it closes with the only thing that was ever going to make any of it possible: grace.

The grace that is in Christ Jesus. The grace Paul leaves with the church is not a general goodwill. It overflowed for Paul, the foremost of sinners, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus (1:14–15), and Timothy is to be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 2:1). Those who swerved aimed at knowledge; the mark was always a person.

What it does not mean. It does not mean those who are truly in Christ can finally fall away. Those who swerve from the faith show that they did not truly belong (1 John 2:19). But we must take the warning seriously, for it is one of the means by which God keeps his own. God keeps to the end those he has truly called (Philippians 1:6). Many faithful Christians hold instead that a believer can finally abandon saving grace, and they take such warnings seriously too. And if you fear you are swerving, the fear itself is a sign of life: those who have truly left the faith are rarely troubled at having left it.

Someone I love has swerved from the faith. Is there hope? Yes, while they live there is hope. Some who wander are true believers in a season of backsliding, and the Shepherd goes after his lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7); Peter denied Christ and was restored. Others were never truly converted, and the God who raises the dead can still call them. You cannot tell from outside which it is, and you do not need to. Keep praying for them by name, without giving up. Keep loving them and keep the door open, without pretending all is well. Speak of Christ when there is an opening, gently. And entrust them to the God who is mighty to save. Grace is the last word of this letter, and it is not too late for grace.

In everyday life. Read the whole of 1 Timothy again this week in one sitting, as the church at Ephesus would have heard it. Then pray for your church as Paul did: for its leaders, its widows, its rich and its poor, its teachers and its young. And end the day as the letter ends, by asking grace for the people you have found hardest to love.

For worship. The letter’s last word is grace, spoken to a difficult church that had to carry the deposit one more generation. It was carried, and it has been carried every generation since, not because the carriers were strong, but because the grace was. The first word of the gospel is grace, and so is the last. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.note: “You” here is plural: the letter was meant for the whole church to hear.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled.<sup>2</sup>Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.<sup>3</sup>If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness,<sup>4</sup>he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions,<sup>5</sup>and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.<sup>6</sup>But godliness with contentment is great gain,<sup>7</sup>for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.<sup>8</sup>But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.<sup>9</sup>But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.<sup>10</sup>For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.<sup>11</sup>But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.<sup>12</sup>Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.<sup>13</sup>I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession,<sup>14</sup>to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>15</sup>which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords,<sup>16</sup>who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.<sup>17</sup>As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.<sup>18</sup>They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,<sup>19</sup>thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.<sup>20</sup>O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"<sup>21</sup>for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
